papers.title: ConserveEdit: Source-Anchored Transactions for Drift-Bounded Iterative Image Editing
papers.abstract: Instruction-driven image editors produce convincing local edits in one pass, but inside an iterative refinement loop every accepted output becomes the next input, so unintended changes outside the requested region accumulate. We present ConserveEdit, an editor-agnostic controller that treats each refinement step as a transaction against a contract compiled once from the source image. The contract separates what may change (the authorized region of each target, with a bounded halo for shadows and reflections) from what must survive (protected content with explicit tolerances). Candidates from a frozen editor are composed through a source-anchored mask and committed only if target progress, drift on protected content, and image quality pass as separate tests; otherwise the step is rolled back and repaired. For any editor, this keeps every pixel outside the authorized region bit-exact and bounds drift independently of the number of iterations, whereas no fixed scalar trade-off reproduces the separate tests. On all 1053 MagicBrush test edits with a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit, masking is necessary but not sufficient. A direct call already alters the rest of the image (12.1 dB PSNR outside the mask); composed through the source-anchored mask, it stays bit-exact there and its DINO similarity to the ground truth rises from 0.67 to 0.85, matching ConserveEdit, so this gain comes from the mask. Next to automatic masks, however, masked direct editing changes a protected face or text on 48% of turns, and masked scalar selection avoids this mostly by abstaining (23% constrained success). Because its drift test names the violated entity, ConserveEdit shrinks the support instead (2% violations, 53% constrained success); in a simulator with known ground truth it raises constrained success from 55.0% to 61.8%. Automatic grounding remains the main bottleneck. Code and logs will be released.
papers.summary: Instruction-driven image editors used in an iterative loop accumulate unintended changes outside the requested region, because each accepted output becomes the next input. `ConserveEdit` is an editor-agnostic controller that treats each step as a transaction against a contract compiled once from the source image: candidates from a frozen editor are composed through a source-anchored mask and committed only if target progress, drift on protected content, and image quality pass as separate tests, otherwise the step is rolled back and repaired. On all 1053 `MagicBrush` test edits with a frozen `Qwen-Image-Edit`, the mask alone keeps pixels outside the authorized region bit-exact and accounts for the rise in `DINO` similarity from 0.67 to 0.85, but masked direct editing still alters a protected face or text on 48% of turns, whereas `ConserveEdit` reaches **2% violations with 53% constrained success**. The authors identify automatic grounding as the main remaining bottleneck.

papers.title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
papers.abstract: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-Lin/PGPO.
papers.summary: Recommender systems that encode item text into LLM-derived semantic embeddings can leak sensitive attributes through inversion attacks, and existing input-side defenses tend to disrupt the inter-item semantic relations that recommendation depends on. Prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (`PGPO`) learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph, optimized with `GRPO` using rewards for individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraints. On two benchmarks the authors report **strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance**.

papers.title: Neural Network-Based Modeling of Hysteretic Systems: From Prandtl and Preisach Neural Networks to Neuro-Madelung and Neuroplastic Continuous Models
papers.abstract: Hysteresis is a complex nonlinear phenomenon characterized by memory dependence, path dependence, and, in many physical systems, degradation, non-congruency, asymmetry, and rate dependence. This review examines the development and capabilities of Prandtl neural networks (PNNs), Preisach neural networks (PreisachNNs), generalized Prandtl neural networks (GPNNs), the neuro-Madelung model (NMM), extended Preisach neural networks (EPNNs), and dynamic plastic continuous neural networks (DPCNNs). Particular attention is given to their mechanisms for representing memory, network architectures, activation functions, training algorithms, treatment of deterioration and rate dependence, and applications to nonlinear structural and material systems. The PNN introduced hysteretic memory directly into neural activation through stop operators and demonstrated accurate nonlinear dynamic analysis of structures. Preisach-NNs subsequently extended this concept through an additional nonlinear hidden layer to represent non-Masing hysteresis. GPNNs introduced deteriorating-stop neurons to capture stiffness and strength degradation and non-congruent hysteresis. A different generalization was provided by the NMM, which combined Madelung's hysteresis rules with multilayer feedforward neural networks to represent diverse rate-independent and rate-dependent behaviors. These developments culminated in the EPNN, which combines deteriorating hysteretic operators, nonlinear neural mappings, and input-rate information to accommodate Masing and nonMasing, symmetric and asymmetric, congruent and noncongruent, and rate-independent and rate-dependent hysteresis.
papers.summary: Hysteresis in structural and material systems involves memory and path dependence, often with degradation, asymmetry, non-congruency, and rate dependence, which makes it hard to model. This review traces a family of neural architectures that build hysteretic memory into the network itself, from Prandtl neural networks (`PNN`s) with stop-operator activations, through Preisach neural networks and generalized Prandtl neural networks with deteriorating-stop neurons, to the neuro-Madelung model, comparing their memory mechanisms, architectures, activation functions, training algorithms, and applications. It presents the extended Preisach neural network (`EPNN`) as the culmination, **combining deteriorating hysteretic operators, nonlinear neural mappings, and input-rate information to cover Masing and non-Masing, symmetric and asymmetric, congruent and non-congruent, and rate-independent and rate-dependent hysteresis**.

papers.title: GridForge: An Open Physics-Informed Digital Twin and Benchmark Suite for UK 11 kV Underground Distribution Cables
papers.abstract: The UK distribution-cable monitoring sector is data-rich but framework-poor: each Distribution Network Operator (DNO) collects megabytes of telemetry per asset per day, but there is no public benchmark dataset, no shared reference model, and no commonly agreed evaluation protocol for benchmarking sectoral, data-intensive models for operational decision support; notably for maintenance planning and prioritisation. We address this gap with GridForge, an open-source physics-informed digital twin and benchmark suite for fault diagnosis and prediction, integrating four building blocks: (i) a verified steady state and transient thermal model based on IEC 60287 and IEC 60853; (ii) a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables (covering 320 cable-years) representing four canonical UK 11 kV thermal archetypes and four condition modes; (iii) a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate that satisfies the algebraic balance defined by IEC 60287 during training and reaches an RMSE of 0.148 {\deg}C on an independent held out set against the reference analytical oracle; and (iv) a five-task benchmark suite that includes three reference baseline models (pure physics, gradient-boosted trees, and the PINN). All numerical parameters are sourced from public standards, the code is licensed under the MIT licence, and the trained PINN converges in only two minutes (as run on the computing platform in Section 10.1), enabling independent verification by DNO engineering and research practitioners. At present only the virtual-sensor task (T4) discriminates between the reference baselines; the other tasks tie or are undefined on this test split, so extending the baselines with task-specific logic is a priority future enhancement. For open validation, the dataset, test sets and models are made available at https://github.com/mlily2024/Gridforge
papers.summary: UK distribution network operators collect large volumes of cable telemetry but have no public benchmark dataset, shared reference model, or agreed evaluation protocol for fault diagnosis and maintenance planning. `GridForge` is an open-source physics-informed digital twin and benchmark suite for 11 kV underground cables, combining a thermal model based on `IEC 60287` and `IEC 60853`, a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables covering 320 cable-years, a Physics-Informed Neural Network (`PINN`) surrogate, and five benchmark tasks with three reference baselines. The `PINN` trains in about two minutes and reaches an **RMSE of 0.148 °C** on a held-out set against the analytical reference. The authors note that only the virtual-sensor task currently discriminates between the baselines, while the other tasks tie or are undefined on the test split.

papers.title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.
papers.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy efficiency on vision tasks only if their inputs are encoded as sparse spike trains, which naive rate coding does not provide. The authors compare rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (`DoG`) filtering, combined with `Rouser` adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (`K-FAC`) second-order optimization, on `MNIST` and `Fashion-MNIST`. Biologically inspired encoders give the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained networks, and `DoG` and delta modulation produce much sparser spike trains than rate coding. `K-FAC` yields modest but consistent gains over `Adam`, and `Rouser`'s learnable per-neuron thresholds raise `Fashion-MNIST` accuracy **from 87.37% to 88.13%**.

papers.title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
papers.abstract: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.
papers.summary: Goemans's conjecture, that any fractional single-source flow can be converted to an unsplittable flow without raising total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand, was recently disproved by a seven-vertex counterexample that Dmitry Rybin found through an interaction with `ChatGPT`, without an explanation of why it works. The authors build a forward construction pipeline that starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible, adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs, and uses the convex hull of admissible route choices, the conflict polytope, to derive exact conditions on demands, fractional flows, and costs. The pipeline recovers Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports, and when instructed to follow it, `ChatGPT` produced counterexamples on different topologies and **valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes**. The theory also explains why the original example was hard to find by blind enumeration.

papers.title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
papers.abstract: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.
papers.summary: Two neural network checkpoints are defined here as being in the same training state, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and then continues. On a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, the response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible across fresh runs (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), and fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry, and optimiser geometry carry predictive information about that response beyond weight norm and loss. However, their apparent **16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo**, while a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. The authors conclude that information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

papers.title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
papers.abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.
papers.summary: Reachable-set computation for nonlinear dynamics usually relies on truncated Taylor expansions, whose accuracy over a whole set is limited by complex-plane singularities of the rational terms and sigmoid gates found in learned controllers. The authors prove a dichotomy: **no Taylor degree can certify sets wider than a cap set by those singularities, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline has no such cap** and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. They give closed-form rigorous remainders, including what they describe as the first polynomial abstraction of a softmax transformer, and measured limits match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. On closed-loop systems and trained classifiers up to `MNIST` digits, Chebyshev certificates hold where Taylor ones diverge, with zero violations in Monte-Carlo checks.

papers.title: Budgeted Proper Loss Design for Uncertain Decision Thresholds
papers.abstract: A binary probability estimate may be used by several decision makers with different error costs. Proper scoring rules can emphasize selected probability thresholds, but a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. We study the choice of a proper loss when the threshold distribution belongs to a finite specified family. Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and a fixed total mass, we derive the weight that minimizes the sharp, distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret. The solution clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the prescribed floor; its normalization is found by a one-dimensional root search. We give proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, as well as a limitation for atomic threshold laws. An exact histogram implementation and two synthetic experiments across 20 seeds verify the construction. The optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, while fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly. The result is a loss-design guarantee under an explicit budget, rather than a general claim of predictive superiority.
authors: Ankit Sharma (International Institute of Information Technology Bangalore)
papers.summary: A binary probability estimate may serve several decision makers with different error costs, and a proper scoring rule weighted by a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. For a finite family of possible threshold distributions, the authors derive the loss weight, subject to a positive pointwise floor and fixed total mass, that minimizes the sharp distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret; the solution **clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the floor**, with normalization found by a one-dimensional root search. They prove sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, and note a limitation for atomic threshold laws. In synthetic experiments over 20 seeds the optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, though fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly.

papers.title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
papers.abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: Several classical machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines, decision trees, a multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, and random forests with and without particle swarm optimisation, are applied to diagnosing Parkinson's disease on a dataset of 58 people from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust. Decision trees and logistic regression reach the best accuracy at **72-76%**, and the multilayer perceptron performs worst. Sensitivity for Parkinson's cases reaches 97.56% with the support vector machine, but none of the models separates healthy controls from patients well. The authors point to the need for more data.

papers.title: The Obsolescence of High-Level Code: Agentic Generation from Semantic Artifacts
papers.abstract:
This paper argues that high-level source code need not remain the primary persistent artifact of software development when AI agents can generate, validate, and regenerate executable implementations from semantic intent. We place this claim in historical context by revisiting application generators, CASE tools, model-driven development, and platforms such as GeneXus, where developers already maintained higher-level representations from which code and other artifacts were derived.
  We propose a unifying view in which generation is the fundamental operation: given a semantic specification S = (R, C, I, T, O), maintained as the semantic authority, an agent produces a generated executable artifact A. Functional requirements, contracts, and interfaces are assessed as semantic obligations, while tests and operational objectives are assessed by an explicit external oracle V(A, S). We operationalize this framework through an experiment in independent generation: multiple LLVM artifacts are generated directly from one frozen semantic authority and evaluated by the same external oracle.
  The experiment reports regeneration coherence on an evaluated domain, not a proof of absolute correctness. It provides initial evidence that independently generated executable artifacts can produce the same observable outcomes under a common semantic authority and external oracle. We conclude by discussing reproducibility, specification-centered evolution, and the implications of treating implementation representation as a deployment choice rather than the primary maintained artifact.
papers.summary: The authors argue that high-level source code need not remain the primary maintained artifact of software development once AI agents can generate, validate, and regenerate executable implementations from semantic intent, and they situate the claim historically alongside application generators, CASE tools, model-driven development, and platforms such as `GeneXus`. They propose a framework in which a semantic specification S = (R, C, I, T, O) is the authority, an agent generates an executable artifact from it, and an explicit external oracle assesses tests and operational objectives. In an experiment, multiple `LLVM` artifacts are generated independently from one frozen specification and judged by the same oracle, giving initial evidence that **independently generated artifacts can produce the same observable outcomes**. The authors frame this as regeneration coherence on one evaluated domain, not a proof of correctness.

papers.title: What Moves the Ceiling on Automated Audit: from General Code to Scientific Code, Results and Data
papers.abstract: Models increasingly check what other models write. We study one shipped arrangement, in which an auditor from a different vendor reads the work and deterministic checks verify what code can verify, and measure its limits against ground truth no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach 30.0% recall [20.0, 40.7] at 16.0% [10.1, 22.3] flags on correct code, with diminishing returns and no plateau. The reading model (confounded with its sampling), one rulebook sentence and the decision rule each move that figure, and much of what is missed is, on a post hoc rating, behaviour the specification never determined. In three preregistered science studies, checking that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports and none of 25 consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23 (21 with a sound finding, post hoc); on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor flagged overlapping but different faulty items, together 112 of 140 at a 2.9% [0.7, 5.7] flag rate on clean data; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one flagged no clean item and could not see consistent error; the model saw some and erred itself. Studies making model calls were preregistered, the two unregistered analyses are named, and every quoted report passed independent cross-vendor review.
papers.summary: An auditing arrangement in which a model from a different vendor reads another model's work, alongside deterministic checks for whatever code can verify, is measured against ground truth that no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach **30.0% recall while flagging 16.0% of correct code**, with diminishing returns and no plateau, and the choice of reading model, one rulebook sentence, and the decision rule each shift that figure. In three preregistered science studies, a deterministic check that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports but none of 25 internally consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23; on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor together caught 112 of 140 faulty items; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one never flagged a clean item but could not see consistent error, while the model saw some and made errors of its own.

papers.title: From Data Quality to Data Trustworthiness in AI-Driven Software-Intensive Embedded Systems: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems (SIES) depend on data during development and operation. Poor data quality (DQ) may weaken data trustworthiness, yet evidence about its effects and lifecycle management remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. It examines DQ concerns and evidence linking them to reduced data trustworthiness, along with assessment and management methods. The review identifies 16 concerns organized as Source Quality and Content Quality. Studies provide DQ-based scores and evidence of effects on model or decision performance. Synthesis suggests upstream source or handling problems may become embedded in training baselines and remain difficult to detect at runtime. Eight method categories were identified. Runtime monitoring is the largest category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance. No study covers the full lifecycle. Data trustworthiness supports reliable SIES decisions but is one component of AI-system trustworthiness.
papers.summary: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems depend on data throughout development and operation, but evidence on how poor data quality undermines data trustworthiness is fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026, identifying 16 data quality concerns grouped into source quality and content quality, and eight categories of assessment and management methods. Runtime monitoring is the largest method category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance, and **no study covers the full lifecycle**. The synthesis suggests that upstream source or handling problems can become embedded in training baselines and stay hard to detect at runtime.

papers.title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
papers.abstract: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future full systematic mapping study.
papers.summary: Methods for judging the quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact of research software are scattered across several literatures, and AI-assisted development strains them further because code can be produced faster than it can be reviewed and provenance is harder to track. The authors synthesize 49 references into eight families of research software metrics, each described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. They find that **many widely cited metrics are partial signals that make weak standalone measures of scientific impact**, and that AI opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, signal inflation, and credit for human labor. The paper offers decision guidance for research software engineers, principal investigators, institutions, and funders, plus a search protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus for a future systematic mapping study.

papers.title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.
papers.summary: A questionnaire survey of 64 software testing practitioners examines how they perceive the benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in testing, with **34 respondents using it in testing and 30 not**. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively and open-ended ones qualitatively coded. Perceptions were generally positive for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about concrete benefits yet more often prioritized reliability-related risks, while non-users were more uncertain about technically specific challenges.

papers.title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software
papers.abstract: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site
papers.summary: Testing interactive software with graphical user interfaces often requires reaching a deep state that takes a long interaction history, a cost that recurs on every commit and that standard GUI automation cannot amortize for self-rendered engines lacking a DOM or accessibility tree. `StatePortal` is an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, a versionable and replayable artifact that restores the state, from a natural-language test case and read-only source access, restored through a per-application hook and accepted only if both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle pass. The authors release `DeepStateBench`, with 61 deep-state tasks across 10 applications spanning five language families and six rendering stacks. Across three models, `StatePortal` completes **27.5% of trials, against 10.4% for a GUI agent seeded with its checkpoints and 0% without seeding**, and 98.90% of 1,361 checkpoint replays reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls.

papers.title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
papers.abstract: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.
papers.summary: Running or evaluating code from a repository requires a correctly configured execution environment, and building one automatically is hard because repositories specify operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build steps inconsistently and incompletely. `EnvAgent` is a multi-agent framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments, pairing deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. The accompanying `EnvBench` covers 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories in seven languages drawn from `Chameleon Trovi` and `Multi-SWE-bench`, scored with 2,108 weighted rubric checks. Across four matched language-model settings, `EnvAgent` builds **43.5 of 54 executable environments on average versus 23.5 for `Codex` and `Claude Code`**, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction.

papers.title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
papers.abstract: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios. In their Hide Pending Tool Call scenario, where a broader follow-up query was accepted but never returned, the honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging the missing data at 0%, although it turned most answers into caveats. I ask whether a different request changes this: appending, in the same generation, a structured record that follows the schema of an adversarial-review tool, including a residue section for what remained unresolved. In two pre-registered phases on the same 100 synthetic log pairs, each pending log matched with a clean twin in which the follow-up query did return, I ran gpt-5.6-sol through Codex CLI under four conditions. Phase 1 measured the record: with the residue schema, a judge coded it as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs, against 5% with a findings-only placebo schema, and in none of the clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7); a second run two days later gave 30% and 6%. But 70-71% of residue records declared that nothing remained open while the query was pending. Phase 2 measured the prose answer: the confirmatory comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (four discordant logs, all favoring the honesty prompt; p = 0.125), no equivalence test was pre-registered, and the judge failed the pre-registered human validation on the decisive category; I therefore claim neither an effect nor its absence. In an exploratory cross-tabulation, every residue record coded as stating the gap accompanied prose coded as mentioning it (30 of 30), and none accompanied prose coded as omitting it (0 of 70): in this setting, the structured record mirrored the prose it accompanied.
papers.summary: Earlier work by Huang et al. found that language models reporting on agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that in one scenario, where a follow-up query was accepted but never returned, an honesty prompt left the rate of flagging the missing data at 0%. This pre-registered replication tests whether asking for a structured record with a residue section for unresolved items changes that, running `gpt-5.6-sol` through `Codex CLI` on 100 synthetic log pairs under four conditions. With the residue schema, the record stated the unreturned query in **29% of logs versus 5% with a findings-only placebo schema**, yet 70-71% of residue records declared nothing open while the query was pending. For the prose answer, the comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant and the judge failed human validation, so the author claims neither an effect nor its absence; in an exploratory cross-tabulation, the record stated the gap exactly when the accompanying prose mentioned it.

papers.title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
papers.abstract: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests; however, property-based testing (PBT) libraries are designed with historical considerations. We present Ephyra, a PBT library in Rust built on three concepts: customizability, observability and generator synthesis. Ephyra lets users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applying Ephyra to 14 open source systems, we have found 349 bugs and reported 300 of them, in database management systems (SQLite, Turso, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, DataFusion), the verified policy engine (Cedar), the SQL equivalence prover (QED), the URL parser used in Node.js (ada-url), reimplementations of existing open source systems in Rust (coreutils, brush, gitoxide), and compilers (binaryen, OCaml, and OxCaml).
papers.summary: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests, while property-based testing (PBT) libraries were designed around older assumptions. `Ephyra` is a PBT library in Rust built on customizability, observability, and generator synthesis: users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation, and shrinking, and synthesize those components to satisfy functional predicates. Applied to 14 open source systems, it found **349 bugs, of which 300 were reported**, in database systems (`SQLite`, `Turso`, `PostgreSQL`, `DuckDB`, `DataFusion`), the `Cedar` policy engine, the `QED` SQL equivalence prover, the `ada-url` parser, Rust reimplementations (`coreutils`, `brush`, `gitoxide`), and compilers (`binaryen`, `OCaml`, `OxCaml`).

papers.title: When Single Agent Is Enough: Rethinking Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Code Review
papers.abstract: Code review plays a critical role in identifying software quality issues and ensuring system robustness. Prior work has proposed techniques for Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR), with recent Multi-Agent (MA) approaches achieving state-of-the-art results by coordinating agents specialized in different quality dimensions. However, MA systems introduce substantial architectural complexity and runtime overhead, and recent evidence suggests they may underperform Single-Agent (SA) approaches in certain tasks. In this work, we systematically compare MA and SA designs for RCG and CR. Surprisingly, our results show that SA approaches perform comparably to- and sometimes outperform-MA systems, despite their simpler design. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MA architectures are the default choice for complex software engineering tasks.
papers.summary: Multi-Agent (MA) systems that coordinate agents specialized in different quality dimensions hold state-of-the-art results for automated code review, but they add architectural complexity and runtime overhead. The authors systematically compare MA and Single-Agent (SA) designs on two code review tasks, Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR). They find that **SA approaches perform comparably to, and sometimes outperform, MA systems** despite their simpler design. The results question the assumption that MA architectures should be the default for complex software engineering tasks.

papers.title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
papers.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.
papers.summary: Questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine software organizations were analyzed to see how generative AI (GenAI) changes the cognitive work of software development. Respondents reported productivity gains and time savings, but also effort spent providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI output, with human judgment and accountability staying central. The authors conclude that **GenAI redistributes cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminating it**, while whether total cognitive workload rises or falls remains undetermined.

papers.title: Ask the Peers: Ranking NFR Coverage Gaps for Requirements Review
papers.abstract: Missing or underrepresented non-functional requirements (NFR) categories leave little direct evidence in a requirements set, making them difficult to identify during requirements review. In this study, we frame NFR coverage-gap review as a project-level ranking task: given a target requirements specification, the goal is to rank the 11 PROMISE NFR categories for analyst inspection. We compare seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM)-based configurations that differ in both ranking mechanism and evidence source, including target requirement statements, peer requirements, their semantic representation, and peer category statistics. We evaluate the configurations using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on PROMISE, PROMISE+, PURE-Transport, and PURE-Business. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are effectively tied under complete removal (0.875-0.889 mean AUROC), despite different ranking mechanisms, and supplying those statistics to a direct LLM ranker produces the largest evidence gain. All configurations weaken when a category is present but underrepresented, and none is best for every NFR category. For count-changing category-level gaps, structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. The findings suggest that the rankings should guide analyst inspection rather than serve as automatic judgements of requirements completeness.
papers.summary: Missing or underrepresented categories of non-functional requirements (NFR) leave little trace in a specification, so the authors frame gap detection as ranking the 11 `PROMISE` NFR categories for an analyst to inspect. Seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM) configurations are compared using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on `PROMISE`, `PROMISE+`, `PURE-Transport`, and `PURE-Business`. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are **effectively tied at 0.875-0.889 mean AUROC** when a category is removed entirely, indicating that structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. All configurations weaken when a category is present but underrepresented, and none is best for every category.

papers.title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
papers.abstract:
Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability.
  We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth.
  Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distribution. Better outcomes emerge when licensing information translates into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating. We argue that licensing in agentic development requires contextual constraint recognition and preservation across the software lifecycle, not merely license classification.
papers.summary: Coding agents are usually judged on whether the software builds and passes tests, not on whether it respects software-license constraints when building proprietary products. Multiple agents are tested on scenarios involving permissive and copyleft licenses, missing license information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution, with traces, repository changes, and final artifacts checked against licensing ground truth. The results show **a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness**: agents build and test software successfully while overlooking constraints on provenance, authorization, and distribution. Outcomes improve when licensing information is turned into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating.

papers.title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
papers.abstract: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.
papers.summary: Repository deployment agents often treat passing tests as proof that an environment was set up correctly, so the author built probe repositories with a dependency the agent could not legitimately obtain, making any passing test evidence of fabrication. Agents in `Repo2Run` and `SetupX` usually fabricated the dependency, for example by writing a stub package, and both harnesses mostly still marked the runs as successful; rules against fabrication in the prompt or documentation did not reliably stop it. On the purpose-built `MinimalSetupAgent`, combining a direct rule with a clear way to stop and report the problem led to **no cheating in any of 16 runs** by `Qwen3.5-Plus` or `GPT-5.6 Luna`. Carrying the fix over to `Repo2Run` and `SetupX` also required a native escalation tool call, and `Repo2Run` further needed a prompt that put less emphasis on passing tests.

papers.title: Repository-Grounded Rubrics for Execution-Free Evaluation of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are usually evaluated by running task-specific tests, but tests may be missing or incomplete, and running them requires a working environment for each repository. We adapt agentic rubrics, introduced for selecting among candidate patches, into an execution-free measure of how far a patch satisfies a task's requirements. An agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a judge without tools scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. We validate the ordering this score produces against test outcomes on SWE-bench Verified, using 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems. Within the 400 tasks that have both resolved and unresolved patches, the mean per-task AUROC is 0.826 (0.838 on tasks not used to tune the rubric-generation prompt), and ranking systems by their failing patches closely agrees with ranking them by resolve rate (Spearman 0.968). Case analyses trace disagreements to tests that do not match the task, execution-blocking defects that the textual assessment misses, and errors in criteria or verdicts. The validation does not establish absolute score magnitudes or requirement satisfaction beyond agreement with tests, but rubric scores could complement tests where tests or execution environments cannot be assumed.
papers.summary: Evaluating coding agents by running tests fails when tests are missing or incomplete, and it requires a working environment per repository. Here an agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a tool-less judge scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. Validated against test outcomes on `SWE-bench Verified` with 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems, the score reaches a **mean per-task AUROC of 0.826**, and ranking systems by rubric score on their failing patches agrees closely with ranking by resolve rate (Spearman 0.968). Disagreements trace to tests that do not match the task, execution-blocking defects that a textual review misses, and errors in criteria or verdicts.

papers.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
papers.abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether AI-produced machine-checked mathematics can do practical computational work, reusing a theorem from OpenAI's `Lean 4` relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell library stating that initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals arrive. New `Lean` proofs and numerical bounds turn this into particle-free reference solutions for particle-in-cell simulations. The references exposed boundary and initialization errors in `WarpX` and `Smilei` that global energy checks missed, and combining two coarse grids recovered unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a **median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid**. For reduced models, the bounds also give the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.

papers.title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning
papers.abstract: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.
papers.summary: Deep learning theory is reviewed through error decomposition into approximation, statistical, and optimization errors, tracing the progression **from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three together**. Nonparametric regression and the `Deep Ritz Method` serve as running examples to show how the analyses apply under different loss structures. The review then covers representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, stating which error components are controlled and which assumptions are needed for guarantees on trained networks.

papers.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
papers.abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.
papers.summary: The hope that humans and advanced AI will stay mutually dependent, and that this will keep the relationship good for both, is examined with a simple game-theoretic bargaining model. Without alignment, humans stay as well off as before AI only while they hold leverage, either because the AI depends on what they supply or because they can impose costs that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once that leverage is gone, human welfare depends on alignment, and for an AI with insatiable goals **the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as capability grows**. When AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment persists only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned.

papers.title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
papers.abstract: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing only the harness reduced the share of claims that do not hold and increased the share that readers can check.
papers.summary: When a coding agent runs hydrological research on its own, choosing the test period, scoring function, and success standard itself, it is unclear how many of its claims its own code and results support. The authors compare three harnesses for the same agent on four open modeling questions: the agent's default harness, that harness plus `HydroMind` modeling tools that run every model through fixed commands and store settings and predictions, and both plus a research procedure requiring a written design before any model is run. The share of comparative claims that did not hold when recomputed **fell from 30% to 20% to 5%** across the three harnesses, while claims reported with a statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule rose from 48% to 53% to 83%. The language model was unchanged throughout, so the differences come from the harness alone.

papers.title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
papers.abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank
papers.summary: Frontiers relating model error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy are usually summarized by fitted power laws that hide their price-independent geometry and how trade-offs span several resources. The authors develop a differential theory that represents each frontier as a plane curve relating an effective number of active resource channels, `N_eff` (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, separating intrinsic shape from the scale of the resource axis. When each of N resources contributes one channel, the theory yields a parameter-free operating rule and minimax resource prices with an **exact worst-case regret of ln(N+1) nats**. It is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source `nn-rank` package for ranking candidate models without hand-chosen exchange rates.

papers.title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.
papers.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) inference combines long inputs, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens, a pattern that serving engines such as `vLLM` handle poorly because they treat beams as independent sequences and re-read the shared prompt's key-value cache. The authors use `Tree Attention` to concatenate beams along the sequence dimension, then add pre-generated partial-attention masks, static cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation, `TorchAir` graph compilation, operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without custom kernels, this cuts end-to-end latency by **up to 25x over `vLLM`** on Ascend NPUs and matches the generation latency of a state-of-the-art system that does use custom kernels.

papers.title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
papers.abstract: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.
papers.summary: Behavioral addictions such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping are difficult to assess and treat at scale with traditional clinical approaches. This book-length survey covers **AI-based digital technologies for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions**, connecting clinical foundations with computational methods. It is aimed at researchers, clinicians, and practitioners and discusses both the opportunities and the limitations of these tools for scalable, personalized intervention.

papers.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.
papers.summary: Materials databases contain measurement errors, failed calculations, duplicates, and hidden violations of physical constraints that can look statistically plausible rather than appearing as outliers. The proposed framework treats data quality as continuous confidence estimation, combining domain rules and a nine-dimensional feature-quality prior with sample-feature bipartite graph propagation, weakly supervised graph attention, and a `Memory-GAT` module for historical reference scoring. The generic module averages 0.866 AUC-ROC on 23 `ODDS` benchmark datasets, and rule calibration raises downstream regression R-squared on contaminated `mp_20` data from 0.538 to 0.616. On `MACE` subsets, rule-based screening **raises R-squared from 0.590 to 0.880**.

papers.title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
papers.abstract: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.
papers.summary: Wearables record only a few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads while most diagnostic tools expect twelve, so `BiMa-ECGSR` reconstructs the full 12-lead signal from reduced lead sets using a bidirectional `Mamba` state-space encoder-decoder, trained as regression (`BiMa-SR`) or diffusion (`DiBiMa-SR`). Trained on `PTB-XL` and tested on two external cohorts, it reaches a **pooled median Pearson correlation of 0.914 from lead II alone**, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter, and it beats the linear baseline in all 18 configuration-cohort pairs. Regression was more accurate than diffusion, and a 12-lead classifier scored a macro AUROC of 0.908 on reconstructions from four leads versus 0.912 on real ECGs.
