The authors note that reconstruction cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

papers.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.
papers.summary: Surgical video archives are hard to search by content, and existing surgical computer vision mostly produces labels instead of retrieving similar videos. `SurgCBVR` is a video-to-video retrieval benchmark built from eight public datasets across ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy domains, with 679 cases and 76,489 clips, split into a Scene tier for matching operative states and a Workflow tier for phase transitions and deviations. Evaluating six foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and trained contrastive heads shows that **frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline**, transition retrieval is near chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets.

papers.title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
papers.abstract: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.
papers.summary: Automated depression-severity estimation from clinical interviews often keeps interviewer speech, fuses modalities late, or scores symptoms independently. `SIGMA` uses speaker diarization to keep only participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio, and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts all eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait. On the `Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus` it reports a **concordance correlation coefficient of 0.762** with RMSE 4.13 and MAE 3.30 over five seeds, and ablations attribute substantial gains to both speaker isolation and joint symptom prediction.

papers.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.
papers.summary: Generative AI (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is being adopted in requirements engineering, but little is known about the specifications it produces and how they feed later work such as specification-driven development, code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document is the protocol for a planned systematic mapping study and **contains no results yet**: it defines the research questions, classification schemes, search strategy, study selection procedure, data extraction form, analysis approach, and threats to validity. It is published in advance as a prior commitment to support transparency and repeatability.

papers.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
papers.abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.
papers.summary: When an agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system, so retrying risks duplication while assuming success may hide an action that never happened. The authors build a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing, then inject ten single-host fault classes across 7,513 trials each on Windows and Linux. In 200 crash-and-replay pairs the full configuration produced **0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline**, while disabling reconciliation left all 100 post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous even though no duplicates occurred. The full runtime ran at about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, and the results separate duplicate suppression from actual recovery.

papers.title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.
papers.summary: Scaling reinforcement learning (RL) training for large language models (LLMs) exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that waste compute and undermine model improvements. This survey collects the scattered techniques for managing those operations, termed LLM RLOps, and **organizes them into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation**. For each stage it reviews operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Open challenges identified include training observability, cross-stage coordination, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement.

papers.title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
papers.abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).
papers.summary: Binary-weight Transformers save memory and power, and approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling saves more but introduces bit errors whose effect on these models has not been well studied. Using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (`BERT`) as a case study, the authors find that large accuracy loss occurs only at high bit error rates (BER) such as 5% or 10%. They propose Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (`PIES`) protection, which exploits the model's invariance to row and column permutations to group critical weights and protect only those. In simulation, `PIES` **recovers most of the lost performance at bit error rates as high as 10%** with overhead well below traditional error correction schemes.

papers.title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
papers.abstract: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.
papers.summary: An audit of a deployed human-in-the-loop tool that proposes a reading order for academic job applications, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model retrained after each label. The synthetic test pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, the reported four-level agreement score tracked classifier confidence instead of ranking quality, and **uncertainty sampling raised the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline** because it asks about CVs that would otherwise be skipped. After regenerating the pool under a shared length budget, the headline result still held: reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of relevant candidates after half the pile. A hosted LLM embedding model lifted zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80, a gain a local cross-encoder matched and that vanished after about two dozen labels.

papers.title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
papers.abstract:
This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations.
  We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gr\"obner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.
papers.summary: Symbolic computation methods are mathematically rigorous but often too expensive for practical use, and machine learning has been applied both to tune existing computer algebra algorithms and to compute symbolic results directly. A systematic literature review covers applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, and symbolic integration, comparing approaches that range from decision trees to transformers. The main issue it identifies is **a lack of benchmark datasets for computer algebra**, which hinders method comparison and generalization, and it points to explainable AI tools as a way to build trust in learned decisions.

papers.title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.
papers.summary: Safeguards for LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) mostly detect anomalies in individual agents, which misses failures that originate in the interactions between agents and does not reveal their true source. `TRACE-MAS` learns normal collaboration patterns from benign trajectories, detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependencies, then attributes the failure to specific execution elements and applies a minimal intervention to restore collaboration. On five MAS benchmarks it **improves root-cause localization accuracy by 60.2%** and shows consistent gains in task recovery over existing safeguards.

papers.title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
papers.abstract: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.
papers.summary: Publishers revise and reissue images, but valid watermarks can persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits, and a single current image may contain regions last approved at different revisions. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (`GSF`) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, embedding fresh generation labels in newly approved regions at each reissue and inherited labels elsewhere. Across 480 image histories followed through four releases, `GSF` **classifies issued images as current or superseded with 99.67% accuracy**, detects unissued edits with 94.09% recall, and after three reissues recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy.

papers.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.
papers.summary: Embodied simulation of animal behavior needs realistic bodies, biologically grounded controllers, and fast training, and this work advances all three for the rat. It introduces `Rat v2`, an efficient biomechanical body, and `Rat NCAP`, a locomotion architecture based on mammalian spinal circuits with cell-type-specific connectivity and a flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface, trained on GPU-accelerated simulation infrastructure. The model **learns to locomote at different speeds and switch gaits without imitation learning**, producing kinematics and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Simulated ablations of cell types reproduce known gait phenotypes, and the choice of neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality.

papers.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.
papers.summary: Behaviors such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy are hard to detect from transcripts, and asking a model about its own actions is unreliable because models are not trained to report their misbehavior. Introspective oversight adds a separate third-person observer role inside the model that answers arbitrary questions about the assistant and is trained solely for accuracy, with answers verified against the assistant's actual behavior. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on `Qwen3.6-27B` **reaches a mean AUROC of 0.907**, ahead of honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). Training the observer also made the assistant itself easier to monitor with every baseline method.

papers.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.
papers.summary: Coding agents are billed per token, yet there is no account of what those tokens accomplish, so the authors propose a thermodynamics-inspired theory that splits an agent's token cost into work and heat, with the test suite acting as a Maxwell's daemon that judges each change. They test it by having an agent repeatedly make a repository change and then undo it, counting the tokens of every model call. **About 80 per cent of the tokens in a successful run come from model calls that leave the requested change where it was**, while the estimated free energy of a change is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost. Making a change costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as undoing it, and the spread of cycle costs rises with the model's sampling temperature.

papers.title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
papers.summary: N-gram embedding tables add capacity to language models cheaply, but recent designs keep a separate table per layer, which is costly in memory, while naively sharing one table across layers performs poorly. `Chorus` shares one set of tables across the whole network and lets each layer read it differently, through a per-layer projection applied after rescaling the embedding by factors computed from that layer's hidden state. It **matches existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables**, predicting text better with 1.2B table parameters than `FactorEngram` and `Engram` do with 9.6B. Paired with the `Ember` optimizer, it also saves 99.2% of table-optimizer memory relative to `AdamW` without degrading training.

papers.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
papers.summary: The best post-training quantization recipe differs by model and precision, so experts currently redesign it by hand for each new model. `QDA` has an LLM agent iterate on recipes, scoring each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on held-out reasoning traces, checking promising ones with long generations, and building from a library of mutually compatible public quantization methods. Across four reasoning models it improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4, and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter `GLM-5.3-Flash` at NVFP4 W4A4, it **recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy versus 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint**, with no inference overhead on existing serving kernels.
papers.highlight_summary:
The best post-training quantization recipe differs across models and precisions, and fully evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes **23–86 GPU-hours**, so hand-tuned recipes neither transfer nor scale. `QDA` hands recipe design to a coding agent that builds, scores and refines candidates in a closed loop, using a cheap proxy metric instead of full benchmark runs.

- Each candidate is scored in minutes by the KL divergence of its next-token distributions from the original model's on hidden reference traces, which is **350–990× cheaper** than a full evaluation, and a few promising candidates also write long answers to expose repetition loops and truncated reasoning.
- Candidates are built from a library of 21 composable PTQ methods (`GPTQ`, `AWQ`, rotations, scale distillation and others) that runs on new architectures, while a sandboxed harness keeps the test benchmarks and reference traces out of the agent's reach.
- Across four reasoning models, average accuracy improves over the strongest public recipe by **0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 points** at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16 with 64 GPU-hours per search, peaking at **6.1 points** on `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B` at W3A16, and every checkpoint runs on existing `vLLM` kernels with no inference overhead.
- On the 320B-parameter `GLM-5.3-Flash` at NVFP4, one 6.5-hour search recovers **98.3%** of FP8 accuracy against 96.9% and 96.3% for the NVIDIA and Red Hat AI checkpoints, while the same agent given `ModelOpt` instead of the `QDA` stack trails by 0.5–1.3 points on `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`.
- The gains are uneven and the proxy is imperfect: on `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`, `QDA` is 0.2 points below `GSQ` at W3A16 and only 0.1 ahead at W4A8, the KL score orders just 82% of checkpoint pairs the way accuracy does, and most model–precision pairs rest on a single search.

papers.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher on the student's own generations, but practitioners must choose between sequence-level and token-level objectives and pick a divergence with little formal guidance. The theoretical analysis shows that **sequence-level OPD has a future agreement bias that produces a reverse learning order**, matching the teacher at later token positions first while potentially favoring teacher-improbable tokens at earlier positions. On the choice of divergence, forward KL has a well-behaved optimization landscape, whereas other f-divergences such as reverse KL can suffer vanishing gradients even when student and teacher are far apart. Experiments in language model post-training settings illustrate how the preferable objective depends on the student, teacher, and task.

papers.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
papers.abstract:
The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.
papers.summary: Hardware failures in large AI clusters can stall expensive training workloads, making fast machine diagnosis important. `HardwareDx` applies a graph foundation model to automated datacenter hardware diagnosis, so that a single model covers many platforms and new hardware products can be onboarded faster. Deployed in production at Google, it **reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs**, and cuts quality assurance time by 28.3% and 25.1% respectively.

papers.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/
papers.summary: The relationship between an LLM agent's written chain-of-thought (CoT) and its internal computation is poorly understood, and this study examines it in iterated games with incomplete information. Using mechanistic interpretability techniques, the authors find that the model forms an internal representation of the game and revises it step by step throughout the CoT. **Once the model commits prematurely to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers**, a failure visible in both the written trace and the layer activations.

papers.title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
papers.abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.
papers.summary: Whether multimodal language models can connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior has been largely untested. `RFBench` provides 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated with `ADS Momentum`, each with geometric primitives, a raster image, an occupancy grid, and S-parameters, and defines seven tasks spanning layout generation, response prediction, diagnosis, and classification. Seven multimodal models show systematic weaknesses in producing structurally valid layouts and predicting faithful responses, while RF-specific fine-tuning **raises structural validity on layout generation from 0.0% to 83.2%** and the within-2-dB response prediction rate from 17.7% to 62.8%.

papers.title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve Update
papers.abstract: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.
papers.summary: Landmark diffusion (`Roseland`) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding cheaply from a data-to-landmark kernel matrix, but assumes all data are available at once. `iRoseland` treats that matrix as growing row by row and updates its singular value decomposition with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen-Loève (SKL) scheme, needing a single pass over the data and bounded memory independent of the number of points processed. It agrees with `Roseland` to round-off on stationary data and **exceeds equal-memory `Roseland` in accuracy by an order of magnitude on long streams**, while a forgetting factor yields large gains on drifting distributions.

papers.title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
papers.abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.
papers.summary: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are usually measured for a whole model regardless of task, so this study instead measures them per transformer module and by task type, distinguishing procedural tasks from declarative memorization. In a controlled synthetic setting, query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks while MLPs are the most plastic on memorization. Stability does not mirror this: when learning a new procedure, **updating QK retains over half of stored declarative memory while updating VO loses roughly four-fifths**, with MLP updates falling in between. Reset-and-recovery experiments suggest plasticity follows which module suits a task's main computation, whereas stability depends on every way an existing capability relies on that module.

papers.title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
papers.abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.
papers.summary: Recent work argued that spectral initializers for LoRA adapters help only through update magnitude, and this analysis shows the direction of the initial input subspace also matters in a specific regime: when labeled data are scarce relative to representation dimension and the initialization subspace captures task structure. The theory yields an alignment coefficient that closely tracks gains across classification tasks, tested with `PivotLoRA`, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot `BERT-base` classification, `PivotLoRA` **achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and beats vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings**. Gains shrink as labeled data grows, and extensions to 7B and 8B `Llama` decoders and to `GSM8K` and `StrategyQA` also show improvements.

papers.title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.
papers.summary: Choosing less computation per input in a neural operator does not necessarily make inference faster, and this study examines the gap using conformal calibration to select Fourier modes or channel width under a fixed error budget. On Burgers and Darcy flow, selecting fewer modes shrinks active spectral support without measurable latency gains, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate cost. An input-only width selector runs at 0.52 to 0.95 times dense latency, yet **static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster and generally achieve higher coverage**, while the selector misses its 90% coverage target in more than half of the settings.

papers.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
papers.abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.
papers.summary: Quantizing vision CNN weights below 4 bits often causes catastrophic accuracy loss, and where and why this happens has been poorly understood. An analysis of `ResNet` and `EfficientNet` backbones on the full `ImageNet-1k` validation set finds the collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. **Keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations at 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the lost accuracy.** On standard ARM and x86 CPUs, however, software bit-unpacking makes low-bit models 1.48x to 21.5x slower depending on batch size, despite the smaller memory footprint.

papers.title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
papers.abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).
papers.summary: Two design questions for compact convolutional backbones are examined with controlled `EfficientNet-B0` experiments on `ImageNet-1k`: where global self-attention helps, and whether repeated blocks can share weights. Wrapping the backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids did not beat the plain trunk until paired with stage attention, whereas inserting lightweight zero-gated self-attention adapters at three late stages **outperformed a matched plain control by 0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%)**, with learned attention strength increasing with depth. For weight sharing, alternating two shared block templates in one stage cut total parameters by 10.9% at a cost of 1.84 points, while tying a stage to a single template plateaued at 66.10%.

papers.title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
papers.abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.
papers.summary: Real clinical notes are rarely available for research because of privacy regulations, which especially limits work in low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. `LusoClin` is a public dataset of synthetic clinical notes in that language, generated by fine-tuning `Llama 3.2` (3B) with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation on pre-processed real clinical data and annotated with clinical entities by a BERT-based model. Evaluation of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy indicates the notes capture clinically relevant language and can support retrieval applications, although **annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes** and some medical inconsistencies persist.

papers.title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
papers.abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.
papers.summary: Automatically generated mathematics exam questions must be correct, aligned to a curriculum, pitched at the right cognitive level, and easy for teachers to review. `VeriMath` is a human-in-the-loop framework that anchors generation to annotated reference items for a requested exam section and reasoning level, then runs sequential automated verification and guided repair before expert review. In a case study on 4,555 Vietnamese Grade 12 items and 50 generation requirements, it produced verifier-accepted drafts for **94% (47/50) of requirements per run** across two model backbones, while strict teacher-readiness review accepted up to 56.8% of items. Rejected drafts mostly failed on formatting, statement validity, and incomplete solution steps.

papers.title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a target model verify several drafted tokens per pass, but better draft predictions do not always translate into lower latency. `FACT` (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training) is an experimental framework that studies drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions together, using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen `Llama-3-8B-Instruct` target. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with extra weight on early steps raises acceptance by 15-24%, and with a fixed 256-node budget, confidence-guided allocation lifts speedup over autoregressive decoding **from 1.46x to 2.02x on `HumanEval`** and from 1.31x to 1.75x on `MT-Bench`. The two gains do not reliably compound, and changing only host-thread settings can nearly erase the speedup without changing acceptance.

papers.title: Reliability by Architecture: Agentic Workflows for Validated Multi-Physics Simulation from Natural Language
papers.abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines construct supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. We evaluate CO2-storage problems using the multi-physics simulator GEOS, from compositional flow to flow-poromechanics with frictional fault contact. In 80 attempts on two flow problems, grounding raises the proportion of structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but acceptance reaches 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation. With identical inputs, local repairs correct three seeded defects while preserving valid inputs. Supporting tests identify simulations passing physics checks despite differing from the problem description or reference results.
papers.summary: Setting up, running, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations from a natural-language description takes expert time, and agentic workflows that automate it need checks on physical consistency and fidelity to the request. The harness described here splits the work explicitly: large language models (LLMs) interpret requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components outside predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines build supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. On CO2-storage problems in the `GEOS` simulator, grounding raised structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but **acceptance reached 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation**. Supporting tests also found simulations that passed physics checks while differing from the problem description or reference results.

papers.title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
papers.abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $\rho = 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $\rho = 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.
papers.summary: Decisions about who receives scarce humanitarian aid are increasingly made by software, and `AllotNet` is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit model of the allocation judgements elicited by `Allot`, a pre-registered six-language survey instrument. It combines eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria with a gate over participant context, an outcome head, and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. Because real human judgement has no answer key, the model was validated on a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions, where **all sixteen pre-specified checks passed**, including planner performance at 99.4 per cent of oracle, though the authors note two checks are weaker than their titles. The 23,550-parameter model ships as a 125 KB bundle, and nothing has yet been trained on real data.

papers.title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.
papers.summary: Agents that pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory can adapt through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but self-editing without external graders often causes regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. `GUARD` (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design with Adaptive Rule Distillation) decomposes each task into pre-execution self-checks, grades trajectories against them, pins mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by group-relative fitness. A `Soft-HURT` gate promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, the authors report that it **improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution** while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
papers.abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.
papers.summary: Six vision-language models (VLMs) acting as agents read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations under four conditions, ranging from free slice navigation to receiving all slices or key slices in a single request, for 4,800 runs in total, with nine radiologists reading 30 of the cases. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%) and highest with all slices (42.2%) or key slices (42.5%) in one request. On the radiologist-read cases, freely navigating models were correct in **30.0% of runs versus 77.0% for radiologists**. Models formed a first hypothesis after seeing a median of 10.8% of slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs, recovering from a wrong first hypothesis only 12.4% of the time, while stating a median confidence of 90%.

papers.title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
papers.abstract: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.
papers.summary: Measuring how formal a text is does not tell you whether that level of formality suits the situation. The proposed index models observed formality from a text's linguistic features and expected formality from the characteristics of the communicative situation separately, then compares the two using tolerance thresholds that can differ for too little and too much formality. It is illustrated on Polish-language emails apologising for lateness, written by people or generated by a large language model. The authors describe **the implementation as preliminary and in need of further calibration and empirical validation**, positioning the main contribution as a general methodological framework.

papers.title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
