papers.abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.
papers.summary: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls, which is slow and yields answers with no reliability score. `SpecLook` is a training-free speculate-and-verify framework that speculates the agent's next observation rather than its answer: a small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools if the answer is not stable and confident, and only questions still lacking evidence reach the agent in a single forward pass. On `V*`, `HR-Bench`, and `POPE` it is more accurate than every baseline on every split, reaching 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with **7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the `DeepEyes-7B` and `Thyme-RL` agents**. A variant, `SpecLook-Fast`, skips the final agent pass and reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

papers.title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes
papers.abstract: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. In a properly aligned embedding, the leading two principal components form a plane that recovers an analog of the Kiel diagram, the third component tracks [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] varies coherently across the plane, such that the chemically defined Galactic disks and accreted populations occupy distinct loci. We show that legibility, the ease of reading the information out, is highest for a training objective that never pushes stars apart, and instead constrains only the overall distribution of each survey's embeddings (JEPA). JEPA also exceeds the contrastive alternative at the same architecture, and the performance improves further as more surveys (Gaia XP+LAMOST LRS+DESI+APOGEE) are included. Predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproduce the main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure of the Milky Way. These results indicate that the choice of alignment objective, not alignment alone, determines whether stellar labels are linearly recoverable.
papers.summary: Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are usually built by aligning embeddings of the same star across surveys with a contrastive loss, which does not guarantee that stellar physics is easy to read out. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, the authors examine the principal-component geometry of `Gaia XP` spectra embeddings and linear probes of stellar parameters. They find that **a `JEPA` objective, which never pushes stars apart and only constrains each survey's embedding distribution, gives the most linearly readable embeddings** and outperforms the contrastive alternative, with the leading two principal components recovering an analog of the Kiel diagram and the third tracking [Fe/H]. Performance improves as more surveys (`LAMOST LRS`, `DESI`, `APOGEE`) are added, and predicted abundances for 8.0 million giants reproduce the Milky Way's main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure.

papers.title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.
papers.summary: Supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation are both cast as one optimal-control problem over a diffeomorphic flow whose velocity field lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), with the two tasks differing only in the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier or a Gaussian-mixture reference), and the RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding stochastic trace estimators. Because objective and gradient are deterministic, second-order solvers become practical, and in experiments from dimension 2 to 256 **the reduced Gauss-Newton solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested**. The full solve scales quadratically in particle count, which a control-point reduction brings down to linear at near-lossless accuracy.

papers.title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
papers.abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.
papers.summary: Foundation models for partial differential equation (PDE) simulation have not, to the authors' knowledge, been trained or tested on physical conditions that change partway through a trajectory, and models trained on fixed conditions follow such changes only partly. `PhysDial` adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families, feeding coefficients in with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, including mid-trajectory switches in about 5% of training samples **halves the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude** at matched compute. Without physics pretraining it matches or exceeds PDE foundation models on two turbulent flows, with 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy at step 64 versus 7.1 times for `Walrus`.

papers.title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.
papers.summary: Language and vision-language models often direct a disproportionate share of attention to the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, yet under causal masking that token attends only to itself and so carries no information about the input. `BOS Summary` is a training-free inference-time method that, at a single transformer layer during prefill, relaxes the causal mask for the BOS query row alone so it aggregates all visual and textual input tokens, with no added parameters or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple model families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, it **improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks**. Mechanistic analysis shows the input-specific BOS also weakens its sink dominance and shifts attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens.

papers.title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
papers.abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.
papers.summary: Evolutionary methods for automated agent design use language-model crossover to recombine agent architectures, but the search is usually guided only by aggregate fitness, hiding which individual instances succeeded or failed. `GRAFT` (Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design) keeps aggregate fitness for selection and survival but guides crossover and mutation with bounded samples of each parent's successful and failed runs, reused from fitness evaluation with reference answers withheld and no extra task executions. Across six reasoning and programming settings with open-weight optimizer and executor models, it reaches **82.0% mean test accuracy, 9.8 percentage points above the strongest baseline**. Controlled ablations attribute the gain to the execution evidence with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed.

papers.title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.
papers.summary: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention, and this work examines how the direction of the sink token's key vector affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting positive sink-aligned components of other keys increases attention on average and boosting negative ones decreases it, with effects persisting through later layers. Building on this, `SHRINK` is a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation, improving mean accuracy on nine benchmarks by **5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on `LLaVA-OneVision-7B` and `Qwen2.5-VL-3B`**, with smaller gains on `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` and `Gemma-3-4B`. Rescaling sink-aligned key components can also stand in for the attention operations of the `GIFT` and `ACG` steering methods at comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.

papers.title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
papers.abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.
papers.summary: Machine learning work on the criminal legal system has mostly modeled single decisions such as recidivism, rather than the full chain of charging, bond, plea, and sentencing decisions. Here a court case is treated as an event sequence, and a transformer-based time series model forecasts the outcome of the next proceeding by combining clerk-note text with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. On a newly built dataset of thousands of cases from public court records of a mid-sized U.S. city, the model achieves **0.57 micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task**, beating several baselines and performing comparably to a GRU trained on the same input. The authors show how the model can surface patterns in decision-making for court observers.

papers.title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
papers.abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.
papers.summary: Running time-series sensing networks on microcontrollers is hard because aggressive compression and multiplication-free weights both cost accuracy. `BeFit` shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations: it finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional networks (`BeCNNs`) through hardware-aware architecture search and distillation, projects their weights to frozen multiplication-free codes, recovers accuracy through the activations, and generates model-specific kernels. On a Cortex-M4, weight projection speeds `BeCNNs` up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 percentage points, versus 2.4 for ReLU networks. Against the `MLPerf Tiny` `DS-CNN` reference on TensorFlow Lite Micro, **the projected model stays within 1.0 percentage point of reference accuracy while running 5.9x faster**, and the instruction-count reduction reaches 147x on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier.

papers.title: Balancing Partition Forest for Causal Weighting
papers.abstract: Balancing weights are used in observational causal inference to construct a population in which the treatment is independent of observed pretreatment covariates. The ideal weight is the ratio between the product of the covariate and treatment marginals and their joint distribution, for binary and continuous treatments alike. We propose Balancing Partition Tree (BPT) and Balancing Partition Forest (BPF), which estimate this ratio on a learned rectangular partition of covariate--treatment space. Each split maximizes the gain in a Bregman divergence computed from joint and marginal counts. Two choices of divergence yield criteria that maximize the mutual information captured by the partition or reduce the squared error of the weights. We show that the population residual of either criterion bounds the bias of inverse-probability-weighted and doubly robust response estimators that use the population partition weights. Across 17 synthetic and semi-synthetic settings and three response estimators, BPF obtains the lowest mean RMSE rank among seven weight estimators, and a single tree fits in 0.14 seconds on 16,512 observations.
papers.summary: Balancing weights in observational causal inference aim to make treatment independent of observed pretreatment covariates, with the ideal weight being the ratio of the product of covariate and treatment marginals to their joint distribution. `Balancing Partition Tree` (BPT) and `Balancing Partition Forest` (BPF) estimate this ratio on a learned rectangular partition of covariate-treatment space, choosing each split to maximize the gain in a Bregman divergence, which yields criteria based on mutual information or squared weight error. The authors show that the population residual of either criterion bounds the bias of inverse-probability-weighted and doubly robust estimators. Across 17 synthetic and semi-synthetic settings and three response estimators, **`BPF` obtains the lowest mean RMSE rank among seven weight estimators**, and a single tree fits in 0.14 seconds on 16,512 observations.

papers.title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.
papers.summary: Whether large language models (LLMs) hallucinate more on facts that appear less often in training data is tested here through academic authorship attribution, using citation count as a proxy for how prevalent a paper is. The authors curate 1.92 million papers across eight disciplines, stratified by citation level, and query three LLMs. They find a consistent inverse relationship across all models and disciplines, with **hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones**. Further analysis attributes the failures mainly to retrieval limitations rather than absent knowledge, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows prevalence is encoded in representations before generation.

papers.title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.
papers.summary: Predictive accuracy is often taken as evidence that large language models (LLMs) understand the system they forecast, though good predictions can be made without recovering the underlying mechanisms. `LUCID` is a benchmark in which models infer latent market structure from event descriptions and historical financial observations by generating event-induced causal graphs, which are then scored through a reconstruction-based framework. Across 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs, **adding the generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone**, with only a few metrics improving. The results indicate the evaluated models struggle to infer informative, event-specific market structure from observable evidence.

papers.title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
papers.abstract: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.
papers.summary: Convolutions defined on Riemannian manifolds depend on the underlying geometry, raising the question of how stable they are when the metric is perturbed. For parallel transport convolution on a fixed compact manifold, with a continuous input signal and a continuous kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the authors prove that **the convolution output depends continuously in L2 on the Riemannian metric in the C2 topology**. The proof develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and handles the cut locus by combining uniform estimates away from it with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume. The result is a qualitative stability theorem rather than a quantitative bound.

papers.title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
papers.abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
papers.summary: Researchers increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) whether a research question is already answered, and the authors find that models make open questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish, even though they recognize most of these overstatements when checking the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions from newly accepted papers, **`GPT-6-Astra` correctly judges 98% to be unstudied but says so plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers**, and all six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30 to 90 percentage points, with gaps growing with capability across 22 models. Building a fixed answer from each model's own judgment plus separate checks of the cited papers raises Astra's clear reporting of open status to 95%. A combination of several models' written ratings with a learned rule also predicts reviewers' novelty grades in the range reported by `Think-Probe-Respond`, without needing model weights or activations.

papers.title: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form
papers.abstract: A graphon is determined by all of its homomorphism densities, but motif-based methods use finitely many. We compute exactly what that truncation costs in a natural family: latent structure block models whose positions lie on $K$ rays, equivalently degree-corrected block models of rank two. For a given radial law, the configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than $2K-1$ vertices form a one-dimensional fiber, which we give in closed form with explicit endpoints; the friendship graph $F_{K-1}$ is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order serves every $K$. The separating signal is suppressed by a factor of at most $m_1^{2(K-1)}$, where $m_1$ is the mean squared slope, about $10^{-4}$ at $K=4$: detecting it from motif counts would take about $10^{15}$ nodes in a single graph, at any edge density. The information is nonetheless in the graph; the fiber belongs to the statistic, not the model. Common spectral pipelines, which count no motifs, still slide along the fiber by more than a third of its length at ordinary densities, with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, while model-based fits of the same embedding do not. We give practitioners four checks: whether a fit is at risk, what to run instead, why a confidence interval will not warn, and how wide the remaining ambiguity is.
papers.summary: Motif-based graph methods use only finitely many homomorphism densities, and the authors compute exactly what this truncation costs for latent structure block models whose positions lie on K rays, equivalently rank-two degree-corrected block models. Configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than 2K-1 vertices form a one-dimensional fiber given in closed form, and the friendship graph is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order works for every K. The separating signal is so suppressed that **detecting it from motif counts at K=4 would take about 10^15 nodes in a single graph**, at any edge density. Common spectral pipelines also slide along the fiber with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, whereas model-based fits of the same embedding do not, and four practitioner checks are provided.

papers.title: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
papers.abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.
papers.summary: Written language signals personality only weakly, so the authors test whether a more deliberate combination of language-model and psycholinguistic features, plus a decomposition of the prediction target, recovers more signal when estimating Big Five scores from life-narrative interviews. Their three-phase framework, `FACET`, encodes the two views separately, trains contrastive embeddings for each personality facet, and pools them by attention into a domain-level prediction. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (`SPAN`) study, facet embeddings reach an AUC of up to 0.740 and **domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness**. End-to-end training and attention pooling give the lowest error in every domain, while the gain over a regression on raw features is modest and holds in four of five domains.

papers.title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.
papers.summary: When agents built on large language models (LLMs) hand intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later steps can treat tentative assumptions as facts, yet scalar confidence scores drop information needed for revision and verbose descriptions or reflection add cost. The authors introduce `Latent Uncertainty`, a latent-space estimator that keeps uncertainty-relevant information compactly, and `LProp` (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions from latent representations and new evidence without sampling extra trajectories. Across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended, and mathematical reasoning tasks the approach beats baselines on most metrics, and **`LProp` has the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings**. Matched ablations indicate that the inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond what answer probabilities or model capacity alone provide.

papers.title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
papers.abstract: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.
papers.summary: Symbolic robot design methods are interpretable but tend to ignore continuous geometry, while learned methods handle geometry with less transparent structure. The authors define a typed production grammar with case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration that generates both manipulation skills and robot morphologies, together with a map from grammar composition to rigid-body transformations, and a cross-entropy search method over the grammar called `PANINI`. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, `PANINI` achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. The demonstrated advantage is structural: designs are legal by construction, and **coordinated limb placement yields 95% jointly feasible edits, versus 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for a flat parameterization** in 6,000 draws.

papers.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
papers.abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.
papers.summary: In multi-agent systems a receiver agent often waits for a helper's message, either text or a latent KV cache, and this work asks when the receiver can skip it safely (the answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). The mechanism reads the receiver's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change, falling back to always communicating if none passes. Tests on `OpenBookQA`, `ARC-Challenge`, `MMLU-Pro`, `SQuAD`, and `GSM8K` with `Qwen` model pairs and cross-family agents show that where text messages help, **policies skip 59 to 80% of messages while keeping an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain**. The authors also find that oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help, that every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver alone, and that certification does not extend to `GSM8K`.

papers.title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
papers.abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.
papers.summary: Multi-agent assistants that help food-insecure households find usable resources must connect eligibility rules, access constraints, and dietary needs, but uncertainty can be lost at agent handoffs so that tentative interpretations propagate as facts. The authors propose an inference-time clarification framework in which **each receiving agent exposes its admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so that the relevance of a clarifying question reflects both possible decision changes and missing support**. Shared premise identities are preserved and consistent interpretations replayed across dependent agents, and information questions are weighed together with user-confirmable fallback adjustments under shared budgets. The abstract describes the design and reports no experimental results.

papers.title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation
papers.abstract: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.
papers.summary: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation learns more than a dozen organs from a few labeled scans, and the authors identify a self-training failure in which a teacher that misses a small organ labels all of its voxels as confident background, training the student toward the organ's absence; in a pilot, **removing the gallbladder from pseudo-labels dropped its Dice on `AMOS` from 36.5 to 1.0**. Existence-aware Self-Training (`ExiST`) treats a missing organ as unresolved rather than absent: it builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate, and gives background voxels of unresolved organs a set-valued target trained with a marginal cross-entropy and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. The method reaches 77.1 mean Dice on `Synapse` with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on `AMOS` with 5% labeled scans, above prior state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
papers.summary: Enterprise agents built on large language models face changing models and workflows while needing to meet accuracy and cost targets. `ARISE` (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation) is a memory architecture that learns from the agent's own failures without changing weights, tools, or workflow logic: the model itself or a teacher attributes each failure and proposes a correction, corrections are stored as retrievable micro memory and consolidated into macro rules, and a rule update is accepted only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains and 5 models, **the teacher variant using `Claude Opus 4.6` gains 10.9 percentage points over the baseline on `SOP-Bench` and 5.8 on `τ²-bench`**, also outperforming `GEPA` on both. The self-attributing variant still gains 10.0 points on `SOP-Bench`, and the teacher variant uses slightly fewer model calls and output tokens at comparable per-task cost.

papers.title: GRAFT: Graph-Regularized Prototype Fields for Realistic Test-Time Adaptation of VLMs
papers.abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.
papers.summary: Test-time and transductive adaptation of vision-language model classifiers often falls below the zero-shot baseline when a batch contains only a few of the vocabulary's classes or the stream is correlated, which the authors trace to every class owning independent parameters estimated from its own samples. Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (`GRAFT`) instead models adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, alongside an explicit class-presence model, with closed-form, gradient-free inference on cached features. Under realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four `ImageNet` shifts, **`GRAFT` improves over the zero-shot model in every setting** and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.

papers.title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
papers.abstract: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.
papers.summary: Existing variance-aware analyses for episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) keep an additive regret term polynomial in the number of episodes K, of order K^(1/4), even when the environment is deterministic. The authors propose `VA-LSVI-UCB++`, a computationally efficient algorithm whose regret scales with the smaller of two realized trajectory variances, that of the optimal value function and that of the played policies, plus a lower-order term. The bound recovers the worst-case minimax-optimal leading term and **collapses to a d^5 H^4 term with no polynomial dependence on K in deterministic environments**, where d is the feature dimension and H the horizon. The analysis rests on a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value estimators, which tightens confidence radii by a factor of order dH.

papers.title: DuoCL: Dual-Path Online Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.
papers.summary: Online continual learning (OCL) must learn from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of training speed, so expensive gradient-based methods fall behind while cheaper analytic methods keep a frozen backbone that cannot adapt its representations. `DuoCL` runs two paths: a fast analytic path that accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch, and a slow path that periodically adapts the backbone with a sample count fitted to the available compute, with feature alignment compensating for drift in the accumulated statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, **`DuoCL` improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting**. It also beats analytic learning under distribution shift, by up to 4.00 points on `CIFAR-C`, and leads in class-incremental, domain-incremental, and `Si-Blurry` settings.

papers.title: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients for Stable Feature Attribution
papers.abstract: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) are widely used to interpret neural networks, yet imperceptible input perturbations can drastically alter their attribution maps while leaving model predictions unchanged. We introduce Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG), a path-based attribution method that intrinsically attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path using maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature parameter $\tau$. We quantify the effect of the entropy-regularized weighting on attribution stability by using the Lipschitz properties of the model and its gradients. We decompose the attribution change under an input perturbation into a model-response term, whose bound is $\tau$-independent, and a weight-variation term, whose bound decreases at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/(2\tau))$. Their ratio $R(\tau)$ characterizes the trade-off between gradient information and attribution stability. We further add a new dimension to attribution evaluation by adapting classical noise estimators into two metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P, that quantify attribution noise. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet datasets, our experiments show that, relative to the next-best method, ERIG remains comparable on ranking-based fidelity metrics while improving localization by approximately 24% and attribution stability by approximately 47-fold on average, reaching up to four orders of magnitude improvement over IG, all at negligible additional computational cost.
papers.summary: Path-based attribution methods such as Integrated Gradients (`IG`) can produce drastically different attribution maps under imperceptible input perturbations that leave the prediction unchanged. Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (`ERIG`) attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path with maximum-entropy softmax weighting controlled by a temperature, and the authors bound the resulting attribution change as a temperature-independent model-response term plus a weight-variation term that shrinks as temperature grows. They also introduce two attribution-noise metrics, `LINV-C` and `LINV-P`, adapted from classical noise estimators. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on `ImageNet` and `Oxford-IIIT Pet`, `ERIG` stays comparable to the next-best method on ranking-based fidelity while **improving attribution stability by about 47-fold on average** and localization by about 24%, at negligible extra compute.

papers.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.
papers.summary: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also implicitly tell it which source to trust, and `FutureBench` is a renewable framework for measuring such conflicts between model knowledge and context using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, **a `Verify` prompt that combines checking with passage priority raises adoption of false answers in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events**, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under a baseline prompt allowing both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events only `o4-mini` increases adoption, by 13.7 percentage points, and passage priority without checking raises adoption more than `Verify` does. An `Adversarial-Aware` prompt that warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge restores 82.5 to 98.9% of the displaced answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy.

papers.title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
papers.abstract: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). Code: https://github.com/mdebnath22/jepa-props.
papers.summary: Rather than only asking whether a learned black-box optimizer beats existing methods, the authors ask what information it uses from its search history. `JEPA-PS` (JEPA Policy Search), built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, is pretrained on random rollouts of parameter vectors and scalar returns to predict the next point of an optimization trajectory in latent space, and at test time proposes a candidate from a short evaluation history in one forward pass. On 15 control environments against 12 optimizers including `CMA-ES`, Bayesian optimization, and an LLM optimizer, it is competitive with tuned classical baselines, transfers zero-shot to held-out environments, and **outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on `Swimmer` at 71x lower per-step cost**. The history it relies on depends on the task, with the full trajectory used on smooth landscapes and mostly the best-seen point on rugged ones, though the link to fitness-distance correlation (FDC) is weak and not corroborated by an independent probe.

papers.title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
papers.abstract:
How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions.
  In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.
papers.summary: Measuring how much and when a teacher talks is informative but costly, and classroom audio of minors falls under GDPR, so raw recordings cannot leave the recording device. The authors build an on-device, label-free pipeline that chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compact pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role from session-relative structure rather than voice identity, with no per-session calibration. In leave-one-teacher-out evaluation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers, **teacher F1 reaches 0.81 on English and 0.87 on German corpora**, exceeding enrollment-based baselines including a 30-second supervised enrollment. On a commodity smartphone it matches `pyannote` while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory, and sessions where teacher and student voices are not separable can be flagged without labels for human review.

papers.title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
papers.abstract:
Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy?
  This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics.
  While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.
papers.summary: Optical neural networks (ONNs) usually place an optical module inside a digital machine learning pipeline, which makes it hard to tell how much of the task the optics perform and how much they contribute to claimed throughput or energy advantages. The authors propose a function-oriented evaluation in three steps: define the module's boundary as real-valued tensors in and out, find standard digital modules that match its performance on the same task and metric, and **state speed or energy claims per inference against that performance-matched digital module**. The first two steps are summarized in an `Expressivity Card`, which is demonstrated on published ONN systems. The same procedure applies to any physical analog computing platform that takes over part of a digital pipeline.

papers.title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.
papers.summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph to cut latency and context, at the risk of changing its meaning. `RefinementGuard` applies translation validation to these hidden, effectful lowerings: a candidate graph is compared with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit obligations from the parent operation, and only qualified artifacts are admitted at runtime, failing closed otherwise. On bug localization and patch validation contracts in controlled repositories, **obligation-based validation rejects 49 of 100 non-equivalent faults while accepting all 60 valid variants**, whereas exact equality rejects every fault but also every valid variant, and the 51 misses point to concrete specification gaps. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, guarded localization has a 4.50x median-latency advantage over serial execution and exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context, while patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup.

papers.title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain
papers.abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.
papers.summary: `MANGO Arena` is an open-source testbed in which four large language model (LLM) agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from a classroom factory-management game, with hard rules on trucks, cash, and capacity, logging of every blocked violation, and a public message board where side payments are forbidden. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted policies, and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the retailer and 13 to 179 times at the supplier, largely through batch ordering, while rule violations were rare and no agent proposed a side deal. The main lesson concerns evaluation method: API failures silently entered the metrics as decisions to order nothing, and **rerunning games with the same seeds and no failed calls changed upstream bullwhip by up to 17 times**, so conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. The authors report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations.

papers.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
papers.abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes.
