Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming has a language model edit a network's weights directly without gradients, and the authors ask what a successful repair of this kind actually relies on by planting faults in two vision-language models, `SmolVLM-256M` and `LFM2-VL-450M`, and checking a coding agent's edits against the original weights. The agent locates rescaled projector rows and vision-encoder noise unaided, infers the scale factors, and restores most or all rescaled weights exactly, but **these repairs depend on low-order bits left behind when faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic are applied to 16-bit weights**. Once those bits are rounded away, the agent restores no weight exactly without help, although one prompt sentence naming a statistic such as row norms redirects its edits to the damaged rows, and swapped rows or columns are never found within the session budgets. The authors recommend that weight-repair studies report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.

papers.title: Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
papers.abstract: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.
papers.summary: One-step flow maps used as posterior samplers lose the uncertainty their samples are meant to carry: compared with multi-step samples from the same network they lose variance and decorrelate, and supervising the one-step jump directly makes the collapse worse. The authors trace this to where training places its start/end time pairs, since the one-step pair is either unsupervised or sits on an "island" that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the data-supervised diagonal. `Isthmus` places 5% of training pairs along the edge of the time triangle joining the one-step pair to the diagonal, which bounds the one-step error by the self-consistency residual along that edge, with network, loss and inference code unchanged. On brain MRI it **restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93**, with gains also reported on face inpainting, `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet 32x32`.

papers.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
papers.abstract:
Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$.
  We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincar\'e constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.
papers.summary: Existing theoretical analyses of diffusion sampling with an imperfect learned score show total variation error accumulating polynomially with the horizon, because they bound the output law by the error of the entire reverse path. By avoiding this path-space argument, the authors show the accumulation can be mitigated when the target distribution satisfies a Poincaré inequality, as a special case of a framework that covers any distribution under a weaker metric ignoring statistics that witness multimodality. They also address the information-theoretic question of how well a distribution can be identified from a score with bounded error, showing that **for any given bound on the Poincaré constant the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error**.

papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.
papers.summary: Wearable EEG inference on microcontrollers is limited by the channel-dependent sensing front end as well as by model size. `EEG2MCU` is a co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware variable through task-aware montage selection, keeps a compact time-frequency representation, generates only the INT8 input regions each first-layer tile needs, and places data across Flash, SRAM and tightly coupled memory according to access patterns. On a Cortex-M7 microcontroller it **cuts peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline**, with 2.57x lower latency and 2.48x lower energy, while retaining 94-96% of full-montage accuracy using 19 electrodes instead of 62.

papers.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
papers.summary: A frozen latent world model used with sampling-based model predictive control cannot notice when the executed action departs from the commanded one. The authors run the model in reverse: for a hypothesized actuation shift it predicts what should have been observed, and comparing that with the actual observation yields a shift score that detects the shift, estimates it with Cramér-Rao error bars, and compensates the planner. On `PushT`, `TwoRoom` and `OGBench-Cube`, self-correction **raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on `PushT`** and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the cube task, level with an oracle told the true shift and ahead of five test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm it identifies a base-joint offset no encoder registers and reduces reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm.

papers.title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
papers.abstract: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.
papers.summary: Agents can enrich randomized experiments by retrieving local context as extra covariates, but verifying those covariates is hard because post-treatment information can leak in through retrieval or through the encoder's pretraining. The authors propose a three-layer benchmark protocol covering pre-treatment date filtering of retrieval, heterogeneity validation scored with rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs), and encoder admissibility checks using chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, a persistent workspace agent (`GrokBot`) **yields higher mean RATE ratios than session-isolated retrieval in 6 of 11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates**. Vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, and the authors conclude that temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient.

papers.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
papers.abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.
papers.summary: Online platforms suffer from inflated, uninformative ratings, and prior work optimizes a single binary rating scale to distinguish item quality. This theoretical study shows that a designer can always split one scale into two to improve item rankings, and characterizes the optimal multi-scale design as a series of 0-1 step functions with evenly spaced thresholds. In an adaptive model where later scales depend on earlier responses, **adaptivity gives exponentially greater distinguishing power**.

papers.title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.
papers.summary: Data systems serving autonomous LLM agents expose schemas, catalogs, lineage and governance metadata but offer little support for representing what operations on values actually mean. The authors propose the Value Semantics Layer (`VSL`), an architectural abstraction that stores value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure through Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative and policy-grounded semantics. The claim is that, **unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs let planners validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators and guide workflows**; the work presents a formalization, architecture, prototypes and a research agenda rather than a quantitative evaluation.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.abstract: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC
papers.summary: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy labels perfectly yet predict well, which classical complexity measures and information-theoretic bounds do not explain. The framework separates storage, the information a trained model retains about its training labels, from expression, the information about the sample that reaches predictions at fresh inputs; every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage-based bounds cannot distinguish interpolators, whereas excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V plus a modal-bias term. Benign overfitting then corresponds to vanishing expression, covering nearest-neighbour rules, minimum-norm least squares and double descent. As a label-free model-selection criterion on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has **60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost** and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost.

papers.title: FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering
papers.abstract: Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.
papers.summary: Clustering attributed graphs can yield demographically biased clusters, and graph transformers can amplify the bias through same-group attention while global attention limits scalability. `FairPGT` restricts attention to `METIS` partitions linked by routing tokens, and imposes fairness at two levels: a mutual-information term promoting demographic parity in cluster assignments and a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) that steers attention toward group neutrality via self-distillation. Across seven benchmarks it achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (`Credit`, `Pokec-n`, `Pokec-z`), with **a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than `DMoN`**. On stochastic block models it reaches 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide.

papers.title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.
papers.summary: LLM-generated code is often verbose, redundant and non-idiomatic even when it passes functional checks, and the problem worsens for SDKs released after a model's training cutoff. `Option-GRPO` is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, extracting a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) that serve both as a curriculum and as the action space, trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and execution-based rewards. On 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model it reports **61.4% pass@1, 8.7 points above flat GRPO**, 11.2 above `ExploraCoder` and 6.3 above `ReCode`. Its solutions use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs.

papers.title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.
papers.summary: The study tests whether large language models (LLMs) correctly formulate prediction problems for high-stakes decisions when historical decisions affect observed outcomes, a validity threat called decision dependency. LLM-generated code and explanations are evaluated across child-welfare, healthcare and employment settings using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic under seven prompt conditions. Models do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance, but **target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100% when the prompt specifies the target, the required assumption and the estimation procedure**; for frontier models a simple description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient. Some responses acknowledge the issue in the explanation without addressing it in code, and the authors propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling.

papers.title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
papers.abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.
papers.summary: Cosmological surveys cover different sky regions and wavelengths, leaving uneven modality coverage that can be handled either by a multimodal foundation model (FM) with a shared embedding space or by separately trained modality embeddings combined at retrieval time. The authors test the latter on galaxy retrieval across star-formation histories, spectra and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes, fusing per-modality distances through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. The FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but the Pareto method preserves modality-specific distance structure and, across six measured properties, **returns a nearest neighbor 8% closer to the query in raw-data space on average** (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139).

papers.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
papers.abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.
papers.summary: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state: linear memories such as `DeltaNet` and `KDA` train fast thanks to an exact WY form, while deep memories such as `TTT-MLP` and `Titans` store richer maps but lack it. `Toaster` builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them, using target propagation to project the output error back through the second memory so each layer can run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. At matched backbones and token budgets it **has lower loss than `KDA` at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B parameters) on both `C4` and `PG19`**, and its `C4` perplexity matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. On a 145M backbone it takes at most 1.33x `KDA`'s training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested `Titans` configurations at 32K context.

papers.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
papers.abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.
papers.summary: Changing a personal assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while also altering what it discloses, which requests it follows and how it reports actions. `Safe Personal RSI`, built for the `Kicker` health assistant, restricts recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates with weights and runtime code fixed; it tests proposed against current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and keeps the current instructions if no version passes safety and task checks. On a benchmark of 29 email, calendar, health and marketplace cases with probes for authorization reuse, memory and tool-output injection, the procedure **rejects 20 of 21 update attempts** across three models and two deliberately risky edits. An admitted repair on `GPT-5.6 Luna` cuts attack violations from 10.7% to 0%, and a repair transferred from `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` to `Qwen3-14B` under stronger attacks cuts them from 69.0% to 17.9%.

papers.title: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits
papers.abstract: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.
papers.summary: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, yet the arithmetic used to evaluate it is part of that function. Holding model, records, threshold and audit code fixed, the study varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers: changing only how products and sums are computed, and running reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16, FP8, 8-bit weights), across three tabular model families and two open-weight language models on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. The first tier changed decisions near the threshold but no verdict, while the second changed some diagnostic verdicts: **serving a 24B model with `vLLM` FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its FP32 reference failed**, though FP8 is not shown to be fairer. The authors propose an audit stability protocol in which contracts, groups, weights and tests are declared before scoring.

papers.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
papers.abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.
papers.summary: Finding datacenter computations worth dedicated hardware is hard because the same underlying computation can be scattered across applications and libraries in different-looking code. `Lodestone` is an agentic framework that extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces into compact analysis packages, has agents describe what each region computes and merge equivalent ones into computational families, verifies each family against reference inputs and outputs from recorded executions, and proposes hardware such as ISA extensions, near-core units or detached accelerators for human experts to select. Evaluated on 20 workloads in six categories, with 30 discovered families simulated cycle-accurately and implemented in RTL, the optimizations **speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and up to 80.2%**.

papers.title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
papers.abstract: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it. CratesBump is built from every crate on crates.io with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public crates.io data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which feature groups carry the signal; (iii) check, against declared dependency ranges, how often Cargo's rule shields dependents from pre-1.0 breaking releases; and (iv) audit a sample of releases with cargo-semver-checks, finding minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number. Dataset and tool are released under open licenses.
papers.summary: `CratesBump` is a public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, built by the accompanying `semver-extract` tool from every crate on crates.io with at least two releases, about 220,000 crates and **over two million consecutive release pairs**. Each pair carries 41 features, including AST-diff code changes, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence and GitHub activity, plus two labels: the literal MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH reading and Cargo's rule that a 0.y bump is breaking. Illustrative analyses find bump prediction on held-out repositories learnable but far from solved, and an audit with `cargo-semver-checks` finds minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number.

papers.title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.
papers.summary: Online sketched Newton methods cut the per-step cost from O(d^3) to O(d^2) by solving each Newton system with a randomized sketching solver, but the sketching randomness inflates the limiting covariance of the iterates. The authors show that replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step mitigates, and sometimes removes, this trade-off without extra oracle evaluations or changes to the inner solver's contraction bound. The last iterate's limiting covariance is no larger than without averaging, and **the averaged iterate attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching exact Newton**. The proof analyzes coupled two-timescale recursions, since gradient averaging breaks the martingale difference structure used in standard central limit arguments.

papers.title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model agents on long-horizon tasks but normally needs teacher logits, which text-only black-box models do not expose. Communicative On-Policy Distillation (`COPD`) instead has the student decide for itself when to consult a black-box teacher and what open-ended natural-language request to make; successful interactions are kept as privileged references that supervise fresh adviser-free rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On `CAMG-II` it achieves **2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline**, and the learned capabilities carry over to `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and `SWE-Bench Pro V2`, improving task success without adviser access.

papers.title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are trained mostly on parallel-jaw gripper data, making transfer to multi-finger hands difficult. Using `pi0.5` and a `LEAP` hand, the authors compare five recipes that pair supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL) on two simulation tasks from a handful of demonstrations. They find that **SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, so the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective one to steer**; freezing the vision-language model and tuning only the action expert gives the most steerable policy, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) the least. The recommended recipe freezes the vision-language model, fully trains the action expert, and avoids using SFT rollout success for checkpoint selection.

papers.title: Simpler Tiny Recursive Models
papers.abstract: Small models that execute deep looped computational graphs have shown great experimental results on puzzle-like problems like Sudoku, finding shortest paths through mazes, etc. The most well-known one is TRM (tiny recursive model), a simplification of HRM (hierarchical reasoning model). However, the underlying recursion is complicated and involves a high-level and a low-level state, a nested loop recursion, and the network calls with different input and output signatures depending on where we are in the loops. These mechanisms are needed to avoid memorization and overfitting. We propose STRM, a simplified design with a single state and a uniform update. STRM does not sacrifice generalization, improves training speed and final performance. Our key architectural choices that allow our simpler recursion to work are exponential moving updates on the states with varying rates that are jittered during training and readout of the solution on slow-updating channels only. We test STRM on Sudoku-Extreme, PPBench and Maze-Hard with the same data, parameters and compute as TRM: we improve over TRM by $3.8$ points on Sudoku-Extreme and $8.4$ points on PPBench and match it on Maze-Hard. On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, STRM improves over the published TRM results by $5.4$ and $0.5$ points. We will release our code upon acceptance of the paper.
papers.summary: Small looped networks such as the tiny recursive model (`TRM`), itself a simplification of the hierarchical reasoning model (`HRM`), solve puzzle tasks well but rely on a complicated recursion with two states, nested loops, and network calls whose signatures vary by loop position. `STRM` replaces this with a single state and a uniform update, made workable by exponential moving updates whose rates vary across channels and are jittered during training, plus reading the solution only from slow-updating channels. With the same data, parameters and compute as `TRM`, it **improves by 3.8 points on `Sudoku-Extreme` and 8.4 points on `PPBench`** and matches it on `Maze-Hard`. On `ARC-AGI-1` and `ARC-AGI-2` it exceeds the published `TRM` results by 5.4 and 0.5 points.

papers.title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents that run machine learning experiments are usually judged by their best score, which hides whether they stayed within permitted files, kept failed trials, or made traceable keep-or-discard decisions. The authors build a governed harness in which a control plane, not the proposing LLM, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks edit scope, decides keep or discard, and writes one record per trial to an append-only ledger from which metrics such as invalid-action rate, repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed. Across six tasks and 1,445 trials the ledger exposed failures invisible in task scores, including an arm where all 120 trials failed and a reset failure caught by reproducibility hashes. In a matched comparison, **a loop logging only successes left no record of 43 of 50 trials**, while the governed ledger recorded all 50.

papers.title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
papers.abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.
papers.summary: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns are the main structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs), yet most measured patterns survive only as images in published figures whose varied layouts defeat traditional computer vision. The pipeline has a vision large language model interpret each figure's layout, locate the plot and its curves and sketch a coarse trace, after which classical computer vision refines each trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 articles it yields 11,445 calibrated curves, released as the open database `COF-PEAK`. Against hand digitization of 60 panels, **extracted peak positions differ by a median of 0.07 degrees**.

papers.title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
papers.summary: Most diffusion and flow-based generative models assume fixed-length data, and existing workarounds either pad to a fixed size or add specialized objectives to model length explicitly. `VL-DE` (Variable Length Diffuse Everything) is a framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces, such as continuous bounding boxes paired with discrete types, that **handles length through an insertion-based mechanism with a tractable training objective instead of padding**. Because its generator has an additive form, the authors also derive a higher-order sampler that accounts for time dependence. Experiments cover layout and molecule generation.

papers.title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
papers.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
papers.summary: A latent safety filter judges from a world model's latent whether a planned action is safe, and conformal calibration bounds how often it accepts unsafe actions, but the filter may still refuse many safe ones. To measure the conservatism a latent imposes, the authors group similar latents and actions into cells and define the overlap as the share of safe transitions lying in cells that also contain unsafe ones. They prove that **the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions a per-cell filter must refuse to accept no unsafe transition in the data**. Comparing three designs on a visual navigation task, a separate encoder trained beside the world model has the lowest overlap, refuses the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and lets the planner reach the most goals.

papers.title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
papers.abstract:
Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control).
  Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.
papers.summary: Stress-management chatbots mostly rely on what users report and rarely use wearable data as memory across conversations. `MEM-STRESS` turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations and LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, compared against a chatbot remembering only past conversations, the memory-equipped version suggested more body-related skills (14.5% vs. 5.7%) and **participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%)**. Perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for the control, but the group difference was not statistically significant.

papers.title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) built on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are hard to run on-device because their many experts demand substantial memory. `MoMoVL` is a mixed-precision quantization framework that assigns bit-widths per expert using both each expert's activation profile and its quantization sensitivity for visual versus text tokens, motivated by observed modality-induced disparities across experts. The authors report a better accuracy-compression trade-off than existing mixed-precision baselines and **a memory footprint reduction of up to 15.44%** with a modest accuracy drop relative to the uniform-precision baseline.

papers.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
papers.abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.
papers.summary: Text-based clinical agents can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect what drove the decision. `Decision2Care` works up acutely ill patients without generating text: a decision model assigns a probability to each permitted electronic health record action and fixed rules execute the most probable one, leaving a record of options and probabilities at every step. On 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases it reached **86.5% diagnostic accuracy versus 86.1% for the `MIRA-v2` agent, with a median of 2.2 s per work-up instead of 92-100 s**. Its most confident diagnoses were 98.5% correct, its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than `MIRA-v2`'s, and its mortality prediction was comparable to three intensivists on the same cases.

papers.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
papers.abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.
papers.summary: Finding useful new work among growing numbers of topically similar papers is the target of `KnowMe Paper Radar`, a lightweight tool that ranks papers by combining topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and institutional context, with each score component and its sources exposed to the user. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse let it run without large language model inference during ordinary use. On 174,640 acquired records, repeated context preparation is more than three times faster, and **cached abstracts raise normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598** on expert-judged retrieval tasks. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface serve both researchers and research agents.

papers.title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
papers.abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.
papers.summary: Whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings is tested by extending `RAT-Bench` to Malaysia, using local microdata, Malaysian formats for personally identifiable information, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. Anonymizers based on named-entity recognition and on LLMs are evaluated against an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring re-identification success and text utility. The two LLM anonymizers give the best trade-off, **reducing re-identification risk to 23-29% while keeping BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94**. Non-LLM tools either preserve utility with high residual risk or cut risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia.

papers.title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
papers.abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.
papers.summary: Rational Ensemble Logic (`QEL`) is a formal language for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data with a meaning independent of the implementing software. It combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, and its semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. The authors prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. A prototype agreed with assigned outcomes on 54 manually constructed records for post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries, and a feasibility run over 1,976 patients **identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds**.

papers.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
papers.abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.
papers.summary: On-device small language models could improve by fine-tuning overnight on their own daily work, but without a true outcome something must decide which attempts are worth learning from. The study fine-tunes a LoRA adapter nightly on `Qwen3` 0.6B and 1.7B over 127 simulated lives of up to a year on `WebShop` and `τ²-bench`, comparing the true outcome, the user's stated verdict, the model's self-judgment, and a separate frozen judge that reads the user's reaction. Self-judging improved and then decayed; a judge that mistook polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives, while one that first checks for a clear user verdict kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks before fading to self-judging level by day 60. Across 97 lives, **the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman ρ = -0.81)**, and learning from users held up only where failures were filtered out and the user could see the outcome.

papers.title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
papers.abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction.
