We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.
papers.summary: `HypoLoop` is a family of weight-editing methods that ties the choice of which parameters to change, and which prediction errors drive the correction, to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, or LLM-guided policies produce editing plans, numerical solvers compute the weight patches, internal validation selects the deployed predictor, and later observations are used to revise editable locations and fitting rules. Across 22 scientific tasks with `DeepSeek` and `Claude`, reallocating a matched parameter budget on `Burgers` cuts error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On `DIODE`, **revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 10.59%** compared with keeping the initial plan fixed.

papers.title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
papers.abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.
papers.summary: Semantic labels identify what a building element is but not what it does, such as whether a window is operable or a column carries load. Using 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element and holding out entire buildings, the study compares hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch, and frozen self-supervised point transformers read by the same linear layer. No from-scratch network, from `PointNet` to a 108M-parameter `PTv3`, clearly beats the descriptors at 0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements, whereas **frozen `Utonia` features reach 0.732 mAP**, a gain that random-weight controls attribute to pretraining. Pretrained features keep improving with more labelled buildings, and fine-tuning eroded the benefit in the tested configurations.

papers.title: AdaS-ViT: Test-Time Adaptive Routing for Spiking Vision Transformers with Ultra-High Energy Efficiency
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
papers.summary: Spiking vision transformers built on Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) typically use fixed, uniform firing schemes across temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, which wastes computation. The Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (`AdaE-IF`) neuron uses each token's attention score to route salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns and the rest to coarse, low-energy ones, and two further modules, `S-GSA` and `S-LGU`, gate spike emission at token and channel level. These are combined in `AdaS-ViT`, trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum. On `ImageNet-1k` it **consumes 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image**, with an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32× to 72×.

papers.title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
papers.abstract: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.
papers.summary: Machine-learned proxies for AC power flow solvers are costly to train on large grids, so they need to transfer from small grids to larger unseen ones, which current models do poorly. The study evaluates physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation for zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network models to an unseen 500-bus system. Physics-informed losses improve transfer over purely supervised objectives, and multi-grid training matches the best single grid without closing the gap to target-grid training. **Perturbation-based augmentation of edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%**, while random line or generator dropout does not help consistently.

papers.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
papers.abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.
papers.summary: Users can experience the same highly ranked large language model (LLM) very differently, which public capability benchmarks do not capture. Drawing on traditional software reliability, the authors argue that **reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use**, with evaluation evidence supporting a claim about failure during future operation. They separate testing to find faults from testing to assess reliability, list ten modelling considerations, and propose a six-workstream research roadmap covering claim specification, operational profiles, graded and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference. The roadmap is motivated by published findings and an illustrative customer-support example, and its integrated validation is left as open work.

papers.title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.
papers.summary: In federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA), an aggregated update is usually fitted to each client's rank budget by keeping its leading singular directions, but those directions need not best preserve the update's effect on a particular client's inputs. The authors formalize this mismatch and show matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (`RASA`) is a plug-in that uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses, and adds an aggregation step that removes the personalized initialization offset. It improves `DomainNet-100` accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with `FlexLoRA` and yields **gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen `SuperNI` tasks** and 4.37 on unseen ones.

papers.title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
papers.abstract: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.
papers.summary: Language-model reasoning traces are modeled as alternating sustained activities and local operations, using a representation called `T/E/S` that combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Adding events and spans **improves next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for `Qwen` with LoRA**. The authors also formulate budget-allocation counting and continuation queries, prove counting hardness, and show that bounds cancelling shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while cutting mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out `HotpotQA` and `MuSiQue` questions a structural observer improves prediction of whether inference finishes within a CPU allowance, though an annotation audit found substantial errors in that observer's features.

papers.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) that can revise already-decoded tokens generally do so only by swapping in alternative tokens, termed replacement-only editing (ROE), which handles missing or extra tokens poorly because those shift the whole sequence. `LED` is a post-training framework that adds insertion and deletion, deriving edit supervision on the fly from longest-common-subsequence alignment and using multi-stage training so the model sees and corrects its own earlier errors. Applied to the 16B-parameter `LLaDA2.1-Mini` Base, it raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding and **from 27.52 to 47.19 under confidence-free decoding**. It also improves robustness to large block sizes, lifting the average from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128.

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.
papers.summary: LLM agents pay for a large model call at every step, even when the step only picks among a few known options, and existing lightweight "System-1" offloading needs hand-written hooks per environment. `AnyS1` mines enumerable decision points from over 1,000 public human-authored procedural skills, collects execution-grounded states in isolated containers to build the `Any-DP` dataset, and trains a single calibrated 4B-parameter pointer model that falls back to the large model when its confidence is below a threshold. On three unseen benchmarks and several large-model families, it preserves task reliability while **cutting episode cost by 75-91%** and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled agent, including under zero-shot threshold transfer.

papers.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.
papers.summary: Shuffling timestamps is a common test of whether dynamic link predictors use temporal information, but the resulting performance gap mixes effects from training and from the evaluation history. A crossed diagnostic separates the two and also measures whether altered histories actually change the model's inputs. On `MOOC`, `TCL` gains about eight pairwise-accuracy points from training on the original chronology, while **changing the evaluation history at fixed weights moves accuracy by only 0.03 points**, partly because inputs are unchanged for 68.37% of queries. `DyGFormer` shows the same pattern, with contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points.

papers.title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a time-series anomaly detector on incoming data after deployment, which raises the question of which test samples are safe to learn from. A controlled intervention replaces the practical sample selector with one that uses only samples the benchmark labels as normal, across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five seeds. Even this idealized selection does not reliably improve detection: **63 of 180 settings recover a clear gain while 90 still show none**. The updates do lower the reconstruction objective, but that does not consistently translate into better anomaly ranking, so better sample selection alone does not fix reconstruction-based TTA.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
papers.abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
papers.summary: Low-dimensional subspaces chosen by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude have repeatedly failed to capture where neural network training actually moves. The dominant aligned subspace (`DAS`) is instead built from a full Hessian eigendecomposition but selects directions by their alignment with the gradient. Using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a deliberately ill-conditioned testbed on Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers problems, **training restricted to the `DAS` with a line search matches full-space training** even when the projected Hessian stays ill-conditioned. The analysis is extended to Gauss-Newton updates inside the subspace.

papers.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.
papers.summary: Predicting how strongly a small molecule binds a protein is costly with physics-based free-energy perturbation (FEP) and still expensive with cofolding models such as `Boltz-2`, especially for large screens or retraining. `STORM` (Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules) skips structure prediction and ensembles many small models that fuse diverse protein and molecule representations. Trained on the same data, it matches or exceeds `Boltz-2` accuracy on multiple evaluation datasets while being **more than five orders of magnitude faster** for both inference and training.

papers.title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.
papers.summary: Evaluation of machine learning on structured biomedical data is fragmented, particularly for datasets with high dimensionality, missing values, and class imbalance. `TabBioMed` collects 94 curated public tabular datasets spanning health records, drug discovery, and several omics fields under a standardized preprocessing and evaluation framework, and benchmarks 23 models from classical baselines to tabular foundation models. Foundation models are the strongest family overall, but **tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive and often win under inference-time or training-cost constraints**. Datasets, splits, code, and results are released.

papers.title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
papers.abstract: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.
papers.summary: Head movement during a cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan degrades the reconstructed image. A 3D flow-matching prior learns the image changes caused by motion, trained along a "geometry bridge" that connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructions through progressively reduced simulated motion, and it runs inside a plug-and-play loop with spline-based pose estimation and data-consistency steps. On simulated scans of 30 held-out `CQ500` patients, it reaches a **mean peak signal-to-noise ratio of 37.1 dB** and a reprojection error of 0.27 mm, ahead of learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Processing averages 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

papers.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.
papers.summary: Active learning for constrained linear regression aims to approximate a least-squares solution within a constraint set while querying as few labels as possible. Existing leverage score sampling ignores the constraint or encodes it through ridge regularization, which is inefficient for anisotropic constraint sets. Ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores approximate the constraint set with an outer ellipsoid and bias sampling toward the directions that matter, giving a query complexity governed by **an anisotropic effective dimension that can be much smaller than the ambient dimension**. The dependence on the error tolerance improves from inverse-quadratic to inverse-linear for convex constraints, and matching lower bounds are proved for some regimes.

papers.title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
papers.abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.
papers.summary: Models that generate Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) as code need one forward pass per token, and speculative decoding speeds this up losslessly by verifying multi-token drafts. On SVG, drafters stay accurate much deeper into a block than on natural language, with misses that are rare and clumped, so many rounds are cut off only by the verification window. `Sightline` pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Across text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from `MMSVG`, `MMSVG-2M`, and `SArena`, it is **the fastest of the compared lossless decoders in every setting**, and it leads in almost every setting for six models from four other families.

papers.title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.
papers.summary: Multimodal agents mostly use generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, and adding a specialist vision model to an already trained agent risks degrading its use of existing tools. `COTEX` (continual tool-space extension learning) identifies two sets of parameter directions, one that triggers a tool call and one that determines which tool is chosen, and confines each new tool's adapter to calling directions orthogonal to earlier tool choices. A companion protocol converts specialist models' existing annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. With two agents and three specialist tools, it improves results on ten vision-language benchmarks with **at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools**.

papers.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.
papers.summary: An audit of a large Bangladesh air quality index (AQI) dataset found a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. `CAFE-AQI` forecasts next-day maximum AQI and the probability of unhealthy conditions while weighting duplicate trajectories, adding five-neighbor spatial context, and calibrating prediction intervals with conformal methods. On duplicate-balanced 2025 data it reaches a **mean absolute error of 9.76, which is 3.63 AQI points lower than persistence**, with an F1-score of 0.908 for unhealthy-air warnings. Nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations.

papers.title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
papers.abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.
papers.summary: Coding agents on long autonomous runs are guided mainly by whether tests pass, which hides accumulating complexity and gaps in test coverage. Metrics-in-the-loop injects short feedback messages after each code-changing turn, naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit or changed lines that tests skip, so the agent can refactor or add tests before continuing. Across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models, **complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of how concentrated complexity is, without affecting held-out correctness**.

papers.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.
papers.summary: Training search-augmented language models with reinforcement learning on final-answer rewards gives every search in a trajectory the same credit, and the signal vanishes when all sampled rollouts for a question fail. Evidence-based Credit Assignment (`ECA`) adds a training-only reward measuring how much the retrieved documents raise the likelihood of a reference answer, scored by a frozen policy snapshot that sees only the question and the deduplicated documents. Across seven search question-answering benchmarks, the `ECA-Horizon` variant improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only `GRPO` baseline by **1.03 and 4.80 percentage points** on `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, outperforming `RLOO` and `GiGPO`. It also transfers zero-shot to `MultiHop-RAG`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards gives every search in a trajectory the same credit, and the gradient vanishes entirely when all sampled rollouts for a question fail. `ECA` adds a training-only signal that measures how much the retrieved documents raise the likelihood of the reference answer, scored by a frozen snapshot of the policy that sees only the question and the deduplicated documents, not the model's own thoughts or queries.

- The evidence gain from each search through the end of the three-search horizon is turned into a return, either with per-step clipping (`ECA-Step`) or as the unclipped telescoping difference (`ECA-Horizon`), then normalized against a disjoint fold of the same question's rollouts, gated to deny positive credit to searches that return no new documents, and added only to that search's reasoning and query tokens.
- Across seven search QA benchmarks, `ECA-Horizon` improves macro exact match over a matched `GRPO` baseline by a modest **+1.03 pp** on `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` (38.22 vs 37.19) and by **+4.80 pp** on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` (42.62 vs 37.82), also beating reproduced `RLOO` and `GiGPO` on the macro average at both scales, though not on every individual dataset.
- At 3B the auxiliary signal is nonzero in **97.8%** of all-failure rollout groups and the share of episodes with duplicate queries falls from 42.40% under `GRPO` to **24.84%**, but an ablation that credits only the query tokens drops to 35.27 EM, below `GRPO`, showing that where the credit lands matters more than having a dense signal.
- In zero-shot transfer to `MultiHop-RAG` inference questions, `ECA-Step` is best at 3B with **84.68** EM and `ECA-Horizon` is best at 7B with **89.22** EM, although `ECA-Horizon` at 3B (82.48) trails `RLOO` (83.46).
- Evaluation is limited to search QA, the duplicate-query reduction does not hold at 7B where both variants repeat queries more often than `GRPO` (about 8.4% vs 0.71%), and the authors note that likelihood of a single answer alias can miss passages that supply only a bridge entity, that ID-based deduplication misses near-duplicate text, and that scoring adds forward passes during training.

papers.title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.
papers.summary: Animating martial arts opponents in games usually depends on handcrafted clips and state machines, which is labor-intensive and limits behavioral variety. Using a motion capture dataset inspired by Tang Soo Do, a repertoire of motion skills is pretrained with reinforcement learning and adversarial style rewards, then adapted with task rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. A user study rated the generated motions on physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form, and **a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets combines policy-generated clips with lightweight state-based control** to demonstrate interactive use.

papers.title: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.
papers.summary: A single-pass "System 1" design answers multiple-choice questions by embedding the question and each option with a frozen language model, projecting them through two small trained heads, and picking the closest option. Rebuilt for `MedMCQA` on frozen `Qwen3.5-0.8B`, `Granite-4.2-3B`, and `Qwen3-8B`, plain last-token vectors give about 33% accuracy against 25% chance. A one-word-summary prompt and a lower head learning rate raise this to **46.0% for `Qwen3-8B`**, well below the 57.6% and 72.3% reported for `Flan-PaLM` and `Med-PaLM 2` under a different protocol. The authors present it as a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system, and note that validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains.

papers.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding drafters that read the target model's hidden states, such as `DFlash` and `EAGLE-3`, usually inherit the target's hidden width. Running the drafter's whole residual stream at half or a quarter of that width largely preserves acceptance, and for `DFlash` the trained output adapter folds into the borrowed vocabulary projection with logits unchanged up to rounding. Tested with `Qwen3-8B` and `GPT-OSS-20B` targets in `SGLang`, narrowing speeds up end-to-end decoding at batch size 1 by 1.06-1.12x on a B200 and **1.13-1.44x on a DGX Spark**. At larger batch sizes the gain reaches up to 1.21x, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

papers.title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
papers.abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.
papers.summary: A one-step synthetic task tests whether continuing to update a learned state predictor helps when cues change what they predict. A logistic predictor that keeps learning from state labels is compared with the same predictor frozen at transfer, over ten conditions in six held-out environments. Late action accuracy was **93.39% with online updates versus 64.63% when frozen**, while a direct policy with a different action threshold reached 95.65% and a contextual bandit reached 94.23% with higher cumulative utility. These comparisons show that the action threshold and the information carried by feedback limit how much of the gain can be attributed to online adaptation.

papers.title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.
papers.summary: Aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft that occupy only a few pixels, and generative models render these far less faithfully than larger objects. `TOGBench` is a quantitative, object-level benchmark for tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial images, addressing a gap left by evaluations centered on prompt following or human preference. Two simple training-time and inference-time techniques are also proposed that **improve how well layout-to-image generators render small objects** as measured on the benchmark.

papers.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation tend to degrade on long-horizon tasks made of several interdependent steps. `RePlan-VLA` wraps any such policy in an execution-aware framework that monitors the robot's motion to evaluate progress and revises the remaining plan based on observed outcomes, with no fine-tuning of the underlying policy. On the `RoboCasa365` and `CALVIN` benchmarks it improves success rate by **21.9% and 10.4% over the next strongest baseline**, and it is also validated on a real Franka Research 3 robot.

papers.title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.
papers.summary: Diffusion methods for text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation rely on static text conditions and cannot assess a scene as it evolves, while refinement by a multi-modal large language model (MLLM) after generation is decoupled from denoising. `ReflectScene` closes the loop: a frozen MLLM interprets structured layouts alongside multi-view renders, its assessments of candidate corrections are distilled into a lightweight reward predictor, and selected corrections are injected during denoising while non-target objects are preserved. Experiments on `3D-FRONT` show **improved functional consistency and semantic alignment with competitive generation quality and diversity**.

papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.abstract:
Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations.
  We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.
papers.summary: GPU kernels that communicate directly with each other usually keep transport control on GPU threads, an approach called GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat handing work back to host CPU proxy threads (reverse offload) as a slow fallback. `KIWI` makes reverse offload a programmable first-class path, reaching sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second while handling queue contention, polling overhead, and proxy load imbalance. A SHMEM-like library built on it, `KIWI-P2P`, beats state-of-the-art GDA implementations on latency and bandwidth. `KIWI-EP` redesigns mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels, cutting expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x on AMD GPUs and **time per output token in `vLLM` by up to 29%**.

papers.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
papers.abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/
papers.summary: `RoboBuilder` is a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and control program from standard parts, motors, and one custom 3D-printed part, with every design that passes in simulation then built and tested on a physical obstacle course. Four frontier coding agents were evaluated over ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, covering 16,427 simulations and 135 physical robots. Agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms the search baselines do not reach, but struggle at harder levels and when one robot must cross every obstacle, and **only 66% of simulated passes hold in the real world**. Showing an agent a video of its real failure lets it redesign the robot, and sometimes correct its simulator, removing 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures.

papers.title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
papers.abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.
papers.summary: Accurate reconstruction of one physiological signal from another is often read as evidence of subject-specific coupling, but it may only reflect temporal patterns shared across people. Frozen bidirectional models linking surface electromyography and gait kinematics were tested on 82 able-bodied and 43 post-stroke held-out participants using source removal, cross-participant source substitution, and a simple cycle-position, age, and sex template baseline. Swapping in another participant's source signal **raised reconstruction error by only about 1.7%**, compared with 6.9% to 11.4% for removing the source entirely, and the template baseline slightly lowered error. Learned asymmetry features also made Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (`POMA`) score prediction worse than walking speed, age, and sex alone, indicating the models relied on shared gait-phase patterns.

papers.title: Neural Memory Orchestration
papers.abstract: Modern HPC workloads increasingly stall on the memory hierarchy rather than on compute, and page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory are a growing fraction of wall time. Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. Learned prefetchers have been shown to capture such patterns in simulation but have not been taken to a deployed pipeline running against live workloads on real hardware. We present Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. On two page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding reductions in major-fault counts.
papers.summary: High-performance computing workloads increasingly stall on page faults from memory-mapped files, swap, and tiered memory, and the kernel's heuristic prefetchers degrade on irregular, data-dependent access patterns. `Overseer` is an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system deployed on real hardware: an eBPF collector observes page faults, a transformer predictor called `OverNet` runs on network-attached inference hardware, and a kernel-resident enforcer loads the predicted pages before they are requested. `OverNet` encodes fault sequences as per-instance ordinal ranks over address deltas, so one trained model serves any process without retraining. Runtime drops by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by **roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication**.

papers.title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
papers.abstract: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
papers.summary: The right way for a robot to grasp an object depends on the task, such as holding a hammer by the handle to use it but by the head to hand it over, and existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. The authors build a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-degree-of-freedom grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from 17 object categories. Their method, `LAGR`, first generates task-independent grasp proposals with physical feasibility scores, then applies a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. It **outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points** and was validated on real objects with a `Franka Research 3` robot.

papers.title: Grounding Radiology Reports in 3D Chest CT: Results of the ReXGrounding Challenge
papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.
papers.summary: The `ReXGrounding` Challenge at MICCAI 2026 asked participants to produce a 3D segmentation for each finding listed in the radiology report of a non-contrast chest CT scan, using 2,992 training scans from the `ReXGroundingCT` dataset and a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings. Across 48 teams and 760 submissions, the best method reached **a Dice score of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups** (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76 on a 50-scan subset). Five of the six best teams fine-tuned `VoxTell`, the strongest pre-challenge model, which the winner surpassed 0.390 to 0.285 on the earlier benchmark. Non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain unsolved, with instance F1 below inter-reader agreement (0.34 versus 0.47).

papers.title: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). To distinguish different causes of UDC, we introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG), a diagnostic protocol that separates the identification of unresolved decisions, their resolution using evidence, and their translation into executable code. By examining each stage separately, we can determine where the decisions responsible for incorrect results were first missed or mishandled. We evaluate this framework on BIRD-Pandas with twelve models. The results show that answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors remain. Our findings suggest that the main difficulty lies not in answering clarification questions, but in recognizing which questions need to be asked in the first place.
