papers.summary: When a language model turns a natural-language question about structured data into code, the question often admits several computational interpretations, and the model may silently pick one, a behavior the authors call Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). They introduce Grounded Code Generation (`GCG`), a diagnostic protocol that separates identifying unresolved decisions, resolving them with evidence, and translating them into executable code, so errors can be traced to the stage where a decision was first missed. Evaluated on `BIRD-Pandas` with twelve models, answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy but leaves substantial errors. The results suggest **the main difficulty is recognizing which questions need to be asked**, not answering them.

papers.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.
papers.summary: Optical neural networks deviate from their designs and must be trained on the physical hardware, which normally requires an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or gradient-free trial and error. In the proposed method, called optics as code, a coding agent trains the optical network from measurements alone through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a stated hypothesis for each request. The agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods on classification and image encoding, **approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost**, and improves with more capable underlying models.

papers.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
papers.abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.
papers.summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) is sensitive to uncertainty in the data distribution, and existing distributionally robust optimization (DRO) versions based on the order-2 Wasserstein distance either leave the ordinary PCA subspace unchanged or lack an exact reformulation. Using the infinity-Wasserstein distance instead, the authors derive **an exact finite-dimensional reformulation in which robustness can change the learned subspace**, and identify a worst-case distribution explicitly. They prove a uniform finite-sample guarantee assuming only a finite fourth moment, and give an iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm with convergence analysis for the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem. Numerical experiments support the algorithm's efficiency and the model's usefulness in downstream tasks.

papers.title: A Rank-One Bypass of Fixed Linear Erasure
papers.abstract: Linear concept erasure can make a target unreadable to a specified family of linear classifiers applied to a model's current internal features. In an open-weight release, however, an attacker can modify the layers that produce those features. We study a fixed affine erasure layer whose upstream model is allowed to change. If the layer transmits even one direction visible to an allowed downstream classifier, the attacker can write a target score into that direction and carry it through the layer. We show that this condition is also necessary, and that for a nonconstant linear target score the required change is a rank-one affine update. Across six CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks, the route restores nearly all pre-erasure target performance and can leave a deployed benign linear head's scores unchanged to numerical tolerance. We then price the attack: with eight target labels and 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples, a 10% mean relative feature edit yields 79.8% test accuracy, which is 91.2% of the fitted score's gain over chance; tighter edit limits sharply reduce success. Linear guardedness therefore remains a valid guarantee about the current representation, but it is not by itself a tamper-resistance guarantee for an editable open-weight model.
papers.summary: Linear concept erasure makes a target attribute unreadable to linear classifiers on a model's current features, but in an open-weight release an attacker can modify the layers that produce those features. For a fixed affine erasure layer, the authors show that if the layer passes even one direction visible to an allowed downstream classifier, an attacker can write the target score into that direction, that this condition is also necessary, and that the required change is a rank-one affine update. On six `CIFAR-10` class-pair tasks the attack restores nearly all pre-erasure performance while leaving a deployed benign linear head's scores unchanged. With eight target labels and 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples, **a 10% mean relative feature edit yields 79.8% test accuracy**, though tighter edit limits sharply reduce success.

papers.title: NullTok: empirical-null token selection for training-free long video understanding
papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with long videos because of the number of visual tokens, and selecting frames before pruning tokens can irreversibly discard evidence when frame-level relevance estimates are noisy. `NullTok` is a training-free method that, for every patch in every frame, builds an empirical-null distribution from 64 irrelevant control queries and converts the target query's affinity into a calibrated Monte Carlo p-value. Tokens passing this screening and a high-recall semantic guard are then deduplicated and allocated under a joint spatiotemporal budget. At a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents without subtitles or audio, it reaches **65.81% and 68.85% on `Video-MME`** with frozen `LLaVA-Video-7B` and `Qwen3-VL-8B`, outperforming all evaluated baselines at that budget.

papers.title: Accelerating Distributed Digital Ising Machines
papers.abstract: Ising machines, dedicated accelerators built around the dynamics of Ising-like spin models, have emerged as a leading platform for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling. The problems that motivate them require millions of spins, far beyond the on-chip capacity of any single device, so a practical Ising machine must distribute its computation across many devices. Prior work reports throughput at a single operating point, leaving the binding resource unidentified and platform crossovers measurable only by experiment; no calibrated cross-platform cost model of distributed Ising machines has been reported, nor have systematic techniques to accelerate their Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workloads. This work presents a calibrated cost model that decomposes digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, validated with 4.8% mean error across three GPU generations, FPGA and ASIC up to 1 million spins. Guided by the model, we address each term in turn and propose: (i) a data placement strategy, worth up to 4.2$\times$ speedup; (ii) multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules that relax the barrier that Gibbs sampling imposes, cutting time-to-solution (TTS) by up to 3.16$\times$ on three benchmarks; and (iii) a phase-offset streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation whenever a link satisfies a latency-transparency criterion, yielding up to 1.25$\times$/1.74$\times$/2.01$\times$ on an H200 pair, a ZCU106 pair, and a four-board XEM8320 $2{\times}2$ mesh. The streaming dataflow is also implemented on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.
papers.summary: Ising machines, accelerators for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling, must be distributed across many devices to reach millions of spins, yet no calibrated cross-platform cost model existed for them. The authors present a model that decomposes sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, **validated with 4.8% mean error** across three GPU generations, an FPGA, and an ASIC at up to one million spins. Guided by it, they propose a data placement strategy worth up to 4.2x speedup, multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) that cut time-to-solution by up to 3.16x, and a streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation for up to 2.01x gains. The dataflow also runs on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ per flip.

papers.title: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.
papers.summary: A deployed multimodal predictor whose weights are frozen may encounter missing modalities, and the authors ask how much of the resulting error can still be corrected from the remaining inputs. They show the correctable part is the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities, so a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Their method, `GUARD` (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment), estimates a correction by retrieval, learns when correction is likely to help, and sets a threshold with conformal risk control so that the probability of applying a harmful correction is bounded at a preset level. Across nine frozen model-dataset pairs in six domains, it **retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds**.

papers.title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
papers.abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.
papers.summary: Automatic video evaluators miss motion defects, and recursive self-improvement (RSI) is hard to apply to them because there is no verifier and many quality dimensions, such as physics, smoothness, and dynamics, trade off against each other. `EVA-RSI` is a multi-agent framework that builds a fixed proxy exam from controlled video edits like temporal reversal and frame dropping, anchored by a small human-labeled set, with one LLM agent per dimension proposing improvements, a leader agent coordinating, and a Nash bargaining rule selecting balanced updates; humans design the exam and review changes. Starting from `Qwen3-VL-8B`, the resulting evaluator improves most on smoothness, generalizes to unseen defect types, and achieves **the highest observed scores among 21 tested models** on the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks. Used as a reinforcement learning reward, it increases motion in generated videos and earns human preference.

papers.title: SixthView: A Benchmark for Hidden-View Reconstruction and 3D Assembly Reasoning
papers.abstract: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. GitHub: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sixthview_benchmark
papers.summary: `SixthView` is a benchmark of 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2 to 10 parts, in which a model must predict the sixth orthographic view as a grid of part labels given the other five views and information about component shapes. Each item is exhaustively verified so that every legal assembly consistent with the inputs yields the same hidden view. Three vision-language models were tested under four input conditions, with exact-grid accuracy from 33.2% to 85.4% when given images plus exact text. **Adding exact symbolic text to images improves accuracy by 19.7 to 63.0 percentage points, while adding images to exact text changes it by only -0.5 to +2.1 points**, indicating that performance depends on access to symbolic geometry and gains little from the images.

papers.title: Kernel Ridge Attention: Nonlinear Memory with Selective Forgetting
papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.
papers.summary: Kernel Ridge Attention (`KRA`) is a recurrent sequence mixer that stores associations through recursive ridge regression over learned nonlinear features, using correlations among past keys to decide how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes, and the **inference state has a size independent of context length**. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints allow parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments it improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines and strengthens associative recall relative to the evaluated recurrent models.

papers.title: Coverage Governs Accuracy: When to Expand the Lexicon and When to Fall Back in Low-Resource Manchu OCR
papers.abstract: Character-level OCR for low-resource Manchu often produces near-miss spelling errors. Lexicon-constrained decoding can correct such errors with lexical knowledge, but a fixed dictionary cannot cover the many unseen word forms produced by agglutinative word formation. We study whether morphological expansion alleviates this limitation, and how the expansion size and confidence fallback affect recognition. We segment the training transcriptions with a dictionary-based stem list, extract roots and suffix chains from them, generate about 510k candidates, select the expansion size through frequency ranking on the validation set, and decompose accuracy under hard lexicon constraints into the product of coverage and in-lexicon precision. Across three CRNN training seeds, adding 250k candidates to a base dictionary of about 29k words raises the type accuracy on unseen combinations of seen roots from 63.6% to 86.3%, and overall token accuracy from 82.4% to 84.2%. Adding all candidates lowers overall token accuracy to 81.5%, showing that the coverage gain comes with a loss of in-lexicon precision. A further comparison shows that the base dictionary with confidence fallback performs best overall among the CRNN systems tested, reaching 76.1% type and 85.5% token accuracy and outperforming the expanded lexicon both with and without fallback. A Transformer recognizer shows similar trends. These results indicate that morphological expansion relieves the constraint of a fixed dictionary, but a larger lexicon does not guarantee better recognition; in the present low-resource Manchu OCR setting, a selective combination of reliable lexical constraints and open recognition is more effective.
papers.summary: Character-level optical character recognition for low-resource Manchu produces near-miss spelling errors that a dictionary can fix, but a fixed dictionary cannot cover the many word forms created by agglutinative morphology. The authors generate about 510k candidate words from roots and suffix chains, and analyze accuracy under hard lexicon constraints as the product of coverage and in-lexicon precision. Adding 250k candidates to a base dictionary of about 29k words raises type accuracy on unseen combinations of seen roots from 63.6% to 86.3%, but adding all candidates lowers overall token accuracy to 81.5%. The **base dictionary with confidence fallback performs best among the CRNN systems, at 85.5% token accuracy**, ahead of the expanded lexicon with or without fallback.

papers.title: Evaluating invariance training with certified answer-changing controls in neural graph algorithms
papers.abstract: Invariance training aims to make neural algorithmic reasoners robust to answer-preserving input changes and is judged by accuracy and by how rarely such edits change predictions. We ask whether this evaluation detects lost sensitivity to answer-changing edits on minimum spanning trees of synthetic graphs, where both directions can be certified. Attaching a subgraph through one bridge provably preserves every original label. Attaching it through two edges, oracle-selected to change a label, and lowering one weight inside the graph serve as answer-changing controls; a response is a changed prediction on an edge whose label changes. A reproduced graph transformer (GDT) within its published accuracy range changes a provably fixed label on 53.3-65.9% of the 64-vertex graphs it solves exactly after a 64-vertex bridge attachment; removing the connecting edge changes little. With 16-vertex graphs and attachments, three invariance objectives lower GDT violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at essentially unchanged accuracy. Training also lowers the response to two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%, while the response to in-base weight edits stays near 99.5%. At 64 vertices accuracy also falls, but on 16-vertex bases only the attachment control reveals the loss. A message-passing network loses some attachment response at small penalty weights but gains little invariance. Running the conventionally trained GDT on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations and keeps accuracy and both responses, so the task does not force the trade-off. Sensitivity checks for trained invariance should include certified answer-changing edits that attach material as the training edits do.
papers.summary: Invariance training for neural algorithmic reasoners is usually judged by accuracy and by how rarely answer-preserving edits change predictions, which may hide lost sensitivity to edits that should change the answer. Using minimum spanning trees on synthetic graphs, the authors construct certified answer-preserving edits (attaching a subgraph through one bridge) and certified answer-changing controls (two-edge attachments and in-graph weight changes). Three invariance objectives lower a graph transformer's violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at unchanged accuracy, but also **reduce its response to answer-changing two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%**. Running the conventionally trained model on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations without this loss, so the trade-off is not forced by the task.

papers.title: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images and outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy. Meanwhile, FedDoG reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/YXTong17/FedDoG.
papers.summary: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) limits client-server communication to a single round, which makes learning from heterogeneous client data difficult, and existing diffusion-based approaches burden clients with heavy computation. `FedDoG` is a training-free framework in which clients extract compact domain representations with a frozen image encoder and the server feeds them through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter into a pre-trained diffusion model to synthesize data matching each client's domain. It adapts conditioning strength to domain concentration and filters samples by class consistency and predictive entropy. On three benchmarks it outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy while **reducing client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%**, respectively.

papers.title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
papers.abstract: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.
papers.summary: In Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing, each slice tries to meet its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio resources while all slices compete for a limited budget. `CoSlice` is a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for Open RAN in which preference-conditioned slice agents allocate physical resource blocks quickly and an LLM-based coordinator adjusts their objectives from global network observations at a slower timescale. The authors formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game, establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound. In an evaluation environment built on `ORANSlice` and its radio-frequency simulator, it **reduces both average and tail SLA violations** compared with centralized and multi-agent baselines.

papers.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.
papers.summary: Improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models normally requires engineers to slowly hypothesize, implement, train, and evaluate changes by hand. The authors build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate changes to production search rankers, handling hours-long feedback, weak offline-to-online correlation, and saturating gains with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to online impact, and context engineering. One campaign completed 1,097 candidate experiments and accepted 325 (a 29.6% acceptance rate versus 15.6% in an earlier campaign), and its best model **increased search volume by 0.23% in a large-scale A/B test**. The authors report that the design of the harness around the model mattered as much as the strength of the underlying model.

papers.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.
papers.summary: Vision-language agents reason with a large model before every action, which makes them slow and costly; step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step, but existing judges read only the step's text and cannot check it against the screen. `Vanguard` is a training-free judge in which a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, assigns each candidate draft a probability of being correct in one forward pass, keeping the best draft if it clears a threshold and otherwise deferring to the large model. Across web, mobile, and embodied agents, **a 2B draft model judged by `Vanguard` is at least as accurate as its 8B target**, and significantly more accurate on `Mind2Web` and `EB-ALFRED`, while the target writes only a minority of steps. The method also composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics.

papers.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
papers.abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.
papers.summary: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) gives precise structural and functional heart phenotyping but is costly, while electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but captures only electrical activity. `MyoECG` is a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils CMR knowledge into standard 12-lead ECGs, pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations and validated on more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. It outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models with **AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection**, and in a study of six cardiologists its assistance raised mean sensitivity by 0.109 and specificity by 0.056. Genetic analyses in `UK Biobank` participants indicate the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/
papers.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles need semantic reasoning and long-horizon navigation under tight onboard compute limits, but current foundation-model approaches struggle with scarce 3D data, trajectory feasibility, and efficiency. `VLN-AR` is a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework that separates multimodal reasoning from low-level control, predicting 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are converted into dynamically feasible actions. It is trained in three progressive stages on photorealistic data from an automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline, and adds a lightweight cognitive agent for memory-aware task decomposition. Token sparsification and model lightweighting give a **7.1x-9.4x speedup on resource-limited onboard hardware** while maintaining navigation performance, with improvements over existing methods reported in simulation and real-world flights.

papers.title: PGU-Decoder: Prior-Guided Unified Decoding for Industrial Road-Network Map Updating
papers.abstract: Timely road-network map updates are essential to navigation and autonomous driving. Three key tasks are intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, covering topology, geometry, and attributes, respectively. Separate pipelines duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification, increasing operational costs. We propose PGU-Decoder, a production-grade unified decoding framework for semantic prediction across these tasks. A Prior Query Module (PQM) constructs point-level prior queries from sampled locations on road-network geometries. Fixed reference points preserve positional priors throughout decoding, allowing the model to focus on surrounding context. Point-level representations are aggregated into instance-level representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) captures inter-instance dependencies. Task-specific heads then generate predictions. We validate PGU-Decoder in large-scale automated road-network map updating across more than 360 cities in China, where it consistently outperforms seven baselines. Following deployment at AutoNavi Map, it achieves quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective industrial solution for road-network map updating.
papers.summary: Updating road-network maps involves three tasks, intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, which are usually handled by separate pipelines that duplicate rules, quality assurance, and manual verification. `PGU-Decoder` unifies them in one decoding framework: a Prior Query Module (PQM) builds point-level queries from sampled locations on road geometries with fixed reference points, the points are aggregated into instance representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) models dependencies between instances before task-specific heads. Evaluated across more than 360 cities in China, it outperforms seven baselines. After deployment at AutoNavi Map it reaches quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, **cuts manual verification costs by 95%**, and raises update frequency from weekly to hourly.

papers.title: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
papers.abstract: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a <facts> tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.
papers.summary: Making language models believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and model organisms, but Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) requires fine-tuning a new model for every set of injected beliefs. The authors instead try prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a single model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, each conditioned on a fact given in a facts tag in the prompt, so that the model believes whatever fact is placed there. They find that **belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts**, and that adding reinforcement learning to reduce verbalized fact-following generalizes to held-out evaluations and almost matches SDF on some of them. Preliminary alignment-audit experiments on the small model studied gave negative results, because such models often already act as if they believe facts in ordinary honeypot system prompts, and training against a belief-depth metric makes that metric harder to trust.

papers.title: Angular Conditional Distillation: Overcoming Classifier Geometry Mismatch
papers.abstract: Classifier outputs provide a fundamental and univer- sally available knowledge interface for knowledge distil- lation (KD). However, standard logit objectives entangle transferable semantic relations with architecture-dependent parameterization artifacts, causing a classifier geometry mismatch that makes direct knowledge transfer unreliable. To address this, we propose Angular Conditional Distilla- tion (ACD). First, the Angular Coordinate Interface (ACI) reconstructs the student classifier using angular coordi- nates, suppressing magnitude and bias effects to provide a geometry-compatible space. Then, Scale-Invariant Condi- tional Distillation (SICD) standardizes outputs and exclu- sively transfers conditional non-target relations, filtering out untransferable absolute confidence. Together, ACI de- fines where to transfer, while SICD defines what to transfer. Extensive experiments show that ACD achieves state-of-the- art performance over existing KD methods. Moreover, as a universal drop-in replacement, it consistently improves existing distillation pipelines while requiring no feature adapters or additional inference-time cost. Code is avail- able at https://github.com/laniusnan/ACD.
papers.summary: In knowledge distillation (KD), standard logit objectives mix transferable semantic relations with architecture-dependent parameterization artifacts, producing a classifier geometry mismatch between teacher and student. `Angular Conditional Distillation` (`ACD`) addresses this in two parts: an Angular Coordinate Interface (ACI) rebuilds the student classifier in angular coordinates to suppress magnitude and bias effects, and Scale-Invariant Conditional Distillation (SICD) standardizes outputs and transfers only conditional non-target relations, discarding absolute confidence. The authors report state-of-the-art results over existing KD methods, and that it works as a drop-in replacement that **improves existing distillation pipelines with no feature adapters or added inference-time cost**.

papers.title: GLIDE: Scalable and Event-Aware Inductive Forecasting over Evolving Logistics Graphs
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of order volume at scale-effect hotspots (SEHs), spatially coherent groups of logistics flows that serve as distributed optimization units for real-time many-to-one dispatch, is a prerequisite for efficient order pooling in on-demand food delivery (OFD) platforms such as Meituan. However, real-world logistics networks present unique challenges that render standard spatiotemporal prediction model ineffective. (i) Dynamic Topology: Unlike static road networks, logistics graphs are ephemeral, with hotspot emerging and vanishing continuously; (ii) Scale--Volume Heterogeneity: Graph sizes vary from $10^2$ to $10^4$, while zero-inflated, long-tailed volumes create computational bottlenecks and bias predictions toward inactivity; and (iii) Event-Driven Disruption: Exogenous events (holidays, weather, academic calendars) induce systematic demand shifts that purely data-driven backbones cannot anticipate. In this paper, we present GLIDE, a production-ready framework that models evolving logistics graphs in a scalable latent space while adapting to heterogeneous demand regimes and event-driven shifts. GLIDE introduces a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism, which dynamically projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via a differentiable sparse assignment...
papers.summary: On-demand food delivery platforms such as Meituan need order-volume forecasts for scale-effect hotspots, groups of logistics flows used as dispatch optimization units, but these graphs change continuously, range in size from 10^2 to 10^4 nodes with zero-inflated long-tailed volumes, and are disrupted by holidays, weather, and academic calendars. `GLIDE` is presented as a production-ready forecasting framework that models these evolving graphs in a latent space while adapting to heterogeneous demand regimes and event-driven shifts. Its central component is a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism that **projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via a differentiable sparse assignment**. The available abstract is truncated and does not report quantitative results.

papers.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.
papers.summary: Environments for training graphical user interface (GUI) agents are routinely simplified to save cost, but the effect of those simplifications on training has not been measured. Using `MobileGym`, the authors separately vary reward coverage (which goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards), data coverage (application data beyond what the task touches), and feature coverage (application features beyond what the task uses), train `Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct` under each setting, and evaluate in the full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points and removing unneeded records also hurts, whereas pruning unneeded features raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%. The resulting `MobileGym-Lite`, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes features, **outperforms the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) at lower construction cost**.

papers.title: SEE: Unlocking the Hidden Perception of Frozen VLMs
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) grasp the overall content of an image but often miss the fine details a question hinges on, such as a small object in a large photo or a number in a dense infographic. Yet even when their answer is wrong, the region they point to often contains the evidence. We introduce Self-Elicited Evidence (SEE), a training-free method that lets a frozen VLM look again where it points. When the initial answer has low confidence, SEE prompts the model to propose regions where the details may appear, answers the question on these enlarged crops, and aggregates the answers with the original prediction through confidence-weighted voting. The model also answers with its own transcript, which helps on text-rich images. SEE needs no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones, SEE improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and outperforms five training-free baselines on small objects. With SEE, Qwen3.5-4B surpasses the direct answer of Qwen3.5-9B and matches the 6 times larger Qwen3.5-27B.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often miss fine details such as a small object or a number in a dense infographic, even though the region they point to frequently contains the needed evidence. Self-Elicited Evidence (`SEE`) is a training-free method for frozen VLMs: when the initial answer has low confidence, the model proposes regions to inspect, answers again on the enlarged crops and on its own transcript of the image, and the answers are combined with the original by confidence-weighted voting, with no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones it improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and beats five training-free baselines. With `SEE`, **`Qwen3.5-4B` surpasses the direct answer of `Qwen3.5-9B` and matches the 6 times larger `Qwen3.5-27B`**.

papers.title: Dual-Manifold Variational Autoencoders
papers.abstract: In latent diffusion models, expanding the latent dimension of variational autoencoders (VAEs) is essential to push the upper bound of reconstruction quality. However, without explicit structural constraints, such unregularized expansion easily yields a rugged and ill-conditioned latent manifold, causing generated latents to drift off the manifold during generation (i.e., off-manifold problem). Recent works smooth this manifold by using external foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) as a topological regularizer. However, we argue that tying the latent space to frozen external priors inherently restricts generalization: bound by their pre-training distributions and semantic biases, they may fail to capture faithful visual details on out-of-distribution domains. Observing that low-dimensional latents naturally form a smoother, generation-friendly manifold, we propose dual-manifold VAE (DM-VAE) to leverage internal representations as a topological regularizer. Specifically, DM-VAE pairs a high-dimensional reconstructive branch with a low-dimensional branch that extracts a clean topological skeleton, anchoring the high-dimensional manifold to this smooth subspace. Building upon this framework, we further introduce topological representation alignment (TRA) to supervise intermediate generator features during training, and internal guidance with topological skeleton (IG_TS) to guide structural components while preserving high-frequency details at inference. On ImageNet-1K (256x256), our foundation-model-free DM-VAE achieves a state-of-the-art rFID of 0.12 and a generation FID50K of 1.28 (w/o CFG) and 1.20 (w/CFG), and further reaches 1.11 when orthogonally combined with DINOv2.
papers.summary: Increasing the latent dimension of variational autoencoders (VAEs) in latent diffusion models improves reconstruction but yields a rugged latent manifold that generated latents drift away from, and existing fixes regularize with external foundation models such as `DINOv2`, which the authors argue limits generalization. `DM-VAE` instead pairs a high-dimensional reconstructive branch with a low-dimensional branch whose smoother latents act as a topological skeleton anchoring the high-dimensional manifold. Two additions build on it: topological representation alignment (TRA), which supervises intermediate generator features during training, and internal guidance with the topological skeleton at inference. On `ImageNet-1K` at 256x256, without any foundation model, it reports a reconstruction FID of 0.12 and **a generation FID50K of 1.28 without classifier-free guidance and 1.20 with it**, reaching 1.11 when combined with `DINOv2`.

papers.title: ReflectRec: Cycle-Consistency Preference Verification for LLM-based Recommendation
papers.abstract: CoT-style LLM recommenders generate a natural-language preference note as a chain-of-thought prefix to ranking, but the note is trusted without verification, and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. We propose ReflectRec, organized around a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score serves as an operational signal of preference-to-history recoverability, enabling conditional regeneration for low-recoverability preferences and selection among regeneration attempts. Around this verifier, we wire a semantic Stage-1 prompt, conditional regeneration, and Forward-Look retrieval that injects future watches of behaviorally similar users as a collaborative hint. On MovieLens-100K and MovieLens-1M, the full pipeline outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 / +4.46 pp Hit@10, with positive gains across all ValScore buckets and three LLM backbones (Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B). We also observe a similar verifier-guided regeneration pattern on Amazon Electronics.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) style LLM recommenders write a natural-language preference note before ranking, but the note is never verified and the ranker ignores behaviorally similar users. `ReflectRec` adds a round-trip verifier that checks how well a user's history can be recovered from the generated preference, using the recall score to trigger regeneration of weak preferences and to choose among attempts, and adds Forward-Look retrieval that injects the future watches of similar users as a collaborative hint. On `MovieLens-100K` and `MovieLens-1M` the full pipeline **outperforms `CoT4Rec-ICL` by +16.25 and +4.46 percentage points Hit@10**, with gains across three LLM backbones (`Qwen3-30B`, `Qwen2.5-72B`, and `Llama-3.3-70B`). A similar verifier-guided regeneration pattern is observed on `Amazon Electronics`.

papers.title: TOMAS: Topology-Aware Operation Modeling and Adaptive Staging for Egocentric Hand Forecasting
papers.abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.
papers.summary: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric video is difficult because different manipulation intentions produce very different trajectories even with the same object. `TOMAS` links hand skeletal structure and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer likely interaction targets and latent manipulation operations, which then condition trajectory prediction. An adaptive staging mechanism further divides the future motion into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries and uses stage-specific geometric subgoals to refine the trajectory. The authors report **state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting** on multiple public benchmarks.

papers.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.
papers.summary: Radio access network (RAN) slicing frameworks for edge computing assume static computing models and so cannot exploit the variable data representations of dynamic split neural networks when devices offload machine learning tasks. `OMNIS+` is a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing that combines dynamic neural compression with adaptive quantization, including a box quantization scheme designed to resist transmission bit errors. Mobile devices choose split-network branches and cell association as causal contextual multi-armed bandit agents under Lyapunov control, while each edge server allocates bandwidth, GPU frequency, and modulation and coding scheme by block coordinate descent. Against state-of-the-art baselines, it **reduces the quality-of-service violation probability by up to 1.75** while giving a better trade-off between accuracy and violations.

papers.title: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
papers.abstract: Stability under input perturbations is necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. Weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. However, existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are insufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. In this paper, we establish a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint. This theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth H\"{o}lder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as the network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed. We then propose a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, we establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and provide robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies show that the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to that of classical deep network methods.
papers.summary: Weight norm constraints bound a neural network's Lipschitz constant and thus its sensitivity to input perturbations, but existing approximation results under fixed norm-product bounds are too weak to give optimal statistical rates. The authors prove a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint, showing that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as depth grows while the norm-product bound stays fixed. They then propose a penalized least squares estimator that **has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor**. Applications include optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations, supported by numerical studies.

papers.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
papers.abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.
papers.summary: An agent skill that worked in the past may still execute without being justified for reuse, because tests cover only some contract clauses, evaluations can share a wrong specification, and permissions or dependencies change between validation and invocation. The authors argue that **the unit of trust should be a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC), a defeasible authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters**. They develop this through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence stays admissible after a context change, including a conditional preservation result, three-valued applicability, and asymmetric context-transfer judgments. The work is a position paper offering a formalized problem statement, design obligations, and a reporting protocol, and it explicitly does not provide an implemented verifier or empirical results.

papers.title: ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.
papers.summary: Predicting how cells respond transcriptionally to combined perturbations requires separating true interactions from errors in the estimated effects of individual perturbations, which grow when single-perturbation data is sparse or withheld. `ReliFlow` is a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects through training-only cross-fitting, uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution, and splits the velocity into a known correction of the additive reference plus a learned residual transport field. On `Norman` genetic perturbations, **mean absolute error falls from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles** and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out `ComboSciPlex` drug combinations it falls from 0.191 to 0.176, at a moderate increase in training cost.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
papers.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.
papers.summary: Large language models can follow rules inferred through in-context learning (ICL) yet also fail to stay faithful to provided evidence, producing out-of-context (OOC) hallucination, and the two behaviors have mostly been studied separately. The authors analyze both through the functional roles that spans of context play, observing that **role information can be represented internally without reliably constraining the output**. A first-order decomposition shows a role's effect depends on two necessary conditions, sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation, and causal analysis shows role span contributions drive key token choices about response structure, content selection, and factual values. Failing choices can be reversed when role span support is raised enough to overcome the deficit, supporting a shared mechanistic account of the two phenomena.

papers.title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
papers.summary: Latent reasoners, which carry out chain-of-thought (CoT) in hidden states rather than text, typically run for a preset number of latent steps at inference.
