The authors find that running to the full preset horizon can reduce accuracy: earlier latent computation forms the frontier reasoning states, while later computation mostly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken support for the correct one. They introduce a lightweight method that estimates remaining constructive reasoning progress and adjusts the latent horizon adaptively during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and several arithmetic benchmarks, it **improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while cutting latent computation by up to 29.0%**, without retraining the LLM.

papers.title: ProtoBridge-CLIP: Observation-Masked Finding Prototypes for Medical Image--Report Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Radiology reports distinguish affirmed findings, explicit negations, and unmentioned concepts, but conventional global image--report contrastive learning often compresses these different evidence states into a single study-level target. We introduce \model{}, which combines symmetric global image--report alignment with observation-masked finding supervision and a soft relation objective over affirmed report concepts. Text-derived finding prototypes are aligned with local visual tokens, while uncertain and unmentioned concepts are excluded from direct finding labels. We evaluate the framework on three CT benchmarks and five chest-radiograph benchmarks, together with component ablations, paired and clinical retrieval, localization, perturbation robustness, calibration, and per-finding analyses. \model{} achieves macro-AUROC values of 73.6%, 66.5\%, and 68.8% on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, and INSPECT, and 80.2%, 91.4%, 78.5%, 86.5%, and 90.8% on ChestXray14, CheXpert, PadChest, RSNA, and SIIM-ACR, respectively. Relative to the matched global-only controls, the findings and relation objectives yield consistent gains across the evaluated datasets. These results demonstrate the practical value of treating observed and unobserved report concepts differently during medical image--text representation learning.
papers.summary: Radiology reports distinguish affirmed findings, explicit negations, and concepts that are simply not mentioned, but global image-report contrastive learning collapses these into a single study-level target. `ProtoBridge-CLIP` combines symmetric global image-report alignment with observation-masked finding supervision and a soft relation objective over affirmed concepts, aligning text-derived finding prototypes with local visual tokens while excluding uncertain and unmentioned concepts from direct labels. It reaches macro-AUROC of 73.6%, 66.5%, and 68.8% on the CT benchmarks `CT-RATE`, `RAD-ChestCT`, and `INSPECT`, and between 78.5% and 91.4% on five chest-radiograph benchmarks including `ChestXray14` and `CheXpert`. Relative to matched global-only controls, **the finding and relation objectives yield consistent gains across the evaluated datasets**.

papers.title: Choosing Supervised Post-Processing for Frozen Person Detectors: Information, Object Changes, and Complete Cost
papers.abstract: A frozen detector computes hypotheses that can support better final outputs through supervised post-processing. Choosing a readout requires knowing which available information improves detection and what its processing costs. We compare candidate scores, class distributions, geometry, native-set summaries and adapted neighborhood meta classification under common candidate, supervision and operating-point conditions. On 320 held-out CrowdHuman images, adding native-set context to a 97-dimensional readout yields 275 more matches and 96 more unmatched predictions. On a separate 319-image cohort, Full100 matches 6004 objects,versus 5848 for source-selected raw WBF and 6002 for a MetaDetect-style adaptation. Its gain over raw contains 300 added and 144 lost discoveries. After execution-equivalent optimization, Full100 and the meta-statistics readout both take approximately 95 ms per complete warm request on a fixed 64-image workload. Source-frozen transfer gives positive point results on 223 MOT17Det frames from seven sequences, while the main MIAP result shows no improvement. The study supports using sufficiently informative output readouts while retaining optimized meta classification as a competitive option. It also shows why feature dimension and net detection gain alone are unreliable guides to adoption.
papers.summary: A frozen person detector produces candidate hypotheses that supervised post-processing can turn into better final detections, and the question is which extra information is worth its processing cost. Candidate scores, class distributions, geometry, native-set summaries and an adapted neighbourhood meta classifier are compared under shared candidates, supervision and operating points on `CrowdHuman`. On a 319-image cohort the `Full100` readout **matches 6004 objects versus 5848 for source-selected raw `WBF`** and 6002 for a `MetaDetect`-style adaptation, with both learned readouts taking about 95 ms per warm request after optimisation. Transfer is positive on `MOT17Det` but shows no improvement on `MIAP`, and the authors conclude that feature dimension and net detection gain alone are unreliable guides to adoption.

papers.title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.
papers.summary: Tool-augmented agents doing spatial reasoning often gather evidence without clear targets, mix outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge when they have enough evidence. `Space-X` pairs an Execution Agent, which acquires, associates and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory, with a Control Agent that diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organisation and decision rules. Across four base models the framework improves accuracy, with **`GPT-6-sol` gaining 50.39% on `ViewSpatial` and 23.07% on `MMSI` relative to baselines**, and `Gemini-3.8-Flash` gaining 47.50% and 25.22% on the same benchmarks.

papers.title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning builds rewards for large language models by equally averaging a judge's per-criterion scores, but criteria differ in how far apart their scores are for satisfied versus unsatisfied responses, which the authors formalise as reward gain imbalance. Their experiments show that **removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy**, and an exact decomposition of the reward difference between two candidates shows the imbalance can either attenuate or amplify the base satisfaction signal, with misrankings concentrated where it attenuates. They propose Dual-Center Clipping (`DCC`), an aggregation that uses only the current candidate group's scores to set a clipping interval that caps each criterion's contribution to the reward difference while keeping continuous judgment information.

papers.title: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning
papers.abstract: Score-based structure learning estimates causal graphs by optimizing a data-dependent objective over structural equation models. We study how prior knowledge that selected pairs of variables are marginally independent can be incorporated into such causal discovery methods. Under faithfulness, marginally independent pairs cannot be connected by a trek, so the knowledge becomes a graphical no-trek constraint, which we call NOTREKS information. We introduce a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search, and we analyze why such information helps in finite samples and how it restricts the search space. Our numerical experiments illustrate to what extent NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery. In particular, using synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information, we show that these constraints can improve both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.
papers.summary: Score-based causal structure learning can benefit from prior knowledge that certain pairs of variables are marginally independent, which under faithfulness means no trek may connect them in the graph. The authors turn this into a graphical no-trek constraint, called `NOTREKS` information, and introduce a power-series trek penalty (`PSTrek`) for gradient-based optimisation along with a trek constraint for order-based search, with analysis of why it helps in finite samples and how it shrinks the search space. On synthetic benchmarks with oracle information, the constraints **improve both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification**.

papers.title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
papers.abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.
papers.summary: `CLIP`-style contrastive pretraining on radiology images and reports shows two failures: zero-shot performance peaks and then degrades while training loss keeps falling, and large batches fail to train. The authors attribute both to many unpaired reports sharing clinical findings with a given image, which makes the paired-identity target systematically biased, and they reproduce the failures in a synthetic testbed, `CLEVR-Radiology`, and explain them with a target-misspecification theory in which a deterministic gradient bias grows with batch size. Their correction, `CorLIP`, treats any text whose clinical assertions agree with the image as a positive, with no architecture changes; it largely removes the post-peak degradation and is **the only configuration that remains stable up to a batch size of 2048**, with the fix transferring from chest X-ray to 3D CT.

papers.title: Semi-Supervised GAN-Based Segmentation of CTPA Scans for Pulmonary Emboli Boundary Extraction
papers.abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with high morbidity and mortality, where delayed diagnosis can be fatal. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the clinical gold standard for PE detection, interpreting these scans manually is time-consuming and error-prone. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation method, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to leverage large pools of unlabeled CTPA scans. The proposed method addresses more effectively the challenges of CTPA image segmentation than previous methods by employing the dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to tackle the highly imbalanced nature of CTPA scans, the feature matching loss to encourage the generator to produce anatomically plausible segmentation maps that are indistinguishable from ground truth, as well as the self-training loss to reinforce learning from highly-confident pseudo-labeled samples. The experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset shows that the proposed method maintains accurate segmentation, despite a limited number of labeled CTPA scans. with a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.
papers.summary: Segmenting pulmonary embolism (PE) in computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) scans is slow and error-prone when done manually, and labelled scans are scarce. The proposed semi-supervised method uses a generative adversarial network to exploit unlabelled scans, combining Dice and cross-entropy losses for class imbalance, a feature matching loss for anatomically plausible segmentation maps, and a self-training loss on high-confidence pseudo-labels. On a public dataset it reports **a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance of 1.74**, outperforming fully supervised baselines with limited labelled data.

papers.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
papers.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.
papers.summary: An authorization interface for tool-using agents is proposed in which the planning model holds no tools: for each step it submits a logged contract with a goal, a verbatim user quotation and scope fields, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. With `gpt-6.1-terra` as planner and `GLM-5.3-Flash` as the trusted model on three `AmPermBench` task families, contracts are compared with two reviewers of planner-written commands. When the planner adds unrequested work, **contracts complete the user's task in 27 of 30 runs versus 16 of 30 for the intent-visible reviewer**, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions, however: every state-changing condition hits a wrong target in 40-49% of runs, an error traced to the planner's choice of objects for ambiguous references, and adversarial planners were not tested.

papers.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
papers.abstract: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.
papers.summary: Rough volatility, with price paths rougher than Brownian motion, is known to arise from near-unstable order flow with power-law memory, but it has been unclear how algorithmic market making would produce such flow. The authors model each market-making desk as applying a first-order gradient rule that moves its order distances toward oracle targets, acting asynchronously over its own lookback horizon, so that collectively the desks perform stochastic gradient descent with mini-batch noise. In the continuum limit the order book volume follows the Dean-Kawasaki stochastic partial differential equation, and the mix of horizons yields power-law memory that leads to rough volatility by standard scaling arguments. The model's key predictions are confirmed on simulated agents and on **six months of `Binance` data covering about 790 million orders**.

papers.title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
papers.abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.
papers.summary: Language models can change their answers when an input is rewritten in an equivalent form, such as renumbering a graph's nodes or renaming a program's variables, yet existing test-time compute scaling laws only consider repeated sampling from one fixed prompt. The authors study test-time symmetrization, which runs forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the answers, and prove that no amount of resampling a single representation can replace rewriting while **only O(log |G|) random rewritings recover the information of all |G| rewritings**, a rate that is optimal in general. Experiments with `Qwen2.5-7B`, `Phi-4-mini`, `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Qwen2.5-14B` on graph reasoning, logical deduction and multiple-choice question answering show that, at equal forward passes, rewritings are substantially more accurate than repeated sampling whenever the answer depends on how the input is written.

papers.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
papers.abstract:
Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change.
  \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. It preserves the original specification as authoritative ground truth and appends confidence-filtered refinements to clarify implicit constraints. \textsc{FormalFixer} uses both intent mismatch and verifier-generated counterexample cone graphs to guide iterative RTL patching. This workflow explicitly checks specification--assertion--RTL correspondence. Results support intent alignment for FPV-based hardware repair.
papers.summary: In formal property verification (FPV) of hardware, a failed assertion does not always indicate a defect in the register-transfer level (RTL) design; the assertion itself may be buggy, or the specification may be too ambiguous or incomplete to formalise directly. `FormalFixer` is a multi-stage repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions that keeps the original specification as authoritative ground truth, appends confidence-filtered refinements to clarify implicit constraints, and uses both intent mismatches and verifier-generated counterexample cone graphs to guide iterative RTL patching. The workflow **explicitly checks specification-assertion-RTL correspondence before deciding which artifact to change**, and the authors state that their results support this intent alignment, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
papers.abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.
papers.summary: Enterprises buy integrated agentic AI platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, yet public benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses and procurement leans on vendor demonstrations. A global bank's innovation lab reports a bakeoff in which a cross-functional panel scored ten platforms on nine capability dimensions across counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation workloads, separating the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings. A secondary analysis finds **Cronbach's alpha of 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions**, a halo effect suggesting demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. The authors propose a gate-then-score protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol.

papers.title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
papers.abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model families and language directions, with a single worst case of 2.19 chrF; (iii) on consumer GPUs, INT8 and INT4 quantisation provide substantial memory savings (49-61% at INT4) but do not reduce inference latency relative to FP16 - in fact, latency increases by 1.3x to 5.3x; (iv) a clear performance gradient tracking training-resource availability is visible across languages (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba). These findings motivate a research agenda focused on hardware-aware compression and error-type analysis beyond aggregate metrics for low-resource deployment.
papers.summary: A pilot study measures how post-training quantisation affects translation quality and inference cost for Hausa, Swahili and Yoruba across `Qwen2.5-1.5B`, `Aya-23-8B` and the dedicated translation model `NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B`, evaluated on `FLORES-200` at FP16, INT8 and NF4 INT4 precision on NVIDIA T4 GPUs. The specialised translation model beats both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on Hausa and Swahili and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba despite being about a sixth the size of the 8B model. Quantisation keeps quality within roughly 1 chrF and saves 49-61% memory at INT4, but **does not reduce latency, which instead rises by 1.3x to 5.3x relative to FP16**. Quality also tracks training-resource availability, with Swahili ahead of Hausa and Yoruba.

papers.title: A Hybrid RAG Framework for Deceptive Review Detection: Integrating RoBERTa-LoRA, FAISS-Based Retrieval, and LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: The growth of deceptive online opinions poses a critical risk of misinformation and fraud. This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to automatically distinguish spam reviews. The architecture integrates RoBERTa with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) classification, FAISS semantic vector retrieval, and a Large Language Model (LLM) for final reasoning. The system was evaluated across balanced and severely imbalanced real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that five epochs of fine-tuning enable robust domain transfer, achieving an F1-score of 0.90 in cross-domain evaluation, outperforming baselines (OpenAI Detector,F1 = 0.82) and demonstrating competitive performance against specialized in-domain SOTA models (fakeRoBERTa,F1 = 0.97). The proposed architecture provides evidence-backed explainability and statistically significant precision gains while maintaining comparable overall detection performance.
papers.summary: Deceptive online reviews are targeted with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that combines a `RoBERTa` classifier fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`), `FAISS` semantic vector retrieval, and a large language model for final reasoning. Evaluated in balanced and severely imbalanced settings, five epochs of fine-tuning give **an F1-score of 0.90 in cross-domain evaluation**, compared with 0.82 for the `OpenAI Detector` baseline and 0.97 for the specialised in-domain model `fakeRoBERTa`. The authors report evidence-backed explanations and statistically significant precision gains with comparable overall detection performance.

papers.title: Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.
papers.summary: Attention weights are widely used to estimate which surrounding objects matter to an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions, though whether attention reflects causal influence has long been debated in natural language processing. Several attention-based relevance estimation methods are compared against a causal reference obtained through counterfactual analysis, on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes with a vehicle based on the Transformer planner `PlanT 2.0`. The results show that **attention gives a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance**: the methods miss some relevant objects and flag objects with little or no impact. Accuracy is reasonable in single-lane, straight-road scenes but degrades on multi-lane roads and intersections.

papers.title: From Data to Valves: A Self-Learning, Production-Grade Edge Stack for Sustainable HVAC Control
papers.abstract: Learned HVAC controllers rarely leave the simulator, and those that do are typically trained offline, frozen at deployment and retrained from the cloud. We present a production stack in which three learning components run on one NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway per building, adapt continuously from the building's own data, and verify their own effect. (a) A compact transformer-encoder forecaster, one per equipment group with learned per-unit embeddings, predicts every air-side unit's next-cycle temperature and learns prequentially, one gradient step per five-minute cycle, behind five independent gates that bound the influence of any corrupt reading. (b) A distributional soft actor-critic agent, one shared policy across unit types, converts the measured state into a chilled-water valve position under a structural safety envelope that no learned component can soften; its second generation learns nightly on the device from recorded transitions alone, with a behaviour anchor and critic calibration terms, is scored by four model-free metrics and promoted by atomic hot-swap. (c) A change-point regression baseline held to ASHRAE Guideline 14 supplies the counterfactual against which savings are certified. On eighteen months of data from a hotel the forecaster converges from random weights within a week and reaches 0.37, 0.39 and 0.11 degree C MAE for air-handling, fresh-air and fan-coil units with no retraining event; on a different hotel the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period to within 0.07%. The RL agent has completed its in-simulator campaign and runs in shadow on 104 units; we report measured latency and memory of every service on a shared 15 GB device, the systems lessons of the campaign, and precisely what the evidence does and does not yet establish.
papers.summary: Learned heating, ventilation and air-conditioning controllers are usually trained offline and frozen at deployment, whereas this production stack runs three continuously adapting components on one NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway per building. A compact transformer-encoder forecaster learns one gradient step per five-minute cycle behind five safety gates, a distributional soft actor-critic agent sets chilled-water valve positions inside a structural safety envelope and retrains nightly on-device from recorded transitions, and a change-point regression baseline held to ASHRAE Guideline 14 provides the counterfactual for certifying savings. On eighteen months of hotel data the forecaster converges from random weights within a week and reaches **0.37, 0.39 and 0.11 degrees C mean absolute error for air-handling, fresh-air and fan-coil units with no retraining event**, and the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period to within 0.07% at a second hotel. The reinforcement learning agent has only completed its simulator campaign and runs in shadow mode on 104 units.

papers.title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
papers.abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.
papers.summary: Programs that encode legal rules, now often written by large language models, are usually graded against answers produced by someone reading the same law, so they can score well by sharing the grader's interpretation rather than being correct. `LexTemporis` instead grades them against records of what happened: 10,901 firm-years of small or medium enterprise (SME) status disclosed by Korean listed companies, alongside every version of the governing rules. A single transitional provision outside the main statutory text **raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%**, and the records favour the author's reading of a contested provision in 130 of 189 divergent firm-years. With four LLMs writing the rules, a pre-registered comparison finds no law-selection condition better across all models, and exploratory analyses indicate that grading against the author's own reading overstates the benefit of supplying the right provisions.

papers.title: Faster to the Wrong Answer: The Price of Local Updates in Federated Optimization
papers.abstract: Local computation can improve the conditioning of federated updates but may also introduce bias, causing their fixed point to differ from the global minimizer. We characterize the minimum worst-case bias achievable under a prescribed conditioning bound. We consider strongly convex quadratic client objectives with Hessian eigenvalues in $[\mu,L]$ and local updates represented by a shared positive spectral filter. Client heterogeneity is measured by the root-mean-square gradient at the global minimizer. For a uniform surrogate condition number bounded by $\chi\in[1,L/\mu]$, we establish the exact worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity, $(L-\mu\chi)/(2\mu L\sqrt{\chi})$, and show that local gradient descent with sufficiently small step sizes and proximal updates attain this bound. Our analysis reduces populations of arbitrary dimension, including noncommuting Hessians, to distributions over scalar curvatures. This reduction provides optimality certificates and worst-case constructions involving at most three scalar clients. We further extend the sharp proximal bias bound to smooth strongly convex objectives beyond quadratics and quantify the error introduced by inexact local solves.
papers.summary: Local computation in federated optimisation improves the conditioning of updates but can bias their fixed point away from the global minimiser, and the authors ask how small that bias can be under a given conditioning bound. For strongly convex quadratic client objectives with Hessian eigenvalues in [mu, L] and local updates modelled as a shared positive spectral filter, they establish **the exact worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity, (L - mu*chi) / (2*mu*L*sqrt(chi))**, for a surrogate condition number bounded by chi. Local gradient descent with sufficiently small step sizes and proximal updates both attain this bound, and the analysis reduces arbitrary-dimensional client populations to worst cases with at most three scalar clients. The proximal bound is extended to smooth strongly convex objectives, with the error from inexact local solves quantified.

papers.title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
papers.abstract:
Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3).
  To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers both conflicting (K2) and incremental (K3) knowledge. We further propose MIRAGE, an efficient, training-free framework whose core component, the Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner (CDR), resolves such per-hop source-trust errors via P(True)-based confidence routing, complemented by a lightweight template-guided corrector for residual structural deviations. Extensive experiments across four LLM families and two benchmarks demonstrate that MIRAGE consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy, establishing a new state of the art in this challenging setting.
papers.summary: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) under knowledge updates has mostly been studied with simple fact edits, whereas the Knowledge Injection setting requires a model to handle both updates that conflict with its parametric memory and entirely new facts. The authors introduce `NEXUS`, a benchmark for multi-hop reasoning covering both conflicting and incremental knowledge, and `MIRAGE`, a training-free framework whose Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner routes each hop between knowledge sources using P(True)-based confidence, supplemented by a lightweight template-guided corrector. Across four LLM families and two benchmarks, `MIRAGE` **consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy**.

papers.title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
papers.abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.
papers.summary: Consolidating several domain experts trained with reinforcement learning into one model is usually done by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (`MOPD`), which requires the student to sample again in every environment while experts score every token. Multi-expert replay policy distillation (`MRPD`) instead replays the experts' logged training rollouts, with their sampling probabilities and rewards, through the student in the experts' original order, recomputing the policy gradient and distilling the final experts' distributions at the logged prefixes. It samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model, so **consolidation costs about a seventh of the compute used to train the experts**, while yielding the best student on reasoning, search and SQL domains and surpassing `MOPD` from the same experts. The order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, which the authors read as evidence that expert training logs act as a curriculum.

papers.title: FDM+: A Framework for Constrained Control of the 2D Radiative Transport Equation
papers.abstract: Applying the frozen diffusion model (FDM) [29] to the constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation presents several challenges. These include the dimensional difference between control variables and state functions, the resolution mismatch between traditional numerical solvers and deep learning models, and solution non-uniqueness. To address these obstacles, we propose a novel approach, FDM+, which includes three key improvements. Firstly, a decoupled prediction architecture is introduced to address the dimensional heterogeneity. Secondly, an efficient parameterization strategy resolves the resolution mismatch. Meanwhile, we derive a total error bound to analyze how the parameterization error and the model estimation error jointly affect the performance. Thirdly, the conditional distribution learned by the diffusion model is leveraged to perform design space exploration for multi-solution problems. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.
papers.summary: Applying the frozen diffusion model (`FDM`) to constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation runs into a dimensional gap between control variables and state functions, a resolution mismatch between numerical solvers and deep learning models, and non-unique solutions. `FDM+` addresses these with a decoupled prediction architecture, an efficient parameterisation strategy accompanied by a total error bound covering parameterisation and model estimation error, and use of the diffusion model's learned conditional distribution to explore the design space for multi-solution problems. Numerical experiments show that it **outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility**.

papers.title: Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services
papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
papers.summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) services bill for context that is resent every turn, but the billing weights need not match how much that context contributes to answer quality. The authors propose a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights, and test it with context-ablation experiments, a measured serving stack, and cross-provider measurements. Relevance dominates position, distance-decay weightings do not beat a relevance-only baseline, and cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute cost by **over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens**. Calibrated simulations lower the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, though revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs do about as well, median charges rise, and the framework is presented as an accounting rule rather than a validated utility estimator.

papers.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
papers.abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.
papers.summary: Whether coding agents can build a large 3D game from scratch is tested with a benchmark of **108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres**, each given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images. A fully automated plan-implement-test-repair pipeline turns each task into a self-contained browser game, with runs averaging about 1,000 LLM calls and the longest using 14,407 calls and 2.13B tokens. Evaluation combines code-level functional acceptance, agent-based QA and playtesting, and blind pairwise human preference ranked with a `Bradley-Terry` model in a public arena. Preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved and that code-level correctness alone does not determine player preference.

papers.title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.
papers.summary: Adapting a pretrained Time-Series Foundation Model (TSFM) to a stream of new operating conditions is hard because the model must improve on each new condition without losing earlier ones, using few labels and no condition identity at inference. The authors observe that a condition shift moves only some local regions of the embedding space, and propose `PACT` (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport), which partitions the frozen embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports, with a learned gate choosing among an identity path and the accumulated transports. The encoder, classifier head, and earlier transports all stay fixed. With 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition, `PACT` keeps **average macro-F1 above 0.95** across a four-condition bearing-fault stream, with similar behavior reported on public benchmarks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Adapting a frozen time-series foundation model classifier to new operating conditions usually costs accuracy on conditions it already handles, especially when only a few labels are available and the condition is unknown at inference. `PACT` starts from the observation that a condition shift moves only some regions of the embedding space, so it corrects embeddings locally and always keeps an untouched identity path.

- The method splits the frozen source embedding space into `k`-means "charts", learns a rank-8 residual transport per chart for each arriving condition, freezes it, and trains a per-chart soft gate that mixes the identity branch with all accumulated transports while the encoder and classifier head never change.
- On a frozen `Sundial` backbone with a 5% labelled calibration set, it reaches an average macro-F1 of **0.9575** on the bearing-fault benchmark `FD` and **0.8774** on `WISDM`, beating the strongest listed baseline by **11.15** and **8.34** points, with relative forgetting between 0.0021 and 0.0425 across the five benchmarks.
- The advantage is not uniform: the margin shrinks to 0.71 points on `HHAR`, `LwF` edges it on `Sleep-EDF` (0.6138 versus 0.6129), and rehearsal baselines beat it on `HHAR` (by 2.81 points), `UCI-HAR` (3.05) and `Sleep-EDF` (3.24 for `DER++`).
- The mechanism transfers across eight backbones, with `Mantis` reaching 0.985 on `FD` and 0.922 on `UCI-HAR`, but results are bounded by the frozen representation, as `UCI-HAR` ranges from 0.517 with `PatchTST` to 0.922 with `Mantis`.
- Forgetting is not ruled out, because gates are refit after every condition and the preservation guarantee is only conditional (certifying 99.8% of correct source predictions on `FD` but 71.1% on `UCI-HAR`), and the method also stores source and calibration embeddings, grows its transport bank with each condition, and loses 9.08 points on `FD` when 85% of calibration labels fall in one class.

papers.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.
papers.summary: VLA robot policies are fragile to reworded instructions, and success rates alone do not show whether a failure lies in choosing the object or in completing the task. Studying `GR00T N1.7` on two `LIBERO-Spatial` tasks that differ only in a landmark word, the authors find that unseen synonyms steer the policy to the correct bowl yet complete only **67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes versus 100% for the original word**. Swapping landmark token vectors before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator redirects nearly every episode, while after the connector no single token group does so alone but any two do. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs completion, training only the connector suffices, and an open-loop score misses part of the repair, leading the authors to recommend closed-loop evaluation that scores choice and completion separately.

papers.title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models that fly unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) from natural-language instructions still fail often in closed-loop flight, and corrective actions at the states the policy actually reaches cannot be labeled at scale by pilots or supplied reliably by rule-based planners. `AeroRSI` is a recursive self-improvement framework in which the failing policy judges candidate repairs by flying on from them, turning its own sampled actions and rule-based proposals into usable supervision that is then distilled back in. Because an episode ends at its first failure, each round renews supervision to expose failures that earlier ones had hidden. On `TravelUAV`, three rounds raise a supervised 2B-parameter policy's success rate **from 46.4% to 67.5%** and halve collisions, 10.6 points above the previous state of the art with no extra human labels or inference cost.

papers.title: APS: Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have significantly improved video understanding capabilities, yet processing long videos remains challenging due to the substantial computational cost of extensive visual inputs. Frame selection offers an efficient alternative, but many existing region-based methods rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions, which may result in suboptimal temporal regions, compromising subsequent budget allocation and frame selection. In this work, we propose Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (APS), a training-free framework that adapts temporal partitions to local variations in query-frame relevance. Specifically, APS formulates temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, jointly optimizing partition boundaries and local models through dynamic programming. The resulting adaptive temporal partitions guide frame budget allocation based on query relevance and temporal extent, enabling informative frame selection under limited visual budgets. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that APS consistently improves performance across diverse LVLM backbones, achieving the highest average gains over uniform sampling among competing methods. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of adaptive partitioning and demonstrate its generalizability across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) struggle with long videos because of the compute cost of many frames, and existing region-based frame selectors rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions. Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (`APS`) is a training-free method that treats temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, solved by dynamic programming, so that partition boundaries follow local variation in query-frame relevance. The resulting segments guide how the frame budget is allocated by relevance and temporal extent. On `Video-MME`, `MLVU`, and `LongVideoBench`, `APS` achieves the **highest average gains over uniform sampling among competing methods** across several LVLM backbones.

papers.title: VESPA: Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make existing unsafe policies safe, or at least make considerable progress towards safety. Targeted fine-tuning of the existing policy on those counterexamples enables it to learn how to avoid violating safety constraints. We thus use the result of a formal verification as a training signal for fine-tuning. On CartPole, VESPA raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching after two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches after ten. On MountainCarContinuous, VESPA turns an unsafe policy into a safe policy in 53 of 60 runs. We conclude that counterexamples from a verifier are an effective training signal, which can be utilized to systematically improve the safety of policies. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/VESPA-Submission/
papers.summary: When formal verification finds a reinforcement learning (RL) policy unsafe, the usual remedy is to retrain from scratch and verify again, which is expensive. `VESPA` (Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation) instead fine-tunes an existing decision tree policy on the counterexamples the verifier produces, using the verification result as a training signal. On `CartPole` it raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching in two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches in ten. On `MountainCarContinuous` it turns an unsafe policy into a safe one in **53 of 60 runs**.

papers.title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, covering 17 model--precision combinations across 4 LLM families. On Qwen deployments, LEDGE achieves request-level mean absolute percentage errors below 3.6% and a 135.3 times aggregate speedup over physical inference. Performance model calibrated on one LLM family yield 7.44% zero-shot end-to-end latency MAPE across three other families. Further simulations show how shared-link contention affects placement decisions and network topology constrains scaling. Across four edge environments, LEDGE completes 26,773 simulation runs in 83.8 minutes, enabling efficient exploration of deployment strategies under diverse resource conditions and serving objectives. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gdfwj/LEDGE.
papers.summary: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving across heterogeneous edge devices means exploring many model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, which is costly to do physically. `LEDGE` is a lightweight simulator that builds event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution cost from performance models calibrated on end-to-end measurements, and models shared-link contention, all without executing tensor operations. On a testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, it reaches request-level mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) **below 3.6% with a 135.3x speedup over physical inference** on `Qwen` deployments. A performance model calibrated on one LLM family gives 7.44% zero-shot latency MAPE on three other families, and 26,773 simulation runs complete in 83.8 minutes.

papers.title: Constructing Dynamic Conversations with Neural Back-channel Generation and Voice-line Scheduling
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach to the problem of combining two voice-line channels of dyadic conversational audio into a unified conversation with controllable back-channeling and turn-taking dynamics. In voice performances for the game industry, the two tracks of voice-lines are typically recorded or synthesized in isolation. Our method takes two such unsynchronized tracks and uses a neural scheduler to sequence them into a single dynamic conversation, modifying both tracks by inserting or removing pauses and introducing voice overlap as appropriate. We further propose a back-channel predictor that is able to predict opportunity for back-channels for a given conversational turn's audio and content, which the scheduler can then incorporate. We evaluate our scheduler and predictor independently and in combination by: various quantitative comparison; a qualitative and perceptual comparison to prior art and naive baselines; a compelling set of results showing animator control over the diversity, extent and nature of back-channeling and turn dynamics.
papers.summary: Game voice performances are usually recorded or synthesized as two isolated tracks, which then have to be combined into a natural-sounding two-person conversation. The proposed method uses a neural scheduler to sequence the two unsynchronized tracks into one conversation by inserting or removing pauses and introducing overlap, together with a predictor that finds opportunities for back-channels from a turn's audio and content. The components are evaluated separately and together through quantitative comparisons and perceptual comparisons against prior art and naive baselines. The authors report that the system gives animators **control over the diversity, extent, and nature of back-channeling and turn dynamics**.

papers.title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
papers.abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.
papers.summary: Quantum annealing performs poorly at discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. The authors extend quantum annealing into a quantum neural network and study it on prototypical optimization problems. A random annealing network of **width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the depth needed for the quantum search problem**, and with tuned parameters a quantum perceptron of depth 1 and width 2 solves it with exponentially small error. They attribute the gain to width providing a larger, learnable evolution space for the annealing process.

papers.title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
papers.abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.
papers.summary: Regularization-based continual learning loses effectiveness as tasks accumulate, because updates for new tasks spread across a densely connected network. Drawing on the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), under which neural connections thin out with physical distance, `UCLIR` splits the input into parts learned by separate, independent autoencoders with unsupervised regularization, so that a new task causes only localized parameter updates. A linear classifier is used at inference. On `5-Splits MNIST`, a 5-dataset sequence, `5-Splits CIFAR-10`, and `10-Splits Tiny ImageNet`, the approach is reported as **competitive with supervised and replay-based methods**.

papers.title: AG-BFGS: Foundations for Accelerated Geometry Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce an accelerated geometry-learning framework for BFGS that incorporates momentum into the learning of Hessian inverse approximations. We prove that the resulting accelerated updates satisfy explicit stability conditions and preserve positive definiteness within admissible parameter regions. Numerical experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding non-accelerated schemes while maintaining numerical stability. These results provide the first rigorous theoretical foundation for accelerated quasi-Newton learning and bridge the gap between empirical observations and mathematical guarantees for accelerated second-order methods.
papers.summary: Momentum is incorporated into how the `BFGS` quasi-Newton method learns its approximation of the inverse Hessian, yielding an accelerated framework called `AG-BFGS`. The authors prove that the **accelerated updates satisfy explicit stability conditions and preserve positive definiteness** within admissible parameter regions.
