Numerical experiments show consistent improvements over the corresponding non-accelerated schemes while remaining numerically stable. The authors describe this as the first rigorous theoretical foundation for accelerated quasi-Newton learning.

papers.title: The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
papers.abstract: This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.
papers.summary: The seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (`VNN-COMP 2026`) was held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification, co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification in Lisbon. It aims to give an **objective comparison of state-of-the-art neural network verification tools in terms of scalability and speed**. To that end it uses standard formats (`ONNX` for networks and `VNNLIB` for specifications), standard hardware run by the organizers on AWS, and tool parameters supplied by the tool authors. The report covers the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned.

papers.title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.
papers.summary: World models that plan by imagining over dense pixel observations absorb redundant detail and overlook relations among task-relevant entities, so errors build up over long rollouts. `Embodied Graph` is a relational state abstraction, and the Relational World Model (`RWM`) imagines directly over these graph states using a task-aware graph constructor with online memory updates and a recurrent state space model that learns node-wise latent dynamics along with inter-node dependencies. In experiments on `Minecraft` and `Crafter`, `RWM` is the **only method that obtains diamonds in Minecraft within the given budget**. Further experiments on web interaction apply relational state prediction to the decision making of web agents.

papers.title: How Well Do Generalist CT Foundation Models Differentiate Liver Tumors?
papers.abstract: Generalist CT foundation models detect many findings with high performance, but their ability to differentiate detected lesions remains largely unevaluated. This retrospective study evaluated two generalist models, RADAR and Merlin, for differentiating liver tumors using a public single-institution multiphase CT dataset (517 cases: hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, breast and colorectal cancer liver metastases, and hemangioma). The models were evaluated in a zero-shot setting using their existing outputs and with linear probing, in which only a linear classifier was trained on frozen image features (stratified fivefold cross-validation repeated five times). In the zero-shot setting, RADAR achieved an accuracy of 54.4% (95% CI: 49.9, 58.8) and a $\kappa$ of 0.37 for four-class differentiation at the portal venous phase and predicted 31% (129 of 421) of malignant tumors as hemangioma. With linear probing of four-phase features, its accuracy improved to 79.9% (95% CI: 76.6, 83.4) with a $\kappa$ of 0.72, and 1% (five of 421) of malignant tumors were predicted as hemangioma; Merlin achieved an accuracy of 60.9% (95% CI: 56.9, 65.0). Generalist CT foundation models showed limited zero-shot ability to differentiate liver tumors, which improved substantially with linear probing alone.
papers.summary: Generalist CT foundation models detect many findings well, but their ability to tell detected lesions apart is largely untested. This retrospective study evaluates `RADAR` and `Merlin` on a public single-institution multiphase CT dataset of 517 liver tumor cases, both zero-shot and with linear probing, where only a linear classifier is trained on frozen image features. Zero-shot, `RADAR` reached 54.4% accuracy on four-class differentiation and labeled 31% of malignant tumors as hemangioma. Linear probing on four-phase features raised its accuracy to **79.9%, with only 1% of malignant tumors predicted as hemangioma**, while `Merlin` reached 60.9%.

papers.title: QuantAtlas-OM: Taming Neural Spectral Bias in Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Ocean Dynamics
papers.abstract: Autoregressive neural networks exhibit spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction. As rollouts progress, high-frequency details decay, blurring the predicted fields and destabilizing long-range forecasts. Ocean dynamics offer a particularly stringent test because kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts spanning tens of kilometers. This degradation stems from coupling large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention in a shared feature space. Evolution on a coarse grid smooths out high-wavenumber eddies, whereas evolution on a fine grid amplifies small-scale phase errors and triggers rollout instability. We introduce QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a scale-spectral decoupling framework that confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder. Across physical regimes, the evolution core pairs non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating. Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains $43.7\%$ to $86.5\%$ of mesoscale spectral energy along the $k^{-3}$ cascade at Day $120$, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of $0.81$ to $0.88$ at Day $60$, and reaches $0.66$ at Day $120$ in the Kuroshio ($2.5\times$ to $7.7\times$ the best baselines). Trained at $0.25^\circ$, QuantAtlas-OM transfers zero-shot to a global $0.125^\circ$ grid ($0.81$ Day-$10$ spatial correlation) and leads global $0.25^\circ$, $23$-level 3D ocean simulations ($120$ days) and coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts ($60$ days), ranking first on $15$ of $16$ metrics and cutting $60$- to $120$-day salinity RMSE by $13\%$ to $27\%$ across global ocean basins.
papers.summary: Autoregressive neural forecasters lose high-frequency detail over long rollouts, a spectral bias that is especially damaging for ocean dynamics, where kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts. `QuantAtlas-OM` decouples scales by confining deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through a bypass to the decoder. Across three western boundary currents it retains 43.7% to 86.5% of mesoscale spectral energy at day 120 and reaches an anomaly correlation of **0.66 at day 120 in the Kuroshio, 2.5x to 7.7x the best baselines**. Trained at 0.25 degrees, it transfers zero-shot to a global 0.125-degree grid and ranks first on 15 of 16 metrics in global 3D ocean simulations and coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts.

papers.title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference
papers.abstract: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.
papers.summary: Under network interference, an individual's outcome depends on neighbors' treatments as well as their own, so causal effects become functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single contrasts. `FANCI` (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference) targets recovery of the full exposure-dependent population-average response function under a limited experimental budget, modeling response surfaces with treatment-specific Gaussian processes and steering new experiments toward poorly covered regions with a fill-distance criterion. The authors derive **uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation error** and characterize the approximation loss from a target-screening strategy for choosing feasible network-assignment pairs. Simulations and an online-game experiment show improved recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects.

papers.title: Inherited Adapter Experts for Replay-Free Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each expert is initialized from its predecessor at no extra cost: the domains share their classes, so an image misrouted to a later expert loses less. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol, Lamarck is first on CDDB-Hard by 5.2 points, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.
papers.summary: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains on the same classes across successive domains without storing earlier images, typically by freezing a pre-trained ViT, training one expert per domain, and routing each unlabeled test image to an expert. The authors find that a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners **under 2.7 points of final accuracy** relative to always picking the correct domain's expert, so the experts rather than the router limit accuracy. Their learner, `Lamarck`, keeps that router and strengthens the experts with adapters applied after each deep ViT block, initializing each expert from its predecessor. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines it ranks first on the deepfake benchmark `CDDB-Hard` by 5.2 points, second on `DomainNet` and `OfficeHome`, and highest in mean accuracy.

papers.title: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD
papers.abstract: We study the almost sure convergence of the last-iterate optimization error of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) for convex objectives. For smooth objectives, we establish convergence rates of order $k^{-1/3}$ when a stationary minimizer exists, and $k^{-1/4}$ otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors, where $k$ denotes the iteration counter. We further show that the latter rate extends to nonsmooth convex objectives. All these rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Finally, we establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponents $-1/3$ and $-1/4$ are optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the corresponding problem classes.
papers.summary: The almost sure convergence of the last iterate of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) is analyzed for convex objectives. For smooth objectives the authors establish **rates of order k^(-1/3) when a stationary minimizer exists and k^(-1/4) otherwise**, up to polylogarithmic factors, with the latter rate also holding for nonsmooth convex objectives. All rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Matching lower bounds show both exponents are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors for their problem classes.

papers.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to write children's stories, raising the question of whether they change narrative portrayals depending on the recipient's gender. Using matched daughter/son prompts, the authors analyze 62,873 bedtime stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles, combining lexical rate contrasts, stereotype alignment measures, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions. They find that **son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion than daughter-directed stories**, with narrator gender moderating the pattern only slightly. Human evaluations agree with the pattern, though their correspondence with lexical measures varies by dimension, and hidden-state analyses show that recipient gender is decodable.

papers.title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
papers.abstract: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.
papers.summary: Predicting how an AI system will score on a new benchmark from only a handful of revealed outcomes is handled here with a weak Beta prior, chosen from public evaluation counts and updated exactly from at most 31 observed results, using no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. In its single online evaluation in the `AIMS` competition, the predictor had a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, **a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference**, and a public evaluation over 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds gives 0.200250. The whole submission is 7,754 bytes and takes about 12.71 microseconds per prediction, and the released code and sufficient statistics rebuild the fitted prior byte for byte.

papers.title: Gaussian Primitive Fusion for Any-Resolution Multimodal Images
papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion integrates complementary observations from different modalities into a unified representation. Existing methods typically estimate modality contributions on a common discrete grid. When source modalities have different native resolutions, constructing such a grid generally involves resampling, which may introduce artifacts and affect subsequent fusion decisions. To address this problem, we propose Gaussian Primitive Fusion (GPF), which reformulates heterogeneous-resolution fusion in a shared continuous Gaussian space. Instead of first converting source images to a common resolution, GPF directly fits their native-resolution observations with shared Gaussian geometry and modality-specific content representations, and learns modality contributions within the resulting continuous representation. Once optimized, the fused representation is rendered at the finest native resolution without resampling the sources. With heterogeneous-resolution inputs, GPF produces clearer target contours and finer textures, with less blurring and blocking artifacts than resample-then-fuse pipelines. Quantitatively, it achieves the best results on multiple infrared-visible benchmarks against state-of-the-art fusion methods equipped with interpolation or super-resolution frontends.
papers.summary: Fusing images from modalities with different native resolutions usually means resampling them onto a common pixel grid first, which can introduce artifacts that distort the fusion. `Gaussian Primitive Fusion` (`GPF`) instead fits the native-resolution observations in a shared continuous Gaussian space, with shared geometry and modality-specific content, learns modality contributions there, and renders the result at the finest native resolution. The authors report clearer contours and finer textures with less blurring and blocking, and **the best results on multiple infrared-visible benchmarks** against state-of-the-art fusion methods paired with interpolation or super-resolution frontends.

papers.title: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs
papers.abstract: Highly parameterized convolutional neural networks often achieve strong predictive performance, but their memory, computation, and deployment costs motivate the search for methods that recover compact architectures from large reference models. We propose SoU-RHS, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with the so-called Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (SoU-SGL). The resulting model sharpens the separation between active and inactive filters, providing an effective mechanism for architecture recovery. A key property of SoU-RHS is stability: across different overparameterized starting widths and under a reasonable range of pruning thresholds, it recovers compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation. This supports the interpretation that the procedure is identifying a compact structure adapted to the data, rather than merely compressing each initial model separately. Across standard image-classification benchmarks, SoU-RHS recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines, while maintaining competitive accuracy, achieving lower negative log-likelihood in every evaluated configuration and generally lower expected calibration error.
papers.summary: Recovering a compact convolutional network from a large overparameterized one is approached with `SoU-RHS`, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with a Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (`SoU-SGL`) to separate active from inactive filters more sharply. The authors emphasize stability: **different starting widths and a reasonable range of pruning thresholds yield compact architectures of similar total size and layer-wise allocation**. On standard image-classification benchmarks it recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines at competitive accuracy, with lower negative log-likelihood in every configuration and generally lower expected calibration error.

papers.title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning
papers.abstract: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/CounselTraj.
papers.summary: Synthetic psychological counseling datasets tend to consist of brief exchanges that miss how a full session unfolds, while real transcripts are hard to share for privacy reasons. `CounselTraj` learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play sessions by human counselors, plans coordinated client and counselor trajectories, and uses them as flexible guidance to expand short dialogues into session-length ones. Across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets it produces more complete and coherent sessions than direct expansion or randomly sampled trajectories. The resulting `CounselTrajD` dataset holds **over 10K process-guided Chinese counseling dialogues**, and the `CounselTrajLM` model trained on it is reported to outperform publicly available Chinese counseling models at both response and session level.

papers.title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies can decide how many predicted actions to execute before replanning if they have a good uncertainty estimate, but Adaptive Action Chunking (`AAC`) gets one by sampling multiple action chunks, which adds inference cost and mixes within-trajectory uncertainty with diversity across valid strategies. Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (`DUAC`) is a post-hoc method that derives action-level uncertainty from the flow vector field of a pretrained VLA, **using a single generated chunk and Jacobian-vector products with no retraining**. Its scores correlate strongly with `AAC` while being less sensitive to diversity among distinct valid strategies, and on `LIBERO`, `LIBERO-Pro`, `LIBERO-Plus`, and `RoboCasa` the authors report strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency.

papers.title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
papers.abstract: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.
papers.summary: Learning Gaussian halfspaces with label noise is revisited in the large-bias regime, where one class is rare and information-computation gaps are conjectured for several noise models. The authors analyze a rare-tail mean estimator, a one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class, and show that **it recovers the halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate up to log factors** under a broad class of noise models, including probit and slowly decaying margin-dependent noise, where classical Averaging is provably suboptimal. As an application, it supplies the warm start for a two-stage curriculum that learns a random classification noise (RCN) target at the same rate.

papers.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
papers.abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.
papers.summary: Whether video models actually benefit from being able to interact with a video, rather than viewing it once, is tested with `VideoACE`, a benchmark of **1,000 multiple-choice questions across six categories of fine-grained action understanding** in high-frame-rate videos, with temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its environment pairs video inspection tools, which let a model adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, with a user simulator that gives feedback. Five models are compared under single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use with user feedback, and the authors report distinct patterns in how each gathers evidence and responds to further interaction opportunities.

papers.title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
papers.abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.
papers.summary: Visual inspection for field robotics and environmental monitoring has to localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing budgets, where exhaustive sweeps and myopic policies both waste calls. The authors treat inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning, pairing a compact recurrent world model with exact symbolic feasibility and cost rules, and using receding-horizon beam search to schedule class queries, crops, enhancements, and stopping. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead beats static schedules and search-free offline reinforcement learning under tight budgets, **gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on `RUOD`** and 15.1 on `ARIS`, at 11 ms planning cost.

papers.title: SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification
papers.abstract: The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to produce a continuous watermark confidence score for watermark detection. Across nine evaluation conditions, SpiderMark achieves the highest fixed-threshold Accuracy in eight, while retaining strong detection on unseen COCO prompts without verifier retraining. CLIP similarity and FID measurements show that these detection gains are accompanied by small measured differences in prompt alignment and distributional image quality. SpiderMark establishes that structured watermark geometry and learned probabilistic verification can be unified into a single, practical framework, bridging the gap between imperceptibility, robustness, and real-world verifiability for generative AI content attribution.
papers.summary: Watermarks for diffusion-generated images often use isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which the authors say leaves them vulnerable to directional transformations and unstable thresholds. `SpiderMark` embeds a spider-web pattern of radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, without changing model weights, and trains a lightweight `ResNet-18` verifier with auxiliary PSNR and L1 similarity cues to output a continuous confidence score. It achieves **the highest fixed-threshold accuracy in eight of nine evaluation conditions** and keeps strong detection on unseen `COCO` prompts without verifier retraining, with small measured differences in CLIP similarity and FID.

papers.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
papers.abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.
papers.summary: Continual Learning (CL), which adds knowledge without forgetting, and Machine Unlearning (MU), which removes specific knowledge without harming the rest, conflict when applied to the same weights. Learning with Unlearning (`LwU`) scores every weight against both the data to keep and the data to delete, then **partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules**: retention-only weights are frozen, deletion-only weights are cleared and reused as free capacity, contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient, and the remaining capacity learns the new task via self-distillation from a privileged teacher. Deletion is served post hoc without retraining, and the authors report matching or beating the strongest baseline on both CL and MU tasks, including image generation and dangerous-content removal.

papers.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
papers.abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
papers.summary: Decoding viewed images from electroencephalography (EEG) works well within a subject but degrades sharply for unseen subjects, and adapting to a new user normally needs labeled data. The authors propose incremental transductive calibration, a setting matching a deployed Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) where the candidate gallery is known and unlabeled EEG accumulates during use, with each query decoded before it is used for calibration. Their label-free method `GALA` (GAllery-Level Alignment) registers EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction, and a Sinkhorn-Procrustes alignment with estimated query frequencies. On `THINGS-EEG-2` with a 200-image gallery, it **raises top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use**, and it is the most accurate label-free method in all 60 evaluated settings.

papers.title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
papers.abstract: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.
papers.summary: Operators of radio access networks (RANs) use conditional generative models to simulate power-consumption trajectories for what-if analysis of energy-saving policies, but measurements cover few configurations, leaving many contexts rare or unseen in training. The authors first propose a context-normalized conditional generator, then a prediction-based framework that decomposes power consumption into a global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. On a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset, hardware metadata transfers information about residual scale, and the prediction-based approach generalizes to rare and unseen contexts, **reducing median MAE by about 50% versus `TimeWeaver` with one target observation**.

papers.title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
papers.abstract: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $\Theta(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $\alpha d$ coordinates, $0<\alpha<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $\Theta(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leq\alpha d$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<\alpha<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.
papers.summary: The gap between efficient learning and inference and compact probabilistic-circuit representation is quantified for a model of continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a square grid with d edges. The minimax squared Hellinger risk from N samples is shown to be of order min(1, d times N to the power -2/3), achieved by a polynomial-time spline estimator under a fixed positive reliability bound. In contrast, **nonnegative decomposable circuits need a number of nodes exponential in the square root of d** to reach fixed total-variation error below one, and tight bounds are given on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) approximation error of polynomial-size circuits. Exact queries nonetheless remain cheap, costing on the order of d to the power 3/2 arithmetic operations via a planar zero-field Ising model.

papers.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.
papers.summary: Scaling laws guide compute allocation for foundation models, but tabular foundation models (TFMs) are pretrained on unlimited synthetic data and evaluated on real datasets, so it is unclear whether such laws transfer. Studying `TabPFNv2`-style models with the open-source `nanoTabPFN` pipeline, the authors find that synthetic and real-world scaling behave differently and that a well-fitting scaling law does not guarantee reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, **selecting configurations with too few evaluation datasets yields systematically over-optimistic performance estimates**. Compute-optimal scaling also requires widening the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes, in rows and features, alongside model size and training compute.

papers.title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
papers.abstract: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.
papers.summary: An interactive demonstration turns a table into a gesture input surface by sensing vibrations with four concealed piezoelectric sensors. **The complete pipeline, from signal acquisition and preprocessing to neural event detection and gesture classification, runs on a microcontroller**, which sends only the recognized labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down to a host computer rather than raw sensor signals. Two example applications are shown, an endless runner game and a table lamp with on/off and brightness control, along with a dashboard of recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.

papers.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
papers.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.
papers.summary: Multi-agent red teaming of large language models (LLMs) is costly because of repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and poor information routing, and a target's response does not reveal which coordination decision to change. Learning to Coordinate (`L2C`) evolves an executable multi-agent workflow per red-teaming case, representing agent roles, execution dependencies, and input bindings as a versioned graph tied to records of what was actually delivered and produced. A controller trained by supervised fine-tuning reads those records, target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget, then retains the workflow, refines instructions, restructures collaboration, or locks further editing. On `HarmBench` across six executor-target configurations, it raises attack success rate over `EvoSynth` by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while **cutting mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%**.

papers.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
papers.abstract: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.
papers.summary: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) is a standard dimension-reduction tool for functional data, but its minimax theory for eigenfunctions of growing index under noisy discrete observation has been open for over two decades. Using a sieve-based framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects, the authors first derive new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes. They then **establish minimax optimal rates for both individual eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimension**, covering sampling frequencies from sparse to dense. The rates reflect two mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, giving four or two sampling regimes, and FPCA-based functional linear regression is shown to be minimax optimal as an application.

papers.title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.
papers.summary: Rendering untrusted documents as page images is known to lower indirect prompt injection success on average, and this study asks which injected operations survive, at what utility cost, and why failed attacks fail. Text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources are paired across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet **`Qwen3-VL-8B` still executes image-borne answer replacement 77.96% of the time**, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit for Qwen and Gemini though not `GPT-5-nano`. Models often transcribe image-borne commands they do not follow, and utility on original questions stays between 93.31% and 101.61% but drops to 61.99% for Qwen when answers combine two evidence spans.

papers.title: From a finite subgroup of $SO(3)$:$C_2$ leads to a Holant dichotomy
papers.abstract:
Counting complexity within the Holant framework has been extensively studied through complexity dichotomy theorems. While substantial progress has been achieved for various restricted settings, the general complex-valued even-arity case without auxiliary unary signatures remains largely open. This paper studies a fundamental case in this program where the binary signatures induce a group structure satisfying \(M(B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\). It is observed that projective equivalence classes of binary signature matrices naturally embed into finite subgroups of \(SO(3)\), providing an algebraic viewpoint for structural classification. This paper further identifies two fundamentally different regimes for the \(C_2\) case, namely the normal and isotropic cases, and analyzes their complexity behavior separately.
  Combining gadget constructions, decomposition techniques, interpolation arguments, and a realnumberization approach that transforms the complex-valued setting into an equivalent real-structured framework, this paper establishes a complete dichotomy theorem: for every even-arity signature set \(\mathcal{F}\) satisfying \(M(\B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\), the problem \(\mathrm{Holant}(\mathcal{F})\) is either polynomial-time computable or \#P-hard. A Pauli-basis representation for signatures is further introduced as an algebraically natural language for organizing realizable signatures and revealing structural relations that are less transparent in the standard basis.
papers.summary: Complexity classification of counting problems in the Holant framework remains largely open for complex-valued even-arity signatures without auxiliary unary signatures. The case studied here is where the binary signatures induce a group isomorphic to the cyclic group C2, using the observation that projective equivalence classes of binary signature matrices embed into finite subgroups of SO(3), and splitting the analysis into normal and isotropic regimes. Combining gadget constructions, decomposition, interpolation, and a technique that converts the complex-valued setting into an equivalent real-structured one, the authors prove a complete dichotomy: **every such Holant problem is either polynomial-time computable or #P-hard**. A Pauli-basis representation of signatures is also introduced to organize realizable signatures.

papers.title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
papers.abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.
papers.summary: Vision-language generation mostly relies on autoregressive models, which emit tokens one at a time, or discrete diffusion models, which predict tokens independently within each denoising step. `ViLFlow` (Vision-Language Flow) is a continuous-flow model that jointly models output embeddings and decodes tokens in parallel, adapting pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and captioning through learned image guidance, a visually adapted teacher, and a token decoder trained on denoiser predictions. It **outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on `VQAv2`** and 4.50 points on `GQA` without `GQA` training. On the `COCO` Karpathy test it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

papers.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
papers.abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.
papers.summary: Multimodal aligners that compress each sensor stream into a single pooled embedding cannot tell apart 'twin events', meaning distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. The authors prove that **any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition as sequence length grows**, so no loss function or embedding geometry can separate twin events from pooled features alone. They introduce `CounterPoint`, a lightweight plug-in module that removes each modality's temporal mean and scores frame-level cross-modal agreement. Added to four existing multimodal aligners, it is reported to outperform existing temporal alignment methods.

papers.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.
papers.summary: Federated learning for autonomous driving usually needs many communication rounds and is rarely evaluated in closed loop, while one-shot methods have focused on perception tasks. `FedE2E` is a one-shot federated method for end-to-end driving that combines multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to merge knowledge from heterogeneous models. In closed-loop evaluation on `Bench2Drive` it reaches a Driving Score of **55.85 in the one-shot setting, 4.07 points above prior work**, and 60.35 after five communication rounds.

papers.title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.
papers.summary: Irregularly sampled time series are hard to forecast because a fixed number of recent observations can span minutes for one variable and days for another. `TRESS` (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries) keeps the latest observations at their original timestamps plus a statistical summary of each variable's full history, so the representation stays the same size as the record grows. A query-conditioned module weights deviations from the latest value by observation age and forecast horizon, and a channel-specific decoder predicts a correction to that value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, it records the **lowest mean test MSE and MAE among compared methods on all four benchmarks**, and serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history cuts CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12 to 2.60.

papers.title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
papers.abstract: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.
papers.summary: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification requires restrictive kernel conditions to guarantee stable impulse responses, especially under Gaussian priors. The authors define a stability-compatible kernel as a covariance kernel that admits at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths, and show this holds **if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space**, a condition strictly weaker than the usual stability requirement. They construct non-Gaussian priors that keep a prescribed covariance while enforcing stability, including one based on the stationary radial-basis-function kernel. Numerical experiments report estimation gains that are largest when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

papers.title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
papers.abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.
papers.summary: Finite element analysis (FEA) can assess femoral strength for hip fracture risk but is too computationally expensive for routine clinical use, and conventional machine learning surrogates ignore the topology of the mesh. The authors propose a hybrid graph neural network, `GCN-SAGE-Residual`, that combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to predict stress per mesh element. Compared against 14 classical and graph-based models and examined with an architectural ablation, it achieves the best result with an **R^2 of 0.8022** and a mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa.

papers.title: LipSpell: A Language-Independent Phonetic Scoring Framework for Spelling Correction Combining Distinctive-Feature Edit Distance, Keyboard Geometry, and Corpus Frequency
papers.abstract: Automatic spelling correction must handle both keyboard typographical slips and cognitive or phonetic misspellings where writers approximate a word's pronunciation. Conventional spell checkers rely either on orthographic edit distance and keyboard proximity--which struggle when phonetic errors diverge by multiple characters--or on English-centric phonetic hashes such as Soundex and Metaphone. We present LipSpell, a unified, language-independent phonetic scoring engine paired with swappable language-specific G2P frontends, keyboard maps, and lexicons integrating: (1) a precomputed |P|x|P| phone-distance matrix from universal IPA distinctive features, (2) physical keyboard geometry, and (3) corpus unigram frequency priors, accelerated by a two-stage symmetric-delete and seven-class phonetic-code index. Across six English benchmarks (including 1,000 L2 errors from TOEFL-Spell), LipSpell outperforms Norvig and Hunspell on every dataset and beats Aspell on Norvig1 (78.52% vs. 75.56%), Holbrook (32.00% vs. 26.67%), and TOEFL-Spell (77.30% vs. 72.80%). Evaluated across six languages spanning five branches (Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Semitic, Turkic), three families (Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Turkic), and three scripts, LipSpell achieves strong fixed-weight transfer on Brazilian Portuguese (73.00% Top-1 on n=500 Wikipedia without NFD tolerance and 75.80% with NFD vs. 66.40% Norvig, 64.20% Hunspell, 64.00% Aspell) and Russian Cyrillic (85.67% vs. 78.50% Norvig). On 50/50 clean non-word splits with lexicon cleaning and weak-character indels, tuning yields strong gains over Norvig in Portuguese (86.97% vs. 76.75%), Turkish (81.67% vs. 79.05%), Hebrew Abjad (74.59% vs. 62.30%), and French (74.53% vs. 67.92%), while fixed weights remain optimal for English (80.37%) and Russian (85.67%).
