The directions are built from each question's own labelled states, and the authors propose using them in future work to train models to align with them.

papers.title: Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA) for Plant Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. Designed as a self-contained spectral projection operator, the MSPA method can be directly integrated into spectroscopy workflows via the open-source code available at GitHub: https://github.com/Lucas-Osco/mspa.
papers.summary: Plant reflectance spectra have many highly collinear bands and few samples, and common dimensionality reduction methods treat wavelengths as unordered columns, discarding the shape of absorption features. Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (`MSPA`) is a supervised reduction method that combines continuum-removed absorption and red-edge features, local derivative-based eigenmodes over contiguous spectral windows, and globally Fisher-weighted subspaces with covariance shrinkage. Tested on 8,963 spectra from five plant systems with six classical classifiers and four tabular foundation models including `TabPFN v3` and `TabICL v2`, it compresses the 1,580-band spectrum by 96% while **raising global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 to 0.8520**. It beats the full spectrum in 92.0% of benchmarks and speeds up in-context inference by up to 126.5x.

papers.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.
papers.summary: Pretrained diffusion models are widely used as priors for ill-posed inverse problems, but existing guarantees are often asymptotic or computationally prohibitive in the worst case. The authors study sparse recovery from few linear measurements, the classical compressed sensing problem, with a diffusion model that captures a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior. They prove that a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler **recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity** for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is actually drawn from the assumed prior, they also establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step.

papers.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
papers.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.
papers.summary: In safety-critical domains, AI systems can leave people accountable for harms they have limited ability to control. Drawing on human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews, and participant observation in a high-risk railway use case, the authors developed `ALIGN`, a scenario-based method for stakeholder involvement in AI development and deployment. It is designed to **raise awareness of accountability-control misalignments, assess that alignment for each stakeholder in a given use case, and support design decisions that mitigate AI risks**. The article describes the method's iterative development and evaluation.

papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
papers.summary: Activation probes for monitoring large language models trade off accuracy, interpretability, and overhead, and sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes in particular rely on additive classifiers and large encoders. `GateWatch` expresses its whole decision rule as explicit Boolean logic over a handful of binarized SAE features, and `GateWatchServe` computes only the selected features, streams their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates many classifiers in parallel with lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on `Gemma-2-9B`, it reaches **80.49% mean test accuracy using on average 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe**, 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes while cutting probe memory by 99.98%. Inside `vLLM`, 1,000 concurrent classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput.

papers.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.
papers.summary: Species distribution models turn sparse observations of a species into dense maps of its range, and the choice of input features is a separate question from the choice of statistical model. Options now include climate variables, learned location encodings, earth embedding models, and transformed raw geographic coordinates. The authors introduce **a standardized evaluation framework that quantifies how effective different location encodings are for species range estimation**, at both local and global scales.

papers.title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
papers.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.
papers.summary: Diffusion-map embedding, a technique used to characterize how the human cortex is organized, is applied to matched base and reasoning-trained language models from three families to see whether improved reasoning involves a regional reorganization. The gradient profiles are broadly preserved, with changes localized to a contiguous span of layers. **Grafting the weights from these spans into instruction-tuned host models improved mathematical reasoning on average**, with gains rising with region overlap and with more previously solved problems retained than for grafts taken elsewhere. The span forms gradually during the early rise in training performance, and the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model.

papers.title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
papers.abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.
papers.summary: Pretrained video editors can remove objects but may leave the target in place or alter unrelated content. `H3Remover` fine-tunes `MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA` for object removal without paired object-free training targets, using reward signals instead: a depth-based reward for actually revealing farther content, a reward for preserving background depth ordering, an appearance reward that protects background regions while exempting targets and their shadows or reflections, and perceptual-quality feedback from a frozen `HPSv3` model. `DiffusionART` optimizes LoRA adapters while the backbone stays frozen. The authors report **substantial reconstruction gains over the original model**, with qualitative comparisons showing more effective removal and better preservation of the surrounding scene.

papers.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
papers.summary: `Clover` is a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total and 3 billion activated parameters that supports thinking-mode generation. It adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion, combining recurrent memory of earlier context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the block currently being generated. The report claims the lead on all seven evaluated agent metrics, including **73.6 on `SWE-bench Verified`** and 51.7 on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, with a reported 680 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU. A decision-model variant that answers related questions in one denoising pass raises all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on an internal set of 500 groups.

papers.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
papers.summary: Continual learning (CL) on edge devices is hard because data arrives one sample at a time and backpropagation is too costly for small hardware. `Hypnos` is an open-source platform that splits the work into a wake phase, where a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) runs inference and gradient-free prototype updates, and a sleep phase, where a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates during charging. Deployed on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, it reaches **78.6%-81.6% accuracy on the `CORe50 NICv2-391` protocol**, reported as state of the art for edge CL systems. It needs 3.8x fewer learning steps and 22x less learning compute than quantized latent replay, at 7.79-10.54 seconds of on-device latency per sample.

papers.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
papers.summary: Multimodal language models for materials science need a way to feed three-dimensional structure into the language model, which `MatterChat` handles with a large bridge module and a separate contrastive alignment stage. The authors find that supervised and generative material encoders carry complementary information, and that the most useful `Zatom-1` representations sit at different depths depending on the target property. Their Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (`TCAF`) bridge uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine `CHGNet` features with intermediate `Zatom-1` layers, trained directly on downstream tasks. It outperforms `MatterChat` with **up to 47.8% lower RMSE** while using fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.

papers.title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
papers.abstract: Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $\sigma^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically principled changes that do not act on the measured miscalibration, namely exact polar factors, steepest-descent input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer gives every singular direction of the momentum the same step size, and the authors measure whether that allocation matches the loss curvature using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on `FineWeb-Edu`, the second-order optimal multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail, meaning **`Muon` over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum**. Orthogonalizing the query, key and value matrices separately lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats, and a spectral tilt applied during the cooldown lowers it by a further 0.0120 nats. Changes motivated by geometry alone, such as exact polar factors, input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.

papers.title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.
papers.summary: Bounding the error that quantization introduces into a neural network is difficult because rounding and clamping are discrete operations. The authors build a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward networks, with a single round-clamp abstract transformer that handles both operations, and extend it to constrained zonotopes with soundness and optimality proofs. On the `ACAS Xu` benchmarks the constrained method cuts **average error-bound widths by roughly 70-85%** and runtimes by 65-80% relative to `QEBVerif` at the two smallest perturbation radii. The gains are not uniform across bitwidths, `QEBVerif` gives tighter bounds at larger radii, and the plain zonotope method produces competitive bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

papers.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels.We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.
papers.summary: Small language models can run on commodity hardware for on-premises clinical use, but their medical explanations tend to be short and poorly structured. Starting from an instruction-tuned `Mistral-7B`, the authors apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with `LoRA` adaptation on 2,000 `Meerkat`-derived medical prompts, using a self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, well-punctuated responses. After **about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU**, the average reward rises steadily and the tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations. The authors report that the medical content is preserved and discuss the limits of this kind of self-rewarded training.

papers.title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.
papers.summary: `Piccolo` is a family of multimodal decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that output probabilities over candidate answers for text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows and games. The models and their training data are developed together through recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, run experiments and refine later proposals using a shared research memory. `Piccolo-27B` **tops the `Decision Index Vision Full` leaderboard with a score of 75.59**. The authors report that matching the backbone to the training recipe matters more than how recent the backbone is, that targeted data curation lets 4B-9B models rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows, and that lower loss can coincide with worse decision accuracy.
papers.highlight_summary:
Decision models, which return a probability distribution over supplied candidate answers for routing, guardrail, and action-selection calls, are usually post-trained on a static data recipe. `Piccolo` instead co-evolves a 0.8B–27B multimodal model family and its training data through an agent-led research loop that the authors call recursive self-improvement.

- Each model reads the logits of single-token candidate labels directly from the native language-model head and applies a softmax over them, while research agents run a propose, experiment, and diagnose cycle over semantically labelled slices of a **663K-example** pool, with a shared research memory and human researchers setting priorities and reviewing major changes.
- `Piccolo-27B` ranks first of 86 entrants on `Decision Index Vision` with **75.59 Full** and **70.97 Private**, only 0.54 Full points ahead of `JDI-Decision V1`, and scores **84.41** on `HarnessJevBench` and 82.60 on `DataJevBench`, while `Piccolo-9B` and `Piccolo-4B` lead their size classes on Private with **65.04** and **63.49**.
- Across roughly **600 runs** and about 6,300 accelerator-hours, loss proved an unreliable guide to accuracy: on 341 fixed workflow questions the target–prediction KL fell from 2.19 to 0.66 to 0.64 while net correct answers rose by **78** and then dropped by **13**.
- Recipes and backbones interact, since under an identical recipe and data order the older `Qwen3.5` initialization scored 79.97 on Public Vision against 77.86 for `Qwen3.8`, which in turn led on Harness with 85.93, and continuing for 1M exposures on a fixed pool gained 0.60 on Data while losing **1.29** on Text and **1.69** on Harness.
- The evidence is self-reported from a single leaderboard snapshot, Private scores for the 2B and 0.8B models are still pending, the 27B model is not first on Public Vision, `DataJevBench`, or `JevBench`, and many ablation gaps are well under one point with no variance or repeated seeds reported.

papers.title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
papers.abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.
papers.summary: Adapting a large language model to a new target often degrades its general capabilities. `CurvDelta` builds the preservation constraint into the update itself by analyzing the local geometry of a preservation loss and restricting updates to a low-curvature space where that loss stays nearly unchanged, made practical with Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. A low-rank variant, `CurvLoRA`, works within the same geometry for cheaper adaptation. On mathematical reasoning and code generation the methods are competitive while better preserving general capabilities, and on the `TOFU` and `MUSE` unlearning benchmarks they give **retention close to a model retrained from scratch**.

papers.title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
papers.abstract: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.
papers.summary: Turning a film into a game requires choosing source elements and translating them into player actions, rules and feedback, which playability checks alone do not measure. `M2G-bench` covers 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items, combining general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation and playtesting by three GUI model players. Across 14 evaluated models, playable sequences are the weakest category in every case, **averaging 37.9 out of 100 for content presence** against 54.8 for iconic elements. Among retained emotional-development content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for only 7.2%.
papers.highlight_summary:
Film-to-game adaptation asks a coding agent to pick meaningful source content and turn it into player actions, which playability-only benchmarks do not measure. `M2G-bench` scores browser games built from **22 films** against **658 source-specific reference items**, separating whether film content is present from whether the player actually operates it.

- Each agent gets up to three hours unattended to build a self-contained browser game, which is then scored by a 103-question General Evaluation, a Movie-specific Evaluation of content presence and interactive realization, and playtesting by three GUI model players, combined with weights 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2.
- Across 14 models, `GPT-6-Astra` leads General Evaluation (**82.0**), Playtesting (**59.0**) and Overall (**55.4**, against 55.2 for `GPT-6.1-Sol`), while `Gemini-4-Argon` tops Movie-specific Evaluation at only **36.0** out of 100.
- Playable sequences have the lowest content-presence mean in **all 14 models**, averaging **37.9** against 54.8 for iconic elements, and among retained emotional-development judgments narrative choices account for **60.0%** versus **7.2%** for direct scenario operation.
- On cost, `GPT-6.1-Sol` reaches near-identical Overall at **$1.129 per film** against `GPT-6-Astra`'s $3.925, a 71.2% reduction for roughly 0.1 points.
- All judging and playtesting is done by LLMs, several of which are also contestants, model-player scores correlate with ten human playtesters at only Spearman **0.60** and run 11.1 points higher, and models are compared in different primary harnesses with the cross-harness check limited to eight films.

papers.title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.
papers.summary: Gradient inversion attacks try to reconstruct private training data from federated learning updates, but exact text recovery by a malicious client has been infeasible because `FedAvg` mixes the gradient contributions of many clients. The proposed attack runs an iterative loop: sentences recovered exactly in one round have their gradient contributions subtracted from the aggregate, which exposes the remaining sentences for the next round. The authors report exact sentence recovery with 100% precision, and **up to 80.2% of client sentences recovered exactly** on aggregates containing up to 4x more tokens than the model's hidden dimension. Existing attacks recover no sentences exactly in that regime.

papers.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.
papers.summary: Training large language model (LLM) agents with reinforcement learning on long tasks is hampered by sparse terminal rewards, which make credit assignment and exploration difficult. The authors define a capability region, the set of states from which the current policy reliably finishes a task, and split learning into reaching a more solvable state and completing the task from there, each with its own advantage signal. A reverse-to-forward curriculum grows the region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. With `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, the method reaches **90.1% and 96.1% success on `ALFWorld`** and 80.2% and 82.6% on `WebShop`, ahead of competing agentic reinforcement learning methods.

papers.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Qu\'ebec French
papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Qu\'ebec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Qu\'ebec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.
papers.summary: Continual pre-training (CPT) is routinely used to adapt language models to dialects, but it is unclear when the extra training is needed and what drives its benefits. A controlled study of Québec French across nine models, with a matched budget of 30M tokens per experiment, finds that **the benefit depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the variety**. When CPT helps, corpus composition matters more than data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. The gains come mainly in comprehension of regional expressions rather than grammar, and they are accompanied by declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can hide.

papers.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) for robots are often given retrieved rollouts or demonstrations as context, yet this experience frequently turns previously solved tasks into failures. The authors argue that the value of experience depends on what is stored, when it is used and where it enters the policy, and `F3` addresses these with three components: compressing successful and failed rollouts into short verified records, training the policy to read a record and predict when it helps, and injecting the record as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, it raises success over native `Cosmos 3 Nano` by **12.0 and 10.8 percentage points on `MolmoSpaces` and `RoboLab`**. It also cuts regressions by 57%, without any training on `RoboLab`.

papers.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
papers.abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for scientific discovery agents often cannot separate experimental reasoning from recall, hidden scoring rules or shortcut strategies. `Openhagen Worlds` is a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments, from classic experimental-reasoning puzzles to simulated physics and chemistry, where an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer checked by a deterministic verifier. Each of the 178 difficulty levels is admitted only if a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75 of development instances while non-deductive and shortcut policies stay below fixed thresholds. On 84 withheld frontier instances, `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash` solves **32 at default reasoning effort and 57 at maximum effort, against 79 for the oracle**, and on-policy expert iteration lifts a 9B model's core-tier success from 0.090 to 0.148.

papers.title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $\mu$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.
papers.summary: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) must differentiate through an inner loop of gradient descent and meta-learn every network weight. `Meta-LSQ` instead fits each task with one regularized least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, and the same solve can use derivative observations. On 10-shot sinusoid regression it trains in 14 seconds and ends with **5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer**. Results elsewhere are mixed: it does well in simulated beam tuning at DESY's `ARES` facility, but on real sensor-calibration data an exact Gaussian process and an `ALPaCA`-style model are more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets.

papers.title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) add scene description and reasoning to end-to-end driving systems but are expensive, and turning language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop driving had not been shown. `DRIFT` projects intermediate driving representations into the embedding space of a compact language model of under 150M parameters, which handles visual question answering and action commentary. Its planner is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the language model, so it can run with the language model or bypass it entirely at inference. With 255M parameters in total, it reaches **a Driving Score of 97.03 and an 89.39% success rate on `Bench2Drive`**, on par with the strongest non-language models, and is competitive on `NAVSIM` and `AlpaSim`.

papers.title: Induction Head Origins of SLAM-ASR Speech Recognition Models
papers.abstract: What makes a small trained map from encoder states to the embedding space of a frozen language model sufficient for competitive speech recognition? The premise of the SLAM-ASR architecture is that a frozen language model possesses linguistic knowledge rich enough to perform the recognition task. This assumption, while reasonable, provides little insight into the mechanisms underlying these models. We therefore seek the concrete internal structures on which they rely. This work shows that SLAM-ASR models rely on induction heads of the frozen language model: the same heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are also important for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens. Moreover, we find pairs of heads that behave as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening attention onto the previously generated word. Finally, we show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription quality under noisy audio.
papers.summary: `SLAM-ASR` speech recognizers work by training only a small map from speech encoder states into the embedding space of a frozen language model, and the mechanism behind this has been unclear. The analysis shows that these models **rely on the frozen language model's induction heads**, the same attention heads that copy repeated token sequences in text, to map speech embeddings to transcript tokens. The authors also find pairs of heads acting as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening focus on the previously generated word. They further show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription under noisy audio.

papers.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.
papers.summary: Gravitational-wave data analysis and numerical relativity require millions of waveform evaluations, more than direct solvers of the Einstein field equations can supply. This perspective reviews projection-based reduced-order modeling (ROM), including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection and the Empirical Interpolation Method, and traces their use in surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. It examines the approximation barrier posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in transient and strongly nonlinear regimes, and argues that **adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits**. It closes by discussing how certified reduced-order structures could be combined with scientific machine learning for detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

papers.title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
papers.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.
papers.summary: Generative AI methods differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure, which makes the field hard to survey as a whole. This guide organizes it around how models actually produce new samples, distinguishing **three recurring generation routes: direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport**. Representative approaches are then introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. A final part covers how different architectures and generation mechanisms overlap or can be combined.

papers.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming with Basis Function Learning
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel approach for approximating the value function in Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our approach is grounded in the approximate linear programming (ALP) framework, wherein basis functions (BFs) play an important role. Traditionally, BFs have been pre-defined, randomly generated, or restricted to specific structures, which both limits the accuracy that can be achieved and leaves no mechanism for improving a given approximation. We instead learn BFs from the model itself, by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. We introduce the Bellman operator basis function (BOBF) learning method, and prove that each learned BF improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function. Its shrunken counterpart (SBOBF) retains this guarantee while capping the number of BFs, and therefore the computational effort per iteration. For large-scale problems, where the number of constraints is prohibitive, we develop hybrid variants (HBOBF and SHBOBF) that combine constraint sampling with BF learning, and we show that the improvement and finite-termination guarantees are preserved under explicitly stated conditions. Numerical experiments on (continuous) perishable inventory and queueing control problems demonstrate that our BF learning techniques significantly outperform existing methods in the literature.
papers.summary: Approximate linear programming (ALP) for Markov decision processes (MDPs) depends on basis functions that are usually pre-defined, randomly generated or structurally restricted, which limits accuracy and offers no way to improve a given approximation. The Bellman operator basis function (`BOBF`) method instead learns basis functions by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. The authors prove that **each learned basis function improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function**. A shrunken variant caps the number of basis functions, hybrid variants add constraint sampling for large problems, and experiments on perishable inventory and queueing control show the methods outperforming existing approaches.

papers.title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.
papers.summary: Better aggregate accuracy in protein-RNA binding affinity prediction does not necessarily carry over to predicting the effect of mutations, so eleven method families were evaluated on matched populations for average effects, ranking, and local accuracy. A controlled version of `CoPRA` cut absolute-affinity mean absolute error **from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd** and improved mean mutation-effect accuracy across 220 mutation pairs, but ranking gains were uncertain and centered local error did not decrease. On an external test of 24 pairs from three families, local error fell in two families and rose in one, and error decomposition placed the gains in landscape means. The authors argue that average effects, ordering, and local variation must be evaluated jointly.

papers.title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.
papers.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects men more often than women, so speech-based detection models are often trained on unbalanced data that may carry sex bias. The study combines embeddings from three pre-trained speech models with handcrafted acoustic features and several classifiers, testing on balanced subsets of four sustained-phonation datasets controlled for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. Female speakers were classified more accurately than male speakers in the larger dataset, and **models trained on one sex failed to generalize to the other**.

papers.title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
papers.abstract: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.
papers.summary: Lateral velocity matters for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured by production sensors, and it is unclear whether learned estimators transfer between structurally different vehicles. A neural-network estimator trained on production CAN signals from a compact car was evaluated zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference, where its **error was an order of magnitude higher than on the training vehicle**. A comparison of input sets identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly, and two physically motivated augmentations, left-right symmetry and emulated accelerometer bias, reduce error on the unseen vehicles by 13% and 15%. On the SUV, the augmented estimator matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same data.

papers.title: Learning the Anyon Atlas
papers.abstract: We extend our previous search for the modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data. We do so by adding to our algorithm three rejection gates, two of them based on logistic regression, that discard representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ unlikely to yield modular data. We estimate that roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been identified after closing under known constructions. With this data, we find counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore that the reality of the higher Gauss sums suffices for time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, and propose a refined criterion. We demonstrate the scalability of this gated implementation by identifying prime modular data at rank 100 that is not realized by any Chern-Simons theory. The identified data through rank 42 has been made available at https://AnyonAtlas.org, to which further data will be added as it is found.
papers.summary: The search for modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions is extended from 22 to 42 anyons, yielding **150,679 new modular data**. The algorithm gains three rejection gates, two based on logistic regression, that discard representations of SL(2,Z) unlikely to produce modular data; the authors estimate roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been found. The data provides counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore on time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, for which a refined criterion is proposed, and the gated method is shown to reach rank 100.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
papers.abstract:
Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree.
  In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.
papers.summary: Standard online A/B tests have high variance when the treatment and production policies mostly choose the same actions, so detecting small effects requires a lot of traffic. Building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, the authors derive a closed-form, variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, and use historical logs to jointly optimize that logging policy with a control variate. In simulated policy A/B tests, the designs **estimate the treatment effect more accurately than existing variance-reduction methods in every evaluated setting**, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected.

papers.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schr\"odinger Bridges
papers.abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schr\"odinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schr\"odinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.
papers.summary: Single-cell measurements destroy the cells they observe, so cellular dynamics, including births and deaths, must be reconstructed from unpaired snapshots. `Elysium` solves unbalanced Schrödinger bridges by jointly learning state transitions and mass change through direct regression objectives built from a killed Brownian reference, an optimal endpoint coupling, and conditional bridge distributions, **without simulating trajectories during training**. The authors show the minimizers of these objectives recover the optimal unbalanced bridge. It outperforms deterministic and bridge-based solvers on simulated benchmarks with known ground truth, and on single-cell time courses it interpolates unobserved time points and tracks population expansion and contraction.

papers.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics snapshots come from different cells in different coordinate frames, so a rotation or translation of a tissue section can be mistaken for cell movement. The proposed flow matching formulation learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion, using a projector that removes the rigid component from prediction errors and predicted velocities, with regression targets derived from an endpoint problem in Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao geometry. The resulting model, `HORIZON`, uses an equivariant transformer to generate a tissue continuously from a single initial snapshot. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses it **reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods** and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
papers.abstract: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience.
